lessons.title: What AI, machine learning, and deep learning actually mean
lessons.goal: Describe the difference between artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning, and name where each one appears in products you already use.

sections.heading: A program that follows written rules
body: Most software you use today follows instructions a person wrote down, step by step, and the same input always produces the same output. A spam filter that moves every message containing the phrase free money into a junk folder is exactly this kind of program. The rule is short, it is visible in the code, and a person can change it in a minute. Nobody showed that filter thousands of examples of spam. Somebody wrote down what spam looks like, and the program checks for it.

Written rules have a strength and a weakness. The strength is predictability: if you can read the rule, you can predict the answer and explain it to a customer. The weakness is coverage. A message that says claim your bonus cash today never contains the phrase free money, so the filter above lets it through, and no amount of reading the code will reveal that this case was never thought of. The decision program you build in this module has the same weakness, and the same cure.

sections.heading: A program that learns from examples
body: Machine learning solves the coverage problem in a different way. Instead of writing the rule, you collect many examples that already carry the right answer, and the program works out the rule for itself. A phone that unlocks by recognising your face has been shown thousands of labelled photographs: this is my face, this is not my face. It never receives an instruction such as if the distance between the eyes is 42 units, unlock. It receives examples and a way to measure how wrong its guesses are.

Learning does not remove the human. Somebody chose which examples to collect, decided what counts as the right label, and checked the results afterwards. When a learned model is wrong, the usual cause is that the examples were unrepresentative, not that the computer was thinking badly. A spam filter trained on messages from 2015 will meet words it has never seen, because the language moved on. This is why the data behind a learned rule matters as much as the algorithm that reads it.

sections.heading: Where deep learning fits
body: Deep learning is machine learning that uses many layers of simple numbers stacked on top of each other. Each layer takes the numbers from the layer below, multiplies them by a set of stored weights, and passes a new set of numbers upward. No layer understands anything. The behaviour appears because the weights were adjusted again and again, until the final layer produced the right answers often enough. Because the layers find their own inputs, you do not write the features by hand.

Face recognition is a good example. The early layers react to simple things such as edges and corners, the middle layers react to parts of a face such as eyes or a mouth, and the later layers react to whole faces. You did not write those steps; they came out of the training. Deep learning needs more examples and more computing power than simpler machine learning, which is why it spread first through image and speech work and then through text work. Deep learning is a way of building a model, not a different goal.

sections.heading: How to tell what a product really uses
body: Marketing language is loose, so read a product description with a checklist. Is the behaviour a written rule you could read in the code, a model trained on examples, or a deep network with many layers? Ask what data was used and when it was collected. A rule that checks a banned phrase keeps working when the phrase becomes popular, because the rule did not change. A model trained on last year's examples starts to fail quietly as the world moves on, and nothing in the interface tells you.

Three questions separate the three kinds of system for you. Does the company describe training on examples, or does it describe conditions written in code? Does the system improve when the team collects more examples of the same kind? Does anyone on the team know the exact rule being applied, or do they inspect a set of numbers instead? The refund decision program you build in this module answers yes to the third question and no to the others, and saying that clearly is a sign you understand the difference.

quiz.question: A rule written by a person and a model trained on examples are two different ways to build the same behaviour. What is the key difference between them?
choices: The trained model gives a different answer each time it sees the same input, while a written rule always gives the same answer.
The written rule was typed by a person, while the trained model worked out its own rule from labelled examples.
A written rule needs a large dataset before it can run, while a trained model needs only the code.
A written rule is always right, while a trained model is wrong on almost every input.
quiz.explanation: The difference is where the rule comes from. A person wrote the conditions in a written rule, so you can read them and change them. A trained model starts with no rule and fits one to labelled examples, so it can catch cases its authors never thought of, including cases it gets wrong. A trained model is still predictable for the same input, and a written rule can be wrong too.

quiz_bank.question: Which of these is an everyday example of deep learning rather than simple rules?
choices: A spreadsheet formula that adds tax to each row of a table.

quiz_bank.question: A product claims it uses AI. Which question best helps you check whether it is really a learned model?
choices: How much does the product charge each month?
How fast does the product run on a laptop?
Does the product show a spinner while it works?
Was the system trained on examples, and what were they?
quiz_bank.explanation: Training on labelled examples is what separates a learned model from a written rule, so ask where the examples came from and what they contained. The other questions describe the product rather than the method, and none of them tells you how the behaviour was produced. Watch out for marketing: the word AI can cover anything from nested if statements to a large neural network, so the training question is the one worth asking.

lessons.title: How a program makes a decision
lessons.goal: Write a decision rule in plain language and turn it into a Python function that always returns the same answer for the same input.

sections.heading: Inputs, rules, outputs
body: Every decision program has the same three parts, and naming them makes the job easier. The inputs are the facts you already know before you decide. The rules are the written steps you apply to those facts. The outputs are the answers you are allowed to produce. In this module the inputs for one support request are the channel it arrived through, the amount of money asked for, and the reason the customer gave. The outputs are three words: approve, review, or decline.

Write the inputs down before you write the code, because a rule cannot use a fact you never collected. If your rule says a request for 50 or more needs review, then the amount has to be one of the inputs, and it has to be a number you can compare with 50 rather than a word such as fifty. Each output should also be a small fixed set. Three outputs are easy to test, twenty are not, and a decision program with an unlimited number of answers is a conversation, not a rule.

sections.heading: From a sentence to a table
body: A written rule such as approve damaged orders is a sentence. A program needs the same rule as a table, because a table can be checked by a person and by a test. For the 12 requests in data/requests.json, the rule table has five rows, and the first row that matches a request produces the answer.

Row 1 says that a damaged or wrong_item reason is approved. Row 2 says that a late_delivery reason goes to review. Row 3 says that an email channel is declined. Row 4 says that an amount of 50 or more goes to review. Row 5 says that a request which matched no other row is approved.

The order is part of the rule, not a detail. Request R10 arrives by email and asks for 102.40, so it matches row 3 and row 4 at the same time. Because row 3 comes first, the answer is decline. Swap rows 3 and 4 and the same request becomes review, and your program no longer matches the table you wrote.

sections.heading: Writing the decision in Python
body: Python writes a chain of rules with if, elif, and else. The keyword if tests one condition, elif tests another condition only when the first one was false, and else runs when every condition was false. A function called decide takes one request and returns the decision as a string, so the caller never has to know how the rule was checked.

Only the first branch whose condition is true runs, and Python stops there, so the order of your rows is the order of your rules. The beginner mistake here is to read every branch as if it were independent: request R10 looks like decline because it is email and also like review because it is large, when in fact the program found one answer and stopped. The second mistake is leaving a return out of a branch, which lets Python run off the end of the function and hand back None instead of a decision. Give every path a return, and keep the final one as the fallback row of your table.

sections.heading: Testing the decision
body: Write down the expected answers before you write the code. If you only decide after the program exists, every wrong answer looks like a reasonable one. For the rule table above, the expected answers for the 12 bundled requests are 7 approvals, 3 reviews, and 2 declines, and the two declines are R05, an email request for 15.00, and R10, an email request for 102.40.

# Each case is a request and the answer it must produce.
cases = [
    ({'channel': 'web', 'amount': 24.50, 'reason': 'damaged'}, 'approve'),
    ({'channel': 'email', 'amount': 15.00, 'reason': 'other'}, 'decline'),
]
for request, expected in cases:
    got = decide(request)
    # Print ok when the answer matches, MISMATCH when it does not.
    print(request['amount'], got, 'ok' if got == expected else 'MISMATCH')

A decision with no test is an opinion. The loop above prints ok for a correct decision and MISMATCH for a wrong one, which means a mistake points straight at the request that caused it. Run the check on all 12 requests before you believe the program, and keep the list of cases in your repository so a reviewer can run them again.

quiz.question: Why does the order of the branches matter in an if / elif / else chain?
choices: Because Python requires the branches to appear from the most specific condition to the least specific one, or the program will not run.
Because only the first branch whose condition is true runs, so moving a rule earlier can change the answer for the same request.
Because each branch may only contain one line of code.
Because the last branch always wins, no matter which conditions are true.
quiz.explanation: Python checks the conditions from the top and stops at the first true one, so the order of the branches is part of the rule itself. R10, an email request for 102.40, matches both the email row and the large amount row; with the email row first the answer is decline, and with the amount row first the answer is review. Python does not require a particular order, and the last branch does not win by itself.

quiz_bank.question: Which test would catch the classic beginner mistake of swapping the amount row with the email row in the rule table?

quiz_bank.explanation: Only the first case can tell the two orders apart. An email request for 102.40 matches both rows, so swapping them changes the answer from decline to review and the check fails. The other three cases match only one row each, so they return the same answer whichever order you use, and a test built from them would pass a broken program.

lessons.title: Python essentials for this course
lessons.goal: Read and write the Python used every day in this course: values, lists, dictionaries, loops, and functions that return a result.

sections.heading: Values and variables
body: A value is a piece of data. A variable is a name attached to a value, so you can use that value later without repeating it. You create a variable with an equals sign, and you change it by assigning to it again. The four value types you will meet constantly in this course are text, whole numbers, decimal numbers, and true or false.

# One support request, with a variable for each of its facts.
request_id = 'R01'        # str: text
channel = 'web'           # str: text
amount = 24.50            # float: a decimal number
reason = 'damaged'        # str: text
# A comparison produces a bool, which is True or False.
needs_review = amount >= 50

Two warnings before you build on this. First, a float is an approximation: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, so never keep money in a float when exact amounts matter, and round only when you show a number to a person. Second, the variable amount holding 24.50 holds a number, not the text 24.50, and text cannot be compared with 50 the way a number can, which is a common first error.

sections.heading: Lists and dictionaries
body: A list is an ordered row of values, written with square brackets and commas between them. A dictionary is a record with labels, written with curly braces: each key is a label and each value is the data under that label. One support request is a dictionary because it has named parts, and the request id is the label that makes it easy to find again. A list keeps the order you typed, so the first decision you wrote stays at position zero.

# A list: an ordered row of values, reached by position.
decisions = ['approve', 'review', 'decline']
amounts = [24.50, 81.00, 17.25]

# A dictionary: labelled parts, reached by name.
# The 12 requests are stored as a list of 12 dictionaries like this one.
request = {
    'id': 'R01',
    'channel': 'web',
    'amount': 24.50,
    'reason': 'damaged',
}

Use a list when the items are the same kind of thing and the order matters, such as the three decisions in order. Use a dictionary when each item has named parts you look up by name, such as one request. The 12 requests are stored as a list of 12 dictionaries, and that shape is what you will meet in every later module of the course.

sections.heading: Loops
body: A loop runs the same block of code once for each item in a sequence. The for loop over a list gives you a loop variable that takes each value in turn, and the indented block under the loop is the body that repeats. The loop variable is an ordinary variable, so you can still read its last value after the loop ends.

# The loop variable takes each request in turn.
# The indented block under the for line is the body of the loop.
# The bundled file has 12 requests, so this prints 12 lines.
for request in requests:
    # Printing inside the body shows one line per request.
    print(request['id'], request['amount'])

Two mistakes are worth naming now. If the body is not indented under the for line, Python reports an error about the indentation, because indentation is how Python marks what belongs to the loop. And a loop over a list of three items runs its body three times, so a counter placed inside the body ends at three, not at one. Writing for item in items gives you the item itself, and saves you from counting positions by hand.

sections.heading: Functions that return a result
body: A function is a named recipe. It takes inputs, runs a block of code, and hands back a result. The keyword return ends the function and gives that value to whoever called it. The name, the inputs, and the result are all written in the definition, so a reader can see what the function promises before reading how it keeps that promise.

def total_amount(rows):
    'Return the sum of the amount value in every row.'
    # total starts at zero and grows with every row.
    total = 0.0
    # The loop adds one amount at a time.
    for row in rows:
        total = total + row['amount']
    # return hands the finished number back to the caller.
    return total

The same three lines written three times become one function you call three times, which means a bug is fixed in one place instead of three. The difference between return and print matters here: a printed value appears on the screen and then disappears when the function ends, while a returned value is held in a variable and can be stored, compared, or passed to another function. A function should do one job and say so in its docstring, the short description under its name.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a list and a dictionary in the terms used in this lesson?
choices: A list holds related items in order and you reach them by position, while a dictionary holds labelled parts and you reach them by name.
A list can only hold text, and a dictionary can only hold numbers.
A list is written with curly braces, and a dictionary is written with square brackets.
A dictionary is always sorted by key, while a list keeps the order you typed.
quiz.explanation: A list is an ordered row of values, such as the three decision words, and you reach an item by its position. A dictionary is a record with named parts, such as one request with the keys id, channel, amount, and reason, and you reach a part by its name. The brackets are the other way round from the third choice: lists use square brackets and dictionaries use curly braces.

quiz_bank.question: What does a function return, and what happens to a value printed inside a function?
choices: A function returns one value to the caller, while a printed value goes to the screen and is gone when the function ends.
A function returns one value to the caller, and a printed value is stored in a variable you can use later.
A function returns nothing at all, and only print statements produce output.
A function returns one value and a printed value is returned as well, so the caller sees both.
quiz_bank.explanation: return hands a value back to the caller and ends the function, while print only writes text to the screen and keeps nothing. That is why total_amount returns its number instead of printing it: the caller can store the number, compare it, or pass it on. The second choice is the classic beginner mistake of treating a printed value as if it had been saved.

quiz_bank.question: A loop over a list of three items runs the body three times. What is the value of the loop variable after the loop finishes?
choices: The first item, because Python resets the loop variable at the start of every pass.
The third item, because Python leaves the loop variable holding the last value it was given.
The number of items in the list, which is 3.
Nothing, because the loop variable is deleted when the loop ends.
quiz_bank.explanation: In Python the loop variable keeps the value from the final pass, so after looping over three items it holds the third one. That is also why a counter placed inside the body ends at 3. The last choice describes languages such as C, where the loop variable goes out of scope, and in Python you can still read the variable after the loop finishes.

lessons.title: Your notebook, your repository, your future employer
lessons.goal: Run Python in a notebook, keep every change in Git, and publish the work on GitHub so that another person can run it and check your result.

sections.heading: Notebook cells and why order matters
body: A notebook is a file made of cells. A cell holds a block of Python code or a block of written notes, and you run a cell when you want to see what it does. Jupyter Notebook is the tool you will use, and Google Colab is the same idea hosted in a browser with nothing to install. When you run a cell, the values it creates stay in memory until you restart the program.

Because of that, the order of the cells matters. If cell 5 uses a variable that cell 2 creates, the notebook only works if you run cell 2 first. A notebook that needs a magic order is broken for everyone else, because nobody else knows your order. Restart the program and run every cell from the top: the command is Restart and Run All in Jupyter, and Restart and Run all in Colab.

Do this before every commit. If the notebook fails from a clean start, you find out now rather than after you publish it. It also catches a common beginner error: a cell that leans on a variable you typed by hand in another cell instead of creating it, which works on your laptop and nowhere else.

sections.heading: What Git records
body: Git is a system for keeping the history of your files. A repository is the folder Git watches. A commit is a named snapshot: the state of the tracked files at one moment, with a message that says why you made the change, the author, and the time.

A branch is a named line of work, so you can try an idea without disturbing the main line. Each commit points to the commit before it, so the history is a list of snapshots from oldest to newest. The command git log prints that list with the messages, and git diff shows what changed between two snapshots. Two commits with clear messages let a reviewer see both what you did and why.

Write commit messages for the person who reads them later, which at first is you. A message like Add the late_delivery rule and the expected answers for R03 and R08 tells the whole story, while a message like fix or update says nothing. Small, focused commits are easier to review and easier to undo than one large commit at the end of the week.

sections.heading: Commit, push, pull
body: The everyday loop has four commands and each one does a single job. git status shows which files have changed since the last commit, and you read it before anything else. git add src/automation.py marks the files you want in the next commit. git commit -m followed by a message records the snapshot locally, on your own machine.

git push sends your commits to GitHub, and this is the step beginners forget: until you push, the work exists on one laptop and nobody else can see it. git pull does the opposite, bringing down commits that other people pushed, and you run it before you start work in a repository that other people also use. If both sides changed the same file, Git stops and shows you both versions instead of choosing for you.

A second beginner mistake is committing everything without reading git status first, which sweeps large data files and secret keys into the history, where they stay forever. Look, add the files you meant to add, and write the message before you commit. GitHub is where you publish: you create a repository, point Git at it with git remote add origin and the web address, then push.

sections.heading: A repository a stranger can run
body: A repository is finished when a stranger can run it without asking you a question. Four things make that possible: a README that says what the project does and the exact commands to run it, dependencies pinned to exact versions so the same code runs next month, tests that run with a single command, and a note about the data that says where it came from and what licence applies.

In this project those four things are the README.md you are reading, the pyproject.toml file that pins pytest, the tests folder that runs with pytest, and the line in this README that says the 12 requests are synthetic. The workflow file in .github/workflows runs the same tests automatically on GitHub every time you push, so a green badge tells a reviewer that the checks pass before they read a line of your code.

Publish the repository as public when you submit it, and put the commit that passes in the submission form. A reviewer should be able to read the README, run one command, and see the same report you pasted. When they cannot, the missing piece is usually the exact command, so write it in the README as a numbered list of commands rather than as a sentence.

quiz.question: What does a Git commit record?
choices: A full copy of every file in the folder, so the repository can be rebuilt from any single commit.
A snapshot of the tracked files at one moment, with a message, the author, the time, and a link to the commit before it.
A diff between your working files and the previous commit, and nothing else.
A message and a list of the files you changed, stored apart from the file contents.
quiz.explanation: A commit is a named snapshot: it stores the state of the tracked files plus the message, the author, the time, and a pointer to its parent commit, which is what makes the history a chain you can walk through with git log. Git stores each version of each changed file, not a full copy of the folder, and the difference between two snapshots is a diff rather than the snapshot itself.

quiz_bank.question: Why should you restart a notebook and run every cell from the top before sharing it?
choices: Because running the cells in order is the only way to get the same result twice.
Because it proves the notebook works from a clean start, so nobody else needs to know the order you clicked.
Because a notebook file only saves the output of the last cell that ran.
Because restarting clears the variables, so the cells use less memory.
quiz_bank.explanation: Values live in memory while the program runs, so a notebook that only works when you click the cells in a particular order is hiding a missing step. Restarting and running everything from the top proves that the cells create everything they need. Restarting does not lose the cells or their saved output, and it is not a memory trick.

quiz_bank.question: A reviewer opens your repository and cannot tell how to run it. Which file is missing, and what should it contain?
choices: requirements.txt, listing the exact version of every package the project needs.
LICENSE, stating who owns the code and the data.
README.md, saying what the project does and giving the exact commands to install, test, and run it.
Makefile, listing the targets for install, test, and run.
quiz_bank.explanation: The README is the first file a reviewer opens, and it is the one that tells them what the project does and which commands to run. A requirements file pins versions but says nothing about the purpose, a licence states ownership, and a Makefile lists targets that a reviewer must already understand. The README also carries the note about where the bundled data came from.

lessons.title: How to read the maths in this course
lessons.goal: Know which numbers you must be able to work with by hand, which you can leave to Python, and how the lessons in this module connect to the models you will build later.

sections.heading: You do not need advanced maths
body: Machine learning sounds like it needs advanced mathematics, and for the models that most people read about in the news, it does. This course does not use those models. It works with plain tables of numbers, small weighted sums, and a training loop that adjusts one number at a time. Every idea in this module is introduced with a worked example first, and the formula comes second.

You also do not need to memorise formulas. In this module you need to work with a mean, a median, a range, a percentage, a weighted sum and one step of a training loop by hand, because those are the numbers you will have to explain to somebody else. Everything else you can leave to Python, which has a function for each summary you will need, so the code does the arithmetic while you check the meaning.

sections.heading: The five ideas you will meet
body: The first idea is describing a dataset: a dataset is a table of rows and columns, and a summary statistic is one number that stands for a whole column. The second idea is probability: a probability is a number between 0 and 1 that says how likely an outcome is under a stated setup, such as a spreadsheet of 1,000 orders.

The third idea is adding features together: a feature is one column of your table, and a weighted sum multiplies each feature by a number and adds the results. The fourth idea is learning by trial: a loss is a number that measures how wrong the model is, and the training loop moves the model parameters to make that number smaller. The fifth idea is uncertainty: an estimate computed from a sample has a range of plausible values, and a good report says how wide that range is.

None of these five ideas needs algebra beyond multiplication and addition, and none of them needs a calculator with more than one button. When a formula appears that you cannot follow on sight, it will be broken into steps you can check with a pencil and paper before you type anything into a cell.

sections.heading: Where each idea is used later
body: You will meet the first idea in the data module, where a table of orders has to be described before a model is built. You will meet the second idea every time you read a flag from a model: a spam filter that flags ten emails only matters if you know how many emails in that mailbox are spam anyway.

The third idea is exactly what a linear model computes, one weighted sum per row of your table. The fourth idea is what happens inside training, where a learning rate decides how big each adjustment is. The fifth idea is how you report an uncertain number to a manager: a mean of 38.29 dollars with a spread of 30.69 dollars tells a different story from a mean of 38.29 dollars with a spread of 3 dollars.

This module ends with a small project: you describe the bundled orders dataset with statistics, you find its data quality problems, and you write down the rules you used. The same numbers are checked by an automated test, so you will know your figures are right before you write the explanation.

lessons.title: Summarize a distribution before modeling
lessons.goal: Calculate and interpret basic measures of center and spread before choosing a model.

sections.heading: Describe the center
body: The mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value once the values are sorted from smallest to largest. The mode is the value that appears most often. These are three different questions about the middle of a set of numbers, and on the same data they can give three different answers.

Take the five values 2, 3, 3, 4, 8. The sum is 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 8 = 20 and the count is 5, so the mean is 20 divided by 5, which is 4. Sorted, the values are already in order, and the third of five is 3, so the median is 3. The mode is 3 as well, because 3 is the only value that appears twice.

The mean and the median differ here because the value 8 pulls the average upward while the middle position stays at 3. That makes the median less sensitive to one extreme value and the mean more sensitive to it. Neither is better in general: the mean is the right choice when you want a total shared out among the values, and the median is the right choice when extreme values would distort that picture.

sections.heading: Describe the spread
body: The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. The variance adds up how far each value sits from the mean, squared, and then divides by the count. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, which puts the number back into the units of your data, so a standard deviation of 2 dollars means dollars.

Using the same five values, the range is 8 - 2 = 6. Each value minus the mean of 4 gives -2, -1, -1, 0 and 4. Squaring each one gives 4, 1, 1, 0 and 16, and those add to 22. Treating the five values as the whole population, the variance is 22 divided by 5, which is 4.4.

The standard deviation is the square root of 4.4, which is about 2.1. Read that as: the values sit roughly 2.1 away from the mean of 4. The spread is 2.1 because the single large value 8 sits 4 away from the mean, while three of the other four values sit within 1 of it.

sections.heading: Summaries are a starting point
body: One summary can hide a lot. In the bundled orders dataset, the eleven recorded order totals have a mean of 38.29 and a median of 29.99, and the gap between them comes from a single negative total of -5.00 sitting below the other ten values, which run from 12.75 to 102.40. A report that gives only the mean hides that row, so the row needs a sentence of its own.

Compare subgroups before you conclude anything. The mean of 38.29 dollars over the eleven recorded totals hides a web channel that averages 44.02 dollars over its five orders and a mobile channel that averages 30.33 dollars over its three orders that have a total. Check the units you are reporting too: a standard deviation of 2 dollars means something very different from a standard deviation of 2 years, and mixing them up changes the story without changing any data.

These summaries are a starting point for modelling, not a conclusion. They help you notice missing values, odd units and hidden groups, and they give you a baseline to compare a later model against. They do not tell you that one feature causes an outcome, and they do not promise that a model trained on this data will work on new data.

quiz.question: For the values 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, what is the mean, and why is it higher than the median?
choices: 4, because the value 8 pulls the average up while the middle value stays 3
3, because the median and the mean are always the same number
4, because there are four values below the average
4.4, because the spread of the values gets added to the middle
quiz.explanation: The sum is 20 and the count is 5, so the mean is 20 divided by 5, which is 4. The median is the third of the sorted values, which is 3. The single large value 8 sits 4 above the mean, so it lifts the average without moving the middle. Adding the spread to the middle is not a step in any of these calculations.

quiz_bank.question: A dataset of yearly incomes has a mean of 60,000 and a median of 42,000. What does the gap suggest?
choices: Half of the people earn exactly 42,000
A small number of very high incomes pull the mean above the middle value
The incomes follow a bell-shaped normal distribution

quiz_bank.explanation: When a few values sit far above the rest, the mean moves up and the median barely moves, because the median depends only on the position of the middle value. A gap of 18,000 is a hint to look at the top of the distribution. It does not tell you that half the people earn exactly 42,000, and the median is a valid statistic on its own.

lessons.title: Reason with probability, base rates, and samples
lessons.goal: Use base rates and conditional probabilities to interpret model flags and data samples.

sections.heading: Start with the base rate
body: A probability is a number between 0 and 1 that describes how likely an outcome is under a stated setup. A base rate is how often that outcome happens in the whole population, before you look at any model signal. A model flag is a small piece of evidence, and the base rate decides how much evidence it really is.

Suppose 1,000 accounts have a churn rate of 10 percent, which means 100 accounts churn. A model flags 80 percent of the 100 accounts that churn, so it catches 80 of them. It also flags 20 percent of the 900 accounts that stay, so it wrongly flags 180. The model produced 80 true positives and 180 false positives, and 260 flags in total.

Only 80 of those 260 flags are real, which is about 31 percent. You spent effort on 180 accounts that would not have churned, and that cost comes from the base rate: when the outcome is rare, false alarms outnumber true catches. Before you trust any flag, ask how often the outcome happens anyway.

sections.heading: Keep conditional questions distinct
body: Recall asks what fraction of the actual positive cases the model caught: 80 out of 100, which is 80 percent. Precision asks what fraction of the flagged cases were actually positive: 80 out of 260, which is about 31 percent. The two questions use different denominators, so they can be very different numbers for the same model on the same data.

Now change the population. If half of a 1,000 account mailbox churns, so 500 accounts churn and 500 stay, the same model catches 80 percent of the 500, which is 400 true positives, and wrongly flags 20 percent of the 500 that stay, which is 100 false positives. The model now makes 500 flags, of which 400 are real, so precision is 400 out of 500, or 80 percent.

The filter did not change at all, and its usefulness changed completely, because the base rate changed. The same reasoning applies to a spam filter: if 1 email in 100 is spam, a flag means far less than it does in a mailbox where 1 email in 2 is spam. When a model score is used as a probability, check whether the predicted rates match the observed rates for the population and the time period where you will act on it.

sections.heading: Ask how the sample was collected
body: A sample is useful when it represents the population your question is about. If one region, one time period or one customer group is missing from the sample, then a summary or a model built on it may not transfer to that group. Write down the sampling frame, which is the list or the rule that says who could have been in the sample.

Random sampling can reduce some selection effects, but it cannot repair an unclear target, a missing population, or a measurement process that changes over time. A survey of 30 people who already use the product tells you how those 30 people feel, and nothing about the people who have not tried it yet. The number 90 percent is a fact about the sample, not about the market.

Sampling also has ordinary variation. Two samples drawn from the same population give slightly different averages even when nothing is wrong, which is why a single number never carries the whole story. Compare important groups, check the counts, and report how many rows the number came from.

quiz.question: In a mailbox of 1,000 emails where 1 in 100 is spam, a filter catches 80 of every 100 spam emails and wrongly flags 20 of every 100 good emails. How many of its flags are spam?
quiz.explanation: There are 10 spam emails, and the filter catches 80 percent of them, which is 8. It also wrongly flags 20 percent of the 990 good emails, which is 198. So the filter makes 8 + 198 = 206 flags, and only 8 of them are spam. That is about 4 percent precision, which is why a rare outcome needs a careful threshold.

So the filter makes 8 + 198 = 206 flags, and only 8 of them are spam. That is about 4 percent precision, which is why a rare outcome needs a careful threshold.

quiz_bank.question: Why is a model's precision as important as its accuracy?
choices: Because accuracy can look healthy when the outcome is rare, while precision says how many of the flagged cases were worth the team's time
Because accuracy cannot be computed on real data
Because precision is measured in the same units as the target
Because a model with high accuracy never needs a threshold
quiz_bank.explanation: Accuracy counts every prediction, so on data where most accounts stay, a model that always predicts 'stays' scores well and catches nobody. Precision asks a different question: of the accounts you flagged, how many actually churned? In the 1,000 account example, precision was 80 out of 260, about 31 percent, while accuracy was 800 out of 1,000, or 80 percent.

quiz_bank.question: A survey of 30 people who already use the product reports that 90 percent love it. Why is that number weak evidence?
choices: Thirty people is too few to calculate 90 percent at all
Ninety percent is too high a number to be believable
The survey needs a second question to confirm the first
Everyone in the sample already chose to use the product, so it says nothing about people who have not started yet
quiz_bank.explanation: The sample was drawn from people who already use the product, so it can only describe people like them. That is a selection problem, not a sample size problem: you could survey 3,000 existing users and still learn nothing about people who have not signed up. The percentage is accurate for the group that was asked, and misleading for the market.

lessons.title: Represent features with vectors and dot products
lessons.goal: Interpret a weighted sum of numeric features as a simple model calculation.

sections.heading: A vector keeps values in order
body: A feature is one column of your table, a single measurement you give the model. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, one per feature, and the order is part of the meaning: a value for size must never be read as a value for age. For a house, a feature vector might be [size in square metres, number of bedrooms, age in years].

A dataset of many such rows is written as a matrix, with one row per example and one column per feature. Every row must carry its features in the same order, or the numbers mean something different in different rows. If you shuffle the values inside a row you have not created a new example, you have created a different house.

A model's weights, which are the numbers the model learns during training, use that same order. Keep the feature names and the units next to your data so the numbers still mean something when the same table is used for training in one week and for scoring in the next. A vector with no names attached is a list of numbers and nothing more.

sections.heading: Compute a dot product
body: The dot product of two vectors of the same length is the sum of the products of matching entries. Take the features [120, 3, 10] and the weights [0.5, 10, -1]. Multiply each feature by its weight: 120 times 0.5 is 60, 3 times 10 is 30, and 10 times -1 is -10. Add them: 60 + 30 - 10 = 80.

That total of 80 is the model's score for this one row. The same operation with two features, x = [2, 3] and weights w = [0.5, -1], gives 0.5 times 2 plus -1 times 3, which is 1 - 3 = -2, and adding a bias of 4 gives a score of 2. A bias is a constant the model adds, and it lets the model produce a score even when every feature is zero.

This weighted sum is the building block of linear regression, of logistic regression, and of every layer in a neural network. A score is not automatically a probability: how the score is read depends on the model and the task, and you learn that reading from the model you actually built.

sections.heading: Check shapes and meaning
body: The number of weights must match the number of features, and they must be in the same order. When they do not match, the operation is not defined, and that error is a useful one: it stops you from training a model that reads the wrong column. Keep the failing check in place instead of hiding it by dropping a feature.

Scales matter as well. A dot product adds the products together, so a feature measured in thousands will dominate a feature measured in units unless you rescale them. Rescaling is normal and useful, but the rescaling parameters must be learned from training data only, and they must be applied in the same way to new data.

A large weight does not by itself prove that a feature is important, because the units and the correlations between features affect what a weight means. In the worked example, the bedroom weight of 10 is the largest per unit, so the model is most sensitive to bedrooms, while the size feature contributed the most to this particular score, 60 of the 80. Read weights together with the units of the features.

quiz.question: What does the dot product of a feature vector and a weight vector produce?
choices: One number for each feature in the vector
One number that combines the features into a single weighted score
A new vector with the same length as the feature vector
The average of the feature values
quiz.explanation: A dot product multiplies matching entries and adds the products, so the result has one number, not one number per feature. A weighted average would divide by the sum of the weights, which a dot product does not do, and a vector of separate averages is not what this operation produces either.

quiz_bank.question: For the features [120, 3, 10] and the weights [0.5, 10, -1], what is the dot product?
quiz_bank.explanation: The three products are 120 times 0.5, which is 60, 3 times 10, which is 30, and 10 times -1, which is -10. Adding them gives 60 + 30 - 10 = 80. The option 60 keeps only the first product, 90 forgets the age term altogether, and 100 treats the negative weight as if it were positive.

quiz_bank.question: In the worked example, why must the feature values and the weights be on comparable scales?
choices: Because the products are added together, so a feature on a huge scale would dominate the whole score
Because the weights have to be whole numbers
Because the dot product is only defined for values between 0 and 1
Because a model with rounded weights is easier to explain
quiz_bank.explanation: A dot product adds the products of matching entries, so if one feature is measured in thousands and another in units, the first one decides the score whatever the weights say. That is why features are often rescaled before training. Weights may be any real number, values may be negative, and rounding is a readability choice rather than a mathematical rule.

lessons.title: Understand gradients and gradient descent
lessons.goal: Explain how a gradient and a learning rate guide a model parameter toward lower loss.

sections.heading: A gradient describes local change
body: A loss is a number that measures how badly the model is doing, and a smaller loss is better. A derivative measures how much the loss changes when you move one parameter a small amount. When there are several parameters, the gradient is the collection of those changes, one per parameter, and it points in the direction where the loss rises fastest right now.

Imagine standing on a hillside in fog. The gradient is the direction of the steepest slope at the spot where you stand, and it changes as you move. Training uses that information in the opposite direction: gradient descent takes a small step downhill, in the direction the loss decreases, and then repeats the calculation from the new spot.

sections.heading: Work a one-parameter step
body: Take the simple loss L(w) = 0.5 times (w - 7) squared, where w is the single parameter. The partial derivative with respect to w is (w - 7), so at w = 10 the gradient is 3. The update rule subtracts a fraction of the gradient: w_new = w - learning_rate times gradient. With a learning rate of 0.1, that is 10 - 0.1 times 3, which is 9.7.

The loss at the new point is 0.5 times (9.7 - 7) squared, which is 0.5 times 7.29, so 3.645, down from 4.5 at w = 10. Repeating the same arithmetic gives 9.43 with a loss of 2.952, then 9.187 with a loss of 2.391. Each step is smaller than the one before it, because the gradient shrinks as w approaches 7.

The learning rate is the fraction of the gradient you take, and it decides how far each step travels. With a learning rate of 1 the same rule moves straight from 10 to 7 in one step and the loss goes to zero. With a learning rate of 2 it swings from 10 to 4 and back to 10 again, so the loss never improves at all.

sections.heading: Check the result, not only the update
body: A rule that runs is not proof that training is working. Plot the loss over many steps and look at it: with a learning rate of 0.1 the loss falls steadily, and with a learning rate of 0.01 it falls so slowly that you might stop before it finishes. An update that looks reasonable can still be moving in the wrong direction if the gradient is wrong.

If the loss goes up after a step, look at the learning rate first, because a rate that is too large overshoots, and then check the gradient itself. Track the loss on the training data and check generalisation on separate validation data, because a model can keep improving on the rows it has seen while getting worse on new ones.

Real models have many parameters and more complicated loss surfaces than this one-dimensional example. That example gives you the direction and the size of each step, not a guarantee that every step in every model improves the result. Knowing which knob to turn, and watching the loss curve while you turn it, is the part that carries over to the models you build later.

quiz.question: What does the learning rate control during training?

Which loss function the model is trained on
How many parameters the model is allowed to have

quiz.explanation: The learning rate is the fraction of the gradient applied at each step. In the worked example a rate of 0.1 moved w from 10 to 9.7, a rate of 1 moved it straight to 7, and a rate of 2 made it oscillate. The batch size, the choice of loss and the parameter count are all chosen before training starts.

quiz_bank.question: The loss goes up after a step. What are the two most likely causes?
choices: The dataset is too small to train on
The learning rate is too large, or the gradient is computed wrongly
The model has too many parameters for the machine

quiz_bank.explanation: A step that is too large overshoots the low-loss region and lands somewhere worse, which is the classic cause when the loss rises on the first few steps. If the loss rises only after many careful steps, suspect the gradient itself, such as a sign error or a badly scaled input. Small data and slow hardware make training painful but do not make the loss climb.

quiz_bank.question: Starting at w = 10 on L(w) = 0.5 times (w - 7) squared with a learning rate of 0.1, what is the parameter after one step?
quiz_bank.explanation: The gradient at w = 10 is 10 - 7, which is 3, so the update is 10 - 0.1 times 3 = 9.7. The option 9.55 comes from multiplying by the loss value 4.5 instead of the gradient, and 10.3 adds the gradient instead of subtracting it, which walks uphill. The value 7 is the minimum, reached in one step only with a learning rate of 1.

lessons.title: Understand probability distributions and sampling
lessons.goal: Distinguish common probability distributions and explain how samples vary.

sections.heading: A distribution describes possible values
body: A probability distribution is a description of the values a quantity can take and how likely each value is, under a stated model. A Bernoulli distribution has two possible outcomes, such as an order being returned or not returned, and a probability for each. A uniform distribution spreads that probability evenly, so a single roll of a six-sided die is uniform over the six faces.

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials that all have the same success probability. The expected number of successes in n trials is n times that probability. For 5 independent trials with a success probability of 0.2, the expected count is 5 times 0.2, which is 1.

An expected count of 1 is a long-run average across many groups of 5, not a promise about any one group. Two groups of 5 with the same probability will often differ, with one holding 0 successes and another 2. A normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped model often used to describe measurement variation, and it is a good description of many measurements rather than a rule that all data follows.

sections.heading: Samples have their own variation
body: A statistic is a number computed from a sample, such as a sample mean or a sample proportion, and it changes from sample to sample. That sampling variation is not the same as a biased collection process. Taking more observations shrinks the random variation, but it does not repair a sample that was collected in a systematically unrepresentative way.

Draw ten values from 0 to 9 and then a hundred values, using the seed 7 in this lesson's task. The ten draws are 3, 1, 6, 0, 5, 3, 0, 5, 0 and 4, which add to 27 and average 2.7. The hundred draws average 4.16. The average of the full set 0 to 9 is 4.5, because they add to 45 and there are 10 of them.

Both sample means sit near 4.5, but the ten-value mean is 1.8 away from it while the hundred-value mean is only 0.34 away. That is why a single small measurement can mislead and a larger sample usually helps. It also explains why two teams analysing the same population can report different numbers without either of them making a mistake.

sections.heading: Match the model to the quantity
body: Use a distribution as a model of uncertainty, not as a label attached by habit. Counts, binary outcomes and continuous measurements have different possible values, and each needs a different model. A Bernoulli model fits a single yes or no outcome, a binomial model fits a count of successes in a fixed number of trials, and a normal model fits a measurement that spreads roughly symmetrically around a centre.

When the choice is wrong, the numbers you compute are wrong even when the arithmetic is right. A normal model applied to a skewed amount understates the spread, and a Bernoulli model applied to a count ignores how the count varies. In machine learning, predicted probabilities and evaluation metrics are estimates from data, and their uncertainty and the population they represent matter when decisions affect people or money.

quiz.question: What does a probability distribution describe?
choices: The values a quantity can take and how likely each value is under a stated model
The exact list of numbers that happen to be in your dataset
How many rows your dataset contains
The order in which the rows arrived
quiz.explanation: A distribution is a model of uncertainty: it lists the possible values and gives each one a probability. Your dataset is one sample drawn from that world, not the model itself. Two datasets drawn from the same distribution can look different while both being normal, which is why a summary number needs its sample size next to it.

With ten draws from 0 to 9, the mean of 4.5 is a target you can miss in either direction, and with a hundred draws you miss by much less. Nothing is broken, and the distribution does not change between draws.

quiz_bank.question: What happens to the average of a sample as the sample grows?
choices: It becomes exactly equal to the population mean every time
It gets closer to the population mean and varies less from one sample to the next
It moves in the same direction on every sample
It stays identical across samples of the same size
quiz_bank.explanation: The average of a larger sample sits nearer the population mean and is more stable, because the luck of the draw has less room to dominate the result. It does not become exactly the population mean, because the data still vary, and it does not move in a fixed direction, because the errors cancel in both directions over many samples.

lessons.title: Use matrices to combine feature vectors
lessons.goal: Read matrix shapes and calculate a small matrix-vector product.

sections.heading: Rows and columns have meaning
body: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers written in rows and columns. In a table of data, rows commonly stand for examples and columns stand for features, and the shape of the matrix, written as rows by columns, tells you how many examples and how many features you have. Four houses with three features each give a matrix of shape 4 by 3.

Here are four houses, with features [size in square metres, number of bedrooms, age in years]: 80, 2, 15; 120, 3, 40; 95, 2, 5; 60, 4, 60. Stacked as a matrix they are 4 rows and 3 columns, so the shape is 4 by 3. Each row is one example, and the columns keep their order and their units.

A vector can stand for one example's ordered feature values, such as [80, 2, 15]. Write the feature names and units down next to the matrix, so a calculation stays interpretable when the same data is used for training and for scoring. A matrix of numbers with no labels cannot be checked by anybody, including you.

sections.heading: A matrix can apply several weighted sums
body: Multiplying a matrix by a vector means taking the dot product of each row of the matrix with the vector, and putting the results in a column. With the weights [0.5, 10, -1] from the previous lesson and the first house [80, 2, 15], the score is 0.5 times 80 plus 10 times 2 plus -1 times 15, which is 40 + 20 - 15 = 45.

Do the same for the other three rows. The second house gives 0.5 times 120 plus 10 times 3 plus -1 times 40, which is 50. The third gives 0.5 times 95 plus 10 times 2 plus -1 times 5, which is 62.5. The fourth gives 0.5 times 60 plus 10 times 4 plus -1 times 60, which is 10. One matrix and one weight vector produce four scores, one per house.

The shape rule follows from that. If the matrix has m rows and n columns, the vector must hold n values and the result holds m values, so a 4 by 3 matrix times a 3-value vector gives a 4 by 1 result. When the shapes do not line up the operation is not defined as written, and you should fix the data rather than quietly dropping a column to make it fit.

sections.heading: Connect the operation to models
body: A linear layer is exactly this operation applied to every row at once, which is why libraries do it that way: one instruction produces a score for every example. The meaning still comes from your choices, because the column order, the units and any bias term decide what the numbers stand for. The multiplication is fast, and it is not automatically correct.

Matrix multiplication is not commutative: changing the order of the two factors changes the result, or makes it undefined, because the inner dimensions have to match. Swapping the order of the rows of the matrix and the values of the vector is the most common beginner bug, and it produces a plausible answer built on the wrong data.

In the four-house example, the age column carries a negative weight of -1, so an older house scores lower on this scale. That is a modelling choice you made, not something the data decided. When you report results, say what each column means and what the weights do, so a reader can tell a deliberate choice from an accident.

quiz.question: What does the shape of a matrix tell you?
choices: The average value of the numbers inside it
Whether the rows are sorted in a useful order
How accurate a model built on it will be
How many rows and columns it has, which tells you what each axis represents
quiz.explanation: A shape written as rows by columns counts the examples and the features. It tells you how many values an input vector needs and how many results come out, so it catches a mismatch early. It says nothing about averages, row order or model performance, which depend on the values and on choices you make later.

choices: Five

One, because a vector has one column

quiz_bank.explanation: Each row of the matrix produces one result, so a matrix with five rows gives five numbers, one per row. In the four-house example the result had four numbers: 45, 50, 62.5 and 10. The number of columns decides how many values the input vector needs, not how many results come out.

quiz_bank.question: A model expects three features but receives four. What kind of mistake is that?
choices: A learning rate that is too small

quiz_bank.explanation: The weights and the features have to line up one for one, so a model built for three features cannot take four. The error appears when the shapes are checked, and the fix is to look at which column was added or dropped, not to loosen the check. A learning rate, a label and an outlier are separate problems that do not cause a shape error.

lessons.title: Interpret partial derivatives
lessons.goal: Explain how a partial derivative measures a loss change for one parameter at a time.

sections.heading: Vary one parameter while holding others fixed
body: A partial derivative measures how a function changes when one input changes while all the other inputs are held still. Take f(a, b) = 2a + 3b. If b stays at any value and only a moves, the function changes by 2 for every 1 that a moves, so the partial derivative with respect to a is 2. Holding b fixed, the partial derivative with respect to b is 3.

The plain-language version is: put your finger on one knob, hold every other knob still, and watch how the output responds. That is why the name says partial, because you are measuring one direction of change rather than the whole picture. When a loss has only one parameter, its partial derivative with respect to that parameter is the ordinary derivative, because there is no second input to hold still.

sections.heading: Read a gradient at a point
body: When a loss has several parameters, the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives, one number for each parameter, all evaluated at the same current point. For J(a, b) = (a - 1) squared + (b + 2) squared, the partial derivatives are 2(a - 1) and 2(b + 2). At the point (0, 0) the gradient is [-2, 4].

Read that vector as directions. The loss goes up fastest in the direction of the gradient, so gradient descent moves in the opposite direction, which here means increasing a and decreasing b, because those are the two moves that bring a towards 1 and b towards -2. The size of each number says how much the loss changes per unit of that parameter.

The derivative is local information. For a nonlinear function the slope changes as the parameters move, so training recomputes the gradient at each step instead of assuming that one direction stays right. A gradient tells you what to do next from where you stand, not what the whole landscape looks like.

sections.heading: Use partial derivatives carefully
body: The numbers in a gradient depend on the function, on the units of the parameters and on where you evaluate them, so a large entry does not automatically mean that parameter matters most in the final model. A large gradient also produces a large step unless the learning rate or the parameter scaling keeps the step in check.

Flat regions slow training down. If the gradient is close to zero where you are, each step moves the parameters only a tiny amount, and progress looks like it has stopped even though the rule is running. A loss that stops improving may be a plateau rather than a bug, so look at the size of the gradient before you rewrite the model.

Automatic differentiation, which is what libraries such as PyTorch use to compute gradients, is exact for the operations it supports, but it checks nothing about whether your loss, your data or your model is the right choice. It computes the slope of the objective you gave it. Verifying that the objective is the one you meant stays your job.

quiz.question: In a partial derivative, what is held fixed?
choices: The variable being differentiated
The learning rate used during training
All the other inputs of the function
The value of the function itself
quiz.explanation: A partial derivative isolates one direction of change: you vary the input you are interested in and keep everything else still. In f(a, b) = 2a + 3b, holding b fixed leaves the coefficient of a, which is 2. The variable being differentiated is the one that moves, and the learning rate and the function value are not part of the definition.

quiz_bank.question: What does the gradient vector at one point tell you?
choices: The direction in which the loss changes fastest at that point
The overall shape of the loss for every possible parameter value
The final parameter values that training will reach
How many parameters the model has
quiz_bank.explanation: The gradient is local: it gives the steepest direction of change at the point where the parameters currently sit, and gradient descent moves the opposite way to reduce the loss. It does not describe the whole landscape, so it cannot tell you the final values. The number of entries equals the number of parameters, but the count is not what the vector means.

quiz_bank.question: Why can training become very slow in some regions?
choices: The dataset becomes too large to fit in memory
The gradient can be close to zero there, so each step moves the parameters only a little
The model has too few parameters to learn the pattern
The learning rate is reset to zero between batches
quiz_bank.explanation: The size of the step is set by the learning rate times the gradient, so a gradient near zero means almost no movement even though the code is running. This is a plateau, not a crash, and the fix is often patience or a different starting point rather than a rewrite. Memory limits, parameter counts and learning rate resets are separate issues.

lessons.title: Interpret confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
lessons.goal: Describe uncertainty in sample estimates and interpret a hypothesis-test p-value without overclaiming.

sections.heading: A confidence interval describes a procedure
body: A confidence interval is a range produced by a repeatable procedure. The interval you see covers a range of plausible values for the population quantity, and the confidence level says how often that procedure covers the true value when it is repeated on fresh samples. A 95 percent confidence procedure covers the true value in about 95 out of 100 repetitions.

It does not mean there is a 95 percent chance that this particular interval contains the true value, because the true value is fixed and the interval is what was produced. It also does not mean 95 percent of your data points fall inside the interval. Read the level as a description of the method, which is why a wide interval is a warning even when the level is high.

A worked example: in a survey of 400 customers, 62 percent kept their accounts. The standard error of that proportion is the square root of 0.62 times 0.38 divided by 400, which is about 0.024, and the margin of error is about 1.96 times 0.024, which is 0.048. The 95 percent interval is therefore roughly 57 percent to 67 percent.

sections.heading: A p-value is conditional on a null model
body: A hypothesis test sets up a null hypothesis, which is usually a statement that nothing is happening, and then asks how surprising the observed data would be if that statement were true. The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as the data you actually saw, under the null hypothesis and the assumptions of the test.

A p-value of 0.03 means that if the null hypothesis and the test assumptions were true, results this extreme would happen about 3 percent of the time. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it is not the probability that your result is correct. It also says nothing about how much the effect matters in practice.

Choose the question and the analysis before you look at the results, and be careful about testing many hypotheses. If you try twenty comparisons and report only the ones with a small p-value, you are very likely to publish a finding that is noise, because about one in twenty comparisons at the 5 percent level looks surprising by chance alone.

sections.heading: Association is not a causal explanation
body: Finding that two variables move together does not tell you that one of them caused the other. A third factor can drive both, and so can the order of events or the way people were selected into the sample. On rainy days more people carry umbrellas and the streets are wet, but the umbrellas do not make the streets wet, because the rain causes both.

In the customer study, users who received onboarding messages kept 12 percent more accounts. That is a real difference in the sample that was studied. It is also compatible with the possibility that the message was sent to more engaged customers, that a product change landed at the same time, or that the extra accounts came from a different mix of customers.

In machine learning, statistical significance is not the same as predictive usefulness or a justified product decision. Report the effect size, the uncertainty, the limitations of the data and the evaluation question together, and let the decision be made on all four rather than on the p-value alone.

quiz.question: What does a 95 percent confidence interval mean?
choices: There is a 95 percent chance that the true value lies inside this particular interval
If you repeated the whole sampling procedure many times, about 95 percent of those intervals would cover the true population value
95 percent of the individual data points fall inside the interval
The estimate is within 95 percent of the true value
quiz.explanation: The 95 percent describes the method: run the same procedure on many fresh samples and roughly 95 percent of the resulting intervals will cover the true value. It is not a probability about one fixed interval, and it has nothing to do with where the individual data points sit. A wide interval still tells you that the estimate is uncertain.

A small p-value says the pattern is hard to explain by chance alone, not that you have found the cause.

lessons.title: Load a table and look at it
lessons.goal: Load the bundled orders file with pandas and describe its shape, its column types and its missing values before you change anything.

sections.heading: Read the file
body: A CSV file is a table stored as plain text, where every line is one row and every comma separates one column. Pandas is a Python library for working with those tables, and a table loaded into pandas is called a DataFrame. You read the bundled orders file with two short lines of code: `import pandas as pd`, then `df = pd.read_csv('starter_kits/machine_learning/module_3_data_problem/data/orders.csv')`. The name `df` is just a label you choose for the table you have loaded.

Two quick commands tell you what you have. `df.head()` prints the first five rows, which here are orders 1001 to 1005: order 1001 on 2025-01-01 for 24.50 dollars from the web channel, order 1002 on 2025-01-02 for 81.00 dollars from mobile, order 1003 on 2025-01-03 for 17.25 dollars from web, order 1004 on 2025-01-04 from mobile with a blank total, and order 1005 on 2025-01-05 for 44.00 dollars from partner. `df.shape` prints `(12, 6)`, which means 12 rows and 6 columns. One row is one order, so the file holds 12 orders and 6 facts about each one.

Reading the file changes nothing, which is exactly why it is the first thing you do. A file can hold numbers where you expected words, or thousands of rows where you expected twelve, and both are cheaper to find now than after you have started cleaning. Keep the file on disk untouched and let pandas load a copy into memory, so that every edit you make later leaves the original exactly as it arrived.

sections.heading: What is in each column
body: `df.dtypes` prints the data type of every column. On this file it reports order_id as int64, order_date as text, order_total as float64, channel as text, returned_within_30_days as int64 and refund_reason as text. A float is a number that can carry a decimal part, which is why a total of 24.50 needs that type rather than a whole-number type. Two columns hold whole numbers, one holds a decimal number and three hold words. Recent versions of pandas print the text columns as str, which is the same idea under a shorter name.

The types tell you what each column can be used for. order_id is an identifier, a label for a row rather than a measurement, so it names an order and should not be handed to a model as if it were a measurement. channel and refund_reason are words, and words have to be turned into numbers before a model can use them. returned_within_30_days is a flag: the number 1 means the order came back within 30 days and 0 means it did not, so it is the column to predict rather than a column to learn from.

`df.describe()` summarises the numeric columns only, so it leaves out the three text columns. For order_total it reports count 11, mean 38.29, standard deviation 32.19, minimum -5.00, maximum 102.40, and the quartiles 16.125, 29.99 and 53.60. The count of 11 tells you straight away that one of the twelve rows has no total, and the minimum of -5.00 tells you that one row holds an amount no customer would ever pay.

sections.heading: Find what is missing
body: `df.isna().sum()` counts the missing values in each column. On this file it prints 0 for order_id, 0 for order_date, 1 for order_total, 0 for channel, 0 for returned_within_30_days and 8 for refund_reason. The one missing total belongs to order 1004 on 2025-01-04 from the mobile channel, and its cell in the file is empty because there is nothing between two commas.

A missing value and a zero are different things. A zero order total would mean the order was free, and pandas stores that as the number 0 and counts it as present. An empty cell means nobody wrote a number down, and pandas stores that as missing and counts it as 1 for that column. If you fill a missing total with 0, the average of the column drops and the model learns that a free order is a normal thing to predict. If you leave the cell empty, the model is told that you do not know.

Eight blank refund reasons is not eight broken rows. A refund reason is only written when an order is returned, and exactly four orders in this file were returned: 1002, 1005, 1008 and 1011. The other eight rows are blank for a good reason. Always check whether a blank is a missing measurement or a blank that carries meaning before you decide to fill it or drop the row.

sections.heading: Look before you change
body: Cleaning decisions change the numbers a model learns, so it pays to see the mess before you tidy it. On this file the inspection has already found three things: one missing total on order 1004, one negative total of -5.00 on order 1007, and a refund reason column that is blank for every order that was not returned. Each of those needs a decision, and each decision changes a row count or an average that somebody will quote later.

Keep the original. `df = pd.read_csv(path)` loads a copy into memory, so `df.copy()` before any edit gives you a version to compare against, and saving a cleaned table to a new file leaves the raw file exactly as it arrived. When somebody asks later why the average is 37.60 instead of 38.29, the answer should be a line of code rather than a memory.

Inspection is cheap and it is the step people skip. Two minutes with `shape`, `dtypes`, `isna().sum()` and `describe()` gives you the size of the table, what each column holds, what is missing and where the impossible numbers are. Everything in the rest of this module rests on those answers being right, so write them down before you change a single cell.

quiz.question: What does the shape of a DataFrame tell you?
choices: The average value of every numeric column
The number of rows and the number of columns
Which columns contain missing values
The order the rows appear in the file
quiz.explanation: The shape of a DataFrame is a pair of numbers written as rows by columns, and for this file it is (12, 6): 12 orders and 6 facts recorded about each order. The shape does not report averages, missing values or row order. Those come from describe(), from isna().sum() and from the order of the rows.

quiz_bank.question: You loaded the file and immediately replaced every empty cell with 0. What goes wrong?

the file on disk is changed, so the original values are lost
a missing total becomes a free order, which is a claim about the business that the data never made
