quiz_bank.explanation: Filling a blank with zero claims the order was worth nothing, and a model trained on that claim learns from a fact you invented. An empty cell says the value is unknown; zero says the value is known and happens to be zero. Filling happens on a copy, so the file on disk is untouched either way, and pandas stores 0 in a float column without complaint.

lessons.title: Fix missing values without inventing data
lessons.goal: Choose a missing-value strategy for the order_total column and explain what information that choice gives up.

sections.heading: Three ways to handle a gap
body: There are three honest moves for a missing value, and they differ in what they assume. You can drop the row, which assumes the missing order is not worth learning from. You can fill with a constant such as 0, which assumes a blank total means the order was free. You can fill with a summary number such as the mean or the median, which assumes the missing order looked like the other orders.

On this file only one row has a missing total: order 1004 on 2025-01-04 from the mobile channel. Dropping it leaves 11 rows and the mean of the present totals, 38.29, unchanged, because the dropped value was never part of that mean. Filling it with 0 adds a zero to the twelve totals, giving a sum of 421.19 and a mean of 35.10.

Filling it with the median of the present totals, 29.99, gives a sum of 451.18 across 12 rows and a mean of 37.60. None of these three numbers is the true total of order 1004, because nobody knows it. The point of choosing a method is not to recover the right value. The point is to make a decision you can defend, and to record what that decision assumes.

sections.heading: Fill with the median, not the mean
body: The median is the middle value once the values are sorted from smallest to largest, and the mean is the sum divided by the count. The eleven present totals, sorted, are -5.00, 12.75, 15.00, 17.25, 24.50, 29.99, 36.10, 44.00, 63.20, 81.00 and 102.40. The sixth of those eleven is 29.99, so the median is 29.99. The sum is 421.19, so the mean is 421.19 divided by 11, which is 38.29.

Those two fill values differ because of one row. The total of -5.00 on order 1007 sits far below the other ten values, and it drags the mean down while it leaves the middle position untouched. On money amounts that can be skewed, the median is the safer fill value, because it is not moved by a single unusual row. Here the mean sits 8.30 above the median, and that whole gap is the -5.00.

Choosing the median still invents a value, which is why the next section adds a column rather than pretending the gap was never there. The rule to remember is simple: fill with a summary that the rest of the column would look like, and then record the fact that you filled it.

sections.heading: Add a missing flag instead
body: The pattern is to fill the value so the model has something to work with, and to add a column that says the value was missing. In pandas that is three lines: `median = df['order_total'].median()` gives 29.99, `df['order_total_was_missing'] = df['order_total'].isna()` marks the gap with True, and `df['order_total'] = df['order_total'].fillna(median)` puts 29.99 in the blank. Order 1004 now carries a total of 29.99 and a flag of True, and the other eleven rows carry a flag of False.

The flag buys you two things. It keeps the information that the value was missing, so a model can learn that missing totals behave differently, and it lets you undo the fill later without hunting for which row was filled. It also lets you report honestly: you can say that the average across the twelve rows is 37.60 while knowing that one of those twelve numbers is the median rather than a measured total.

The cost of the flag is one more column and one more decision to explain. If you drop the flag, the filled row looks like every other row and the missing-ness disappears. If you keep it, a reader of your audit can see exactly which rows you changed and why, which is the difference between a cleaned dataset and a quietly altered one.

sections.heading: Missing can mean something
body: Not every blank is a gap in your knowledge. The refund_reason column is blank on eight of the twelve rows, and those eight rows are exactly the orders that were not returned: 1001, 1003, 1004, 1006, 1007, 1009, 1010 and 1012. The blank means this order was never returned, so there is no reason to give. The four returned orders carry the reasons damaged, wrong_item and late_delivery.

If you dropped every row with a blank refund_reason, you would be left with the four returned orders and nothing else. The returned rate in your table would jump from 4 in 12, which is 33 percent, to 4 in 4, which is 100 percent, and the table would no longer describe the orders the shop actually received. That is the danger of dropping rows on a blank that carries meaning.

So the rule is to ask what the blank means before you act on it. If the blank means the event did not happen, keep the row and treat the blank as information. If the blank means the event happened and nobody recorded it, you have a genuine gap, and you choose a fill or a drop and say which one in your notes.

lessons.title: Turn text categories into numbers
lessons.goal: Encode the channel column as numbers a model can use, without pretending that web, mobile and partner have an order they do not have.

sections.heading: Why a model cannot read a word
body: A model that learns from numbers has no way to measure how far the word web is from the word mobile, because a distance between two words is not a number it can compare. A text column therefore has to be turned into numbers before training. How you turn it changes what the model is able to learn, which is why the choice is a modelling decision and not a formatting detail.

There are two broad options. You can give each category a single number, such as web = 0, mobile = 1 and partner = 2, which is called ordinal encoding. Or you can give each category its own column of ones and zeros, which is called one-hot encoding. The first is compact and cheap. The second is wider and safer, and the reason why is the next section.

The order you assign in ordinal encoding is arbitrary. If you number web = 0, mobile = 1 and partner = 2 today, a model may treat a partner order as being twice as far from web as a mobile order, even though nothing in the business says partner sits between web and mobile. The number is a label you made up, and a model cannot tell a label from a measurement.

sections.heading: One number per category
body: One-hot encoding gives each category its own column, and every row gets a 1 in the column of its category and 0 in the others. In pandas the call is `dummies = pd.get_dummies(df['channel'], dtype=int)`, which returns three new columns named mobile, partner and web, one row for each of the twelve orders.

The resulting table looks like this. Order 1001 is web, so its row is mobile 0, partner 0, web 1. Order 1002 is mobile, so its row is mobile 1, partner 0, web 0. Order 1003 is web, so its row is mobile 0, partner 0, web 1. Order 1004 is mobile, so its row is mobile 1, partner 0, web 0. Order 1005 is partner, so its row is mobile 0, partner 1, web 0. The last seven rows follow the same pattern: 1006 web, 1007 mobile, 1008 web, 1009 partner, 1010 mobile, 1011 web and 1012 partner. Every row has exactly one 1.

Summing each of the three columns gives 4 for mobile, 3 for partner and 5 for web, which are the same counts that `df['channel'].value_counts()` reports. What the columns mean is simple: web = 1 tells the model that this order came through the website, and the same for the other two. Because each category has its own column, the model can learn a separate effect for each channel and cannot accidentally learn that partner is more than web. The cost is width: three channels become three columns, so fifty channels would become fifty columns.

sections.heading: When a category really has an order
body: Some categories genuinely sit in a sequence, such as a size column with small, medium and large, or a satisfaction score from 1 to 5. Ordinal encoding is right there, because the categories have a real order and a real gap between neighbours. You write the mapping yourself, such as `{'size_small': 0, 'size_medium': 1, 'size_large': 2}`, and apply it with `df['size'].map(mapping)`.

The trap is using ordinal encoding where no order exists, and channel is the example. Web, mobile and partner are names, not positions on a line. A model that sees partner = 2 and mobile = 1 treats the gap between them as real, and it treats web = 0 as being closer to nothing. One-hot encoding does not have this problem, because three separate columns carry no implied distance between them.

A second trap is pretending that the categories are equally spaced. Even with size_small, size_medium and size_large, the jump from small to medium may matter far more to a customer than the jump from medium to large, so one number per step hides that difference. When the gaps matter, one-hot encoding each level leaves the model free to learn them from the data instead of inheriting your guess.

sections.heading: Keep the categories you saw
body: The categories in your training data are not necessarily the categories that turn up later. If you fit one-hot encoding on rows from January and then score an order from a channel called kiosk, that order has no column of its own: every one-hot column is 0, which looks like an order from no channel at all. Keep the list of categories you saw during training, and give unseen categories their own handling, such as an other column or an explicit refusal to score.

A column with hundreds of distinct values has the opposite problem: one-hot encoding turns it into hundreds of columns and the table stops being readable. In this file the refund_reason column holds three distinct reasons among the four returned orders, damaged twice, wrong_item once and late_delivery once, so three extra columns would be reasonable here. On a column with one reason per order you need a different plan, such as grouping rare reasons into an other bucket.

Before you encode, count what is there. `df['channel'].value_counts()` gives web 5, mobile 4 and partner 3, and `df['refund_reason'].value_counts()` gives the three reasons with their counts. Counting first tells you how wide your table is about to become and shows you a category with a single row, which is often a typo rather than a real category. You will meet this same counting step again when you decide which rows to train on.

On this file the twelve rows produce web 5, mobile 4 and partner 3 when you sum each column, which matches value_counts(). The first option is ordinal encoding, which is the approach this lesson warns against for names.

lessons.title: Put features on a comparable scale and catch outliers
lessons.goal: Scale the order_total column so no single column dominates a distance, and decide whether an unusual total is an error or a real case.

sections.heading: Why scale
body: Many models measure how similar two rows are by adding up the squared differences between their feature values, which is the distance formula. If one column is measured in dollars and another in ones, the dollars column contributes most of the total even when the ones column is the one that carries the meaning. The rule is to put columns on comparable scales before you measure distance, so that the model listens to every column.

Take two orders from this file. Order 1005 is a partner order of 44.00 dollars that was returned, and order 1012 is a partner order of 36.10 dollars that was not returned. Their totals differ by 7.90 and their returned flags differ by 1, so the raw distance is the square root of 7.90 squared plus 1 squared, which is the square root of 63.41, about 7.96. The dollar gap does nearly all the work, and order 1012 ends up the closest order to order 1005 among the eleven rows that have a total.

Scale the dollar column into z-scores and the same comparison changes. Order 1005 becomes 0.19 and order 1012 becomes -0.07, so the total gap shrinks to about 0.26 while the flag gap of 1 stays. The distance becomes the square root of 0.26 squared plus 1 squared, about 1.03, and the closest order to order 1005 is now order 1008, a web order of 63.20 that was also returned, at about 0.63. Scaling changed which orders count as similar, which is exactly why the choice has to be yours.

sections.heading: Standardisation and min-max
body: Standardisation, also called z-score scaling, centres a column on its mean and divides by its standard deviation. In words: take the value, subtract the mean of the column, then divide by the spread of the column. The eleven present totals have a mean of 38.29, because they sum to 421.19 over 11 values, and a population standard deviation of 30.69. A total of 44.00 becomes (44.00 - 38.29) divided by 30.69, which is 5.71 divided by 30.69, about 0.19.

Min-max scaling does something different: take the value, subtract the smallest value in the column, and divide by the range, which is the largest minus the smallest. The eleven present totals run from -5.00 to 102.40, so the range is 107.40, and 44.00 becomes (44.00 - (-5.00)) divided by 107.40, which is 49.00 over 107.40, about 0.46. Min-max puts every value between 0 and 1. Standardisation puts the average at 0 and the spread at 1, and it copes better when a few values sit far from the rest, because one extreme value does not stretch the whole column.

In pandas and scikit-learn you do not have to do the arithmetic by hand. `from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler`, then `scaler = StandardScaler()`, `scaler.fit(train[['order_total']])` and `scaler.transform(train[['order_total']])` gives the scaled column, and the scaler stores the mean and the spread it learned as `scaler.mean_` and `scaler.scale_`. One detail worth noticing: `df['order_total'].describe()` shows a standard deviation of 32.19 because it divides by ten, while StandardScaler divides by eleven and uses 30.69. Both are standard conventions, so write down which one you used.

sections.heading: Fit the scaler on training data only
body: A scaler learns numbers from the rows it is fitted on: the mean of 38.29 and the spread of 30.69 come from the rows you hand to fit. If you fit on all twelve orders, the four evaluation orders have already told the model their own average and spread before the evaluation starts, and your score on those rows is optimistic. The rule is that the scaler learns from training rows and is applied unchanged to everything else.

The same rule applies to the median you used to fill the missing total and to the one-hot columns you created for the channel. Each of them learns something from the data: the median 29.99, the list of three channel names, the mean and the spread. Every one of those must be learned from training rows only and then reused for rows the model has not seen. Breaking that rule is called data leakage, and the next lesson looks at the wider problem.

The practical habit is to split first and fit second. Create the training rows and the evaluation rows, fit the scaler on the training rows, then apply it to the evaluation rows without refitting. In code that is two steps, `scaler.fit(train[['order_total']])` followed by `scaler.transform(test[['order_total']])`, and the second line never looks at the test values to decide anything.

sections.heading: Outlier or unusual customer
body: The interquartile range, written IQR, is the width of the middle half of the values. The first quartile, Q1, is the value that has a quarter of the data below it, and the third quartile, Q3, is the value that has three quarters below it. On the eleven present totals, Q1 is 16.125 and Q3 is 53.60, so the middle 50 percent of orders sits between about 16.13 and about 53.60, and the IQR is 53.60 - 16.125, which is 37.475.

Values outside that middle band are worth a look: order 1007 at -5.00 sits below 16.13, and order 1011 at 102.40 sits above 53.60. The stricter and more common fence widens the band by one and a half IQR on each side, which on this file runs from -40.09 to 109.81 and so flags neither row. That difference matters, and you have to decide it before you look: on a table of thousands of orders the fence is stable, and on a table of eleven values the quartiles move as soon as one row changes.

Even when a value is flagged, decide whether it is an error or a real case before you touch it. A total of -5.00 is impossible, so order 1007 is a data error, probably a refund recorded as a negative sale, and someone has to correct or exclude it. A total of 102.40 is a perfectly ordinary amount for a large order, and the customer who placed it is real, so deleting it would remove a genuine case and quietly narrow what your model has seen. Flag the row, look it up, and write down what you did.

In the orders file the total gap of 7.90 between two orders produced a distance of about 7.96, while the flag gap of 1 contributed almost nothing. Scaling puts both on comparable footing so the model listens to both.

lessons.title: Frame the prediction problem
lessons.goal: Write down the decision a model must support, the column it predicts, the columns available at that moment, and the simple rule a model has to beat.

sections.heading: Start with the decision
body: A model earns its place by changing a decision that somebody has to make. Start by naming the person who acts, the action they can take, and the moment they need the answer. For the bundled orders file, the decision could be this: a returns team checks orders by hand before they ship, and the model should say which orders are likely to come back within 30 days. The team can only act on an answer at the moment the order is placed, so the prediction time is order time and the outcome window is 30 days.

Those three choices fix everything else. The prediction unit is one row of the table, which here means one order. The outcome window decides which rows count as returned, and the file already gives you that column: returned_within_30_days is 1 for four orders and 0 for eight. If you had instead wanted to predict returns within 7 days, this file could not answer the question, because it does not record when a return happened.

Writing this down first is what stops the common beginner mistake of choosing an algorithm first and then bending the data to fit it. A logistic regression and a decision tree can both be trained on the same table, but only one decision makes sense here. The decision, the prediction unit and the window are yours to choose; the columns and the rows you are given are not.

sections.heading: Choose the target and baseline
body: The target is the column the model learns to predict. Here it is returned_within_30_days, and it takes two values, so this is a classification problem. The features are the columns that exist at prediction time: order_total, channel and order_date. The refund_reason column is not a feature, because it is only written when an order is returned, which is after the answer you are trying to predict. That column is a leakage feature, and a later lesson deals with it properly.

A baseline is the simple rule you would use if you had no model at all. The usual baseline here is to predict not returned for every order. On these twelve rows that rule gets 8 right out of 12, because 8 of the 12 orders were not returned, which is 66.7 percent accuracy. A model has to beat that number to be worth anything, and on a table where a third of the orders come back, a rule that always guesses not returned is strong enough to hide a useless model.

Write the baseline down in the same sentence as the target, so that nobody can later claim a model is good without saying what it beat. The returned rate across the whole table is 4 in 12, which is 33.3 percent, and a model that predicts that rate exactly gets about a third of the rows right. If your model scores below 66.7 percent on these rows, it is worse than the rule you would have used anyway.

sections.heading: Write an evaluation contract
body: An evaluation contract is a short written promise about how you will test the model, made before you see any result. It names the rows you will test on, the number you will report, and the threshold you will judge it against. For the bundled file a workable contract says this: train on the eight earliest orders, 1001 to 1008, evaluate on the four latest, 1009 to 1012, report accuracy and recall on those four rows, and accept the model only if it beats the 66.7 percent baseline.

Fixing the contract in advance is what stops you from moving the goalposts. Without it, the natural thing to do after a disappointing score is to change the test rows, drop the awkward order 1004 with its missing total, or pick the metric that flatters the model. Each of those changes the rules after seeing the score, and the score that results then tells you nothing about future orders.

Keep the contract in the repository next to the code, and treat any change as a new experiment with a new name. On these four evaluation rows the baseline rule predicts not returned and gets three of the four right, because only order 1011 was returned. A perfect four out of four would be worth checking for leakage rather than celebrating, and that check comes later in this module.

quiz.explanation: The decision sits upstream of everything technical. If the returns team needs to know which orders to check before shipping, then the prediction unit is the order, the prediction time is order time, and the target is a return within 30 days. The algorithm choice comes last and can change without altering that. Baselines are computed without any model, so they are always available.

lessons.title: Inspect and validate a tabular dataset
lessons.goal: Find structural and quality problems in the orders table with checks you can rerun, and report each problem together with the row that caused it.

sections.heading: Treat a dataset as a contract
body: A dataset is not just a file of numbers. It is a promise: these columns, this many rows, one row per order, an order total that is a positive amount of money, a channel from a known list. When you write the promise down, a check can fail loudly the moment the file stops matching it, instead of the problem surfacing three weeks later as a strange model score.

For the bundled orders file the contract reads like this: 12 rows and 6 columns named order_id, order_date, order_total, channel, returned_within_30_days and refund_reason; 12 distinct order ids; order_total a number of 0 or more; channel one of web, mobile or partner; returned_within_30_days equal to 0 or 1; and a refund reason only on rows where the order was returned. Write it as one sentence per rule, because a rule you cannot state is a rule you cannot check.

Schema checks and quality checks answer different questions. A schema check asks whether the shape is right: are the expected columns present, with the expected names and types, and is the id unique. A quality check asks whether the values are sensible: are totals positive, are channel names from the known list, is a refund reason present exactly when an order came back. Both kinds belong in the pipeline, and the second kind is where the real problems live.

sections.heading: Inspect with safe summaries
body: Start with counts, because they are cheap and they catch the worst problems. `df.shape` gives 12 rows and 6 columns. `df['order_id'].nunique()` gives 12, so no order appears twice. `df['order_total'].isna().sum()` gives 1, the gap on order 1004. `df['order_total'].le(0).sum()` gives 1, the -5.00 on order 1007. And `df['refund_reason'].notna().sum()` gives 4, exactly the number of returned orders, so the refund reasons and the returned flag agree with each other.

Those five counts between them find both real faults on this file. A missing total is a gap in the record, and a negative total is impossible for a sale, so order 1007 is either a refund signed as a sale or a typing error, and somebody has to decide which. Averages hide both problems: the mean of 38.29 looks like a normal amount for an order, and it tells you nothing about a row that is missing or a row that is negative.

Compare across groups as well as across columns. `df.groupby('channel')['order_total'].mean()` gives 44.02 for web over 5 orders, 30.33 for mobile over the 3 orders that have a total, and 36.70 for partner over 3. The web and mobile averages differ because of which orders sit in each group and because of one negative row inside mobile, so a single overall average hides both the group difference and the bad row.

sections.heading: Make failures actionable
body: A check that reports only failed has told you almost nothing, because you still have to find the bad rows yourself. A useful failure names the rule, the value that broke it and the row it came from: order_total must be 0 or more, order_id 1007 has -5.00. Now the fix is a decision about one order rather than a search through twelve.

In pandas the pattern is a function that returns a list of problems, each one a string, and a caller that raises an error when the list is not empty. Writing the checks as strings that name the rule also means the output can go straight into the audit report the project asks for, so the evidence of what was found is written down rather than remembered.

Keep one important limit in mind. A check can tell you that a value breaks a rule, and it cannot tell you whether the rule was wrong. If the business allows negative totals for refunds, then the check that demands a positive total is the thing to fix, not order 1007. Decide which rules are promises from the business and which are assumptions you have made, and label the assumptions.

quiz.question: What makes a dataset a contract rather than just a file of numbers?
choices: It is stored in a CSV file so that it can be opened in a spreadsheet
It has a promised shape, column meanings and value rules that checks can test
It contains more than a thousand rows
It has been checked at least once by a person
quiz.explanation: A contract is a written promise about structure and values: 12 rows, 6 named columns, unique order ids, positive totals, channels from a known list. Because the promise is written down, a check can fail loudly and point at the row that broke it. Storage format, dataset size and past human inspection do not make a dataset checkable.

df.isna().sum().sum() equals 1
df['order_total'].le(0).sum() equals 1

quiz_bank.question: Your validation function prints validation failed. What is missing?
choices: The function needs to be run more than once
The rule that broke, the offending value and the row it came from
The name of the library that was imported
The number of columns in the file
quiz_bank.explanation: A bare failure leaves you searching the table yourself, which is the slow part. Naming the rule, the value and the row, as in order_total must be 0 or more, order_id 1007 has -5.00, turns the failure into one decision about one order. Running it twice, or noting the library and the column count, tells you nothing about what broke.

lessons.title: Choose a split that matches the real question
lessons.goal: Split the orders table so the evaluation rows look like future orders, and check that the split itself is sound.

sections.heading: Random splits are not always realistic
body: A random split throws each row into the training pile or the evaluation pile at random, and that is the right choice when rows are independent and future rows resemble a random pick from today's rows. It is the wrong choice when the question is about the future. If the model will be used to predict whether a customer's next order comes back, then training on an order from 2025-01-12 and testing on one from 2025-01-02 has mixed up time.

The orders file is an order book, so its rows arrive in time order: 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-12, one order per day. The honest split for a model that will predict future returns is therefore a time split. Take the earliest eight orders, 1001 to 1008, as development rows and the latest four, 1009 to 1012, as evaluation rows. The evaluation rows are then orders that had not happened yet when the development rows were collected.

A random split would also be wrong when the same customer appears many times, because the model would meet that customer in training and in evaluation and score better than it would on new customers. Group the rows by customer before splitting in that case. The rule to remember is simple: match the split to the question you will be asked, not to the split that gives the nicest number.

sections.heading: Keep the test set for final evaluation
body: Three sets, three jobs. The training set is what the model learns its parameters from. The validation set is what you use to choose between options: which features to include, which fill value to use, which threshold to set. The test set is what you score once, at the end, to estimate how the model will do on orders it has never seen.

The test set is worth protecting, because every time you look at it, it stops being a test set. If you check the test score after every experiment and keep the experiment with the best test score, you have fitted the model to the test data and the number you report is optimistic. Keep the test rows untouched until the choices are settled, and decide the sizes in advance: 8 development rows and 4 evaluation rows for this file.

With only twelve rows the sizes are small, and that is a real limitation to state rather than hide. Four evaluation rows means one mistake moves the score by 25 percentage points, so a single evaluation is noisy. Cross-validation, which repeats the split over several folds, gives a sense of that variation once you have more rows to spend. For now, write down the split rule and the row counts, and say plainly that the sample is small.

sections.heading: Check the split itself
body: Before you trust a split, look at it. Three checks catch most problems. Does the split keep a similar proportion of returns? The development rows 1001 to 1008 contain three returned orders, which is 3 in 8 or 37.5 percent, and the evaluation rows 1009 to 1012 contain one, which is 1 in 4 or 25 percent. On four rows that difference is noise rather than a shift, but on a large table a big gap would be a warning.

Do the two parts look alike, and do they share identifiers? Here they share nothing: the 12 order ids are distinct, so the 8 and the 4 have no order in common, and you can check that with `set(train_ids).isdisjoint(test_ids)`, which returns True. The ranges differ more than the balance does. The development rows hold the missing total on order 1004 and the negative total on order 1007, while all four evaluation rows have totals, ranging from 15.00 to 102.40.

Notice what that last check revealed. Every messy row in this file landed in the development half and none landed in the evaluation half, so a model that mishandles missing or negative totals would look fine on the evaluation rows and fail on real orders. That is exactly what a split check is for. A split that hides your data problems is a split that makes you feel better than you should.

quiz.question: When is a random split the wrong choice?
choices: Whenever the dataset has more than a hundred rows
When the model will be used on future rows, or when the same customer appears in several rows
Whenever the target column takes only two values
Whenever the data contains a missing value
quiz.explanation: A random split mixes the past and the future, and it lets the model meet the same customer in both halves. The orders file is a time-ordered order book, so training on 1001 to 1008 and evaluating on 1009 to 1012 matches the way the model will actually be used. The size of the table, the number of target values and a missing cell do not decide the split.

quiz_bank.question: Which check reveals a leaky split?
choices: Printing the row count of each part
Checking that no order id appears in both parts
Checking that both parts have the same number of columns
Sorting both parts by order date
quiz_bank.explanation: If the same order id sits in both halves, the model can recognise the row instead of generalising from it, and the score will be too high. On this file the 12 ids are distinct, so the check returns True and the split is clean. Equal row counts, equal column counts and sorting by date say nothing about whether information crossed the boundary.

lessons.title: Build features and detect leakage
lessons.goal: Decide which columns a model may use by asking when each one exists, and recognise the results that mean information leaked in.

sections.heading: Availability defines a valid feature
body: A feature is a column of your table that you hand to the model as input, and a valid feature is one that exists at the exact moment you need the prediction. The test is simple and unforgiving: if the column is written after the outcome happens, it is not available at prediction time, whatever its value turns out to be.

The refund_reason column fails that test. It is blank on the eight orders that were not returned and holds damaged on 1002 and 1008, wrong_item on 1005 and late_delivery on 1011, so it is written at the moment of a return, which happens up to 30 days after the order. A model that reads it is reading the answer. The columns available when an order is placed are order_total, channel and order_date, and returned_within_30_days is the target rather than a feature.

Leakage also arrives through less obvious routes. A feature computed from a count over all orders, including the ones you will test on, has already seen the future. A duplicate customer id in two splits lets the model recognise a customer it has met before. And preprocessing fitted on the whole file, such as a scaler or a filled median, mixes the test rows into the training. Each of these makes an offline score look better than the model will be in use.

sections.heading: Fit transformations on training data
body: A transformation is a step that learns numbers from your data: filling a missing total with the median 29.99, turning channel into three one-hot columns, or standardising order_total around a mean of 38.29 and a spread of 30.69. The learned part is where the risk sits. If those numbers come from all twelve rows, then the four evaluation orders have already shaped the model before you test it.

So the rule is: fit on training rows, then apply to everything else with the numbers you have already learned. `scaler.fit(train[['order_total']])` learns the mean and the spread from the development rows, and `scaler.transform(test[['order_total']])` applies exactly those numbers to the evaluation rows without looking at them. The fill for a missing total has to use a median computed on the development rows, and the one-hot columns have to come from the channels seen in development.

Keep the mapping from raw column to model input in one place, with the names, the units and the missing-value behaviour written down next to it. A feature called order_total_z means something specific: the number of standard deviations above the training mean, with the median fill applied first. Without that note, a later reader cannot tell whether two runs used the same transformation, and a comparison between them means nothing.

sections.heading: Audit suspiciously strong results
body: A near-perfect score is a warning, not a celebration. On this file you can see why without building anything: every one of the four returned orders has a refund reason and all eight unreturned orders have none, so the rule that says if refund_reason is not empty then the order was returned gets 12 rows out of 12 right. A hundred percent on the training table, from a column that will be empty for every order you ever score.

The usual causes of a suspiciously strong result are the same four every time: a feature that is written after the outcome, duplicate identifiers shared across splits, a statistic computed over the full dataset, or a target column that is quietly part of the inputs. The checks are the same every time too. Take the score again with the suspect feature removed and see whether it collapses. Check for shared ids between training and evaluation. Check every feature for the moment it is written.

A lower honest score is worth more than a high dishonest one. The number you can defend is the one that would still be roughly true on orders from next month, when the refund_reason column is empty for every order you score and the feature cannot help at all. Record what you checked in your audit, because the person reading the report cannot see inside your pipeline, and an unexplained perfect score will be assumed to be a mistake.

quiz.question: What makes a column a leakage feature?
choices: A column with too many missing values
A column that is written after the outcome you are trying to predict, so it is not available at prediction time
A column measured in dollars rather than in ones
A column with a high number of distinct values
quiz.explanation: Leakage is a timing problem: the column exists, but only after the answer is known. refund_reason is written when an order comes back, so a model that reads it has been handed the target. Missing values, units and the number of distinct values are data quality questions, and none of them makes a column unavailable at prediction time.

quiz_bank.question: Why must a scaler be fitted on training rows only?

Because the mean and the spread it learns would then include information from the evaluation rows
Because StandardScaler cannot handle more than 100 rows

quiz_bank.explanation: A scaler learns a mean and a spread from the rows it is fitted on. If those come from all twelve orders, the four evaluation rows have already told the model their own average before the test, and the resulting score is optimistic. Fit on the development rows, then apply the stored mean and spread to the evaluation rows without refitting.

lessons.title: Predict a number with linear regression
lessons.goal: Fit a straight-line model that predicts a number, and read its error with MAE, MSE and R squared.

sections.heading: What a straight line can and cannot do
body: A linear regression predicts a number by adding up your features, each multiplied by a weight, plus a constant called the intercept. A feature is one column of your table and a weight is the number the model learns for that column. This is the dot product from the maths module, which you have already met as a way of turning a row of measurements into a single score. In the bundled houses file the features are size_sqm, bedrooms and location_score, and the target is price.

Here is the fitted model, taken from a least-squares fit on the first 12 houses: price = 4661.82 times size_sqm, minus 17239.04 times bedrooms, plus 8232.73 times location_score, minus 77001.34. To price a house of 80 square metres with 3 bedrooms and a location score of 3 you multiply and add: 4661.82 times 80 is 372945.45, 17239.04 times 3 is 51717.13, 8232.73 times 3 is 24698.18, and the intercept is 77001.34. The prediction is 372945.45 minus 51717.13 plus 24698.18 minus 77001.34, which is 268925.17.

A straight line through data is a starting point, not the answer. With three features the model is not even a line on the page: it is a flat surface in three dimensions, so it cannot bend, cannot peak, and cannot notice that size matters more in one location than in another. The negative weight on bedrooms is the first hint that a single flat surface is a simplification, because size and bedrooms move together in this table: their correlation across the 12 training houses is 0.96.

sections.heading: Fitting the line
body: Fitting means searching for the weights that make the model as close as possible to the prices you already have. For any candidate set of weights you predict a price for each of the 12 training houses, subtract each prediction from the real price, square each mistake, and add the squares up. The weights that give the smallest total are the fitted weights. Squaring is what makes a prediction that overshoots and one that undershoots by the same amount count equally, and it makes a mistake of 10000 count 100 times more than a mistake of 1000.

The numbers for this dataset make the tightness visible. The fitted weights are 4661.82 for size_sqm, minus 17239.04 for bedrooms, 8232.73 for location_score and minus 77001.34 for the intercept, and on the 12 houses it was fitted on the average mistake is 5664.75 and R squared is 0.9892. That looks wonderful, and it tells you almost nothing about new houses, because the model was scored on the very rows it was built from.

You do not have to derive those weights by hand. The LinearRegression class in scikit-learn does the search for you: you give it a table of features and a column of targets, call fit, and it stores the weights it found. A numpy least-squares call on a matrix with an extra column of ones does the same job. Whichever route you take, the column order of your features must match the order of the weights, and the beginner bug here is a sensible-looking score produced by a column read in the wrong order.

sections.heading: Read the error three ways
body: MAE, the mean absolute error, is the average size of the misses, keeping only their size and throwing away their direction. On the four houses held back for testing, the model's predictions were 370711.58, 398682.49, 401181.63 and 437385.26, and the real prices were 372000, 396000, 408000 and 448000. The four mistakes are 1288.42, 2682.49, 6818.37 and 10614.74; they add to 21404.02, and dividing by 4 gives an MAE of 5351.00. Because the mistakes keep the units of the target, you can say the model is off by about 5351 currency units on a typical house.

MSE, the mean squared error, squares every mistake before averaging. The same four mistakes squared are 1660028.81, 7195742.08, 46490213.17 and 112672638.23, which add to 168018622.28, and dividing by 4 gives 42004655.57. The square root of that, 6481.10, is the root mean squared error, which puts the number back into the units of the target. The point of squaring is that a large miss is punished hard: the mistake of 10614.74 contributes 112672638.23 of the 168 million, which is 67 percent of the total from one row out of four.

R squared answers a different question: how much of the movement in the target did the model explain? The four real prices have a mean of 406000, so they sit 34000 below it, 10000 below it, 2000 above it and 42000 above it; squaring those four gaps gives 1156000000, 100000000, 4000000 and 1764000000, which add to 3024000000. The model's squared mistakes add to 168018622.28, so R squared is 1 minus 168018622.28 divided by 3024000000, which is 0.9444. Read that as: on these four houses the model explained about 94 percent of the variation in price.

sections.heading: Predict a house price
body: Put the pieces together on the first held-back house, which has 102 square metres, 4 bedrooms, a location score of 5 and a real price of 372000. The model gives 4661.82 times 102, which is 475505.45, minus 17239.04 times 4, which is 68956.17, plus 8232.73 times 5, which is 41163.64, minus 77001.34, and the answer is 370711.58. The real price is 372000, so the mistake is 1288.42, which is about 0.3 percent of the price.

Is the model worth anything? Compare its MAE of 5351.00 with the simplest reference you can build. The average price of the 12 training houses is 231500, so predicting 231500 for every house gives four mistakes of 140500, 164500, 176500 and 216500, which average 174500. The fitted model cuts the average miss from 174500 to 5351, and its MAE is 1.3 percent of the average price of the four test houses.

Keep three cautions in your report. Four test houses is a very small sample, so the 0.9444 rests on thin evidence. The negative bedroom weight comes from size and bedrooms moving together in the training rows, so do not read it as more bedrooms making a house cheaper. And the model has only seen houses up to 96 square metres, so a prediction for a 200 square metre house is an extrapolation you should not trust.

quiz.question: What does MAE measure, and why is it in the units of the target?
choices: The average size of the prediction mistakes, in the same units as the target
The share of the variation in the target that the model explains
The average mistake after every mistake has been squared
The number of features the model used to make its prediction
quiz.explanation: MAE averages the absolute differences between predictions and real values, so it stays in the units of the target and you can say the model is off by about 5351 currency units on a typical house. The share of variation explained is R squared. The squared version is MSE, which is not in the target's units, and a feature count is not an error.

quiz_bank.explanation: MAE adds up the size of every mistake, so one huge miss and several small ones can reach the same total. The model is 40 percent better than predicting the average every time

quiz_bank.explanation: R squared compares the model's squared mistakes with the spread of the target around its own mean. A value of 0.4 means 40 percent of that spread was removed by the model and 60 percent was not. It is not an accuracy, and it is not measured against a baseline, so it does not say on its own how good the model is.

lessons.title: Predict a label with k-nearest neighbours
lessons.goal: Predict a label by looking at the most similar examples in the training data, and see how the choice of k changes the answer.

sections.heading: The idea in one sentence
body: A k-nearest neighbours model, usually shortened to KNN, learns nothing at all. To predict a new row it finds the rows in the training data that are closest to it, the neighbours, and answers with their answers. The letter k is how many neighbours you look at. For a label such as churned or stayed you take the label that appears most among the k neighbours, and for a price like the houses file you take the average of their prices.

Take a house of 80 square metres with 3 bedrooms and a location score of 3, and use the first 12 houses of data/houses.csv as the training data. With k = 1 the closest training house is the one with 78 square metres, 3 bedrooms and a location score of 3, priced at 258000, and the raw distance between them is 2 because only the size differs. The prediction is therefore exactly 258000.

With k = 5 the model looks at five houses: 78 square metres at 258000, 85 at 288000, 74 at 226000, 92 at 312000 and 64 at 214000. Their prices add to 1298000, and dividing by 5 gives 259600. Nothing was fitted and nothing was learned: the prediction is a lookup in the training table, and the only thing you chose was how many rows to read.

sections.heading: Distance needs comparable features
body: Closest has to be measured, and the usual measurement adds up the raw differences between columns. That works only when the columns sit on comparable scales. Across the 12 training houses the standard deviation of size_sqm is 15.53, while the standard deviation of bedrooms and the standard deviation of location_score are both 1.03, so a difference of 10 square metres counts ten times as much as a difference of one bedroom.

The fix is scaling, which turns each column into a spread of ones: subtract that column's mean and divide by its standard deviation, so a one-step change in any column means the same distance. On the example house above, scaling changed which rows were the five nearest. The raw five were the houses of 78, 85, 74, 88 and 70 square metres, and the scaled five were the houses of 78, 85, 74, 92 and 64 square metres.

That swap changed the number. Averaging the raw five prices gives 250800, and averaging the scaled five gives 259600, a difference of 8800 on a single prediction. The lesson is not that one neighbour set is wrong. It is that a choice as quiet as scaling changes your numbers, so the choice belongs in the report next to the score.

sections.heading: Choosing k
body: With k = 1 the model copies a single neighbour, so its prediction jumps from one row's price to the next with no smoothing, and one odd training row can decide the answer for a whole region of input space. With k = 5 the model averages, which is steadier. The second example house, 100 square metres with 4 bedrooms and a location score of 5, is predicted at 344000 when k = 1, because the nearest training house is the one of 96 square metres, and at 297600 when k = 5, the average of 344000, 288000, 312000, 258000 and 286000.

Push k to the far end and the model stops using the features at all. If k equals the number of training rows, every training house is a neighbour of every new house, so the prediction is always the average price of the 12 training houses, 231500, no matter what the new house looks like. A 60 square metre flat and a 200 square metre house would get the same answer.

So k = 1 is too jumpy and k = the whole training set is too smooth, and the useful range sits between them. With 16 houses in this file, values from 3 to 5 are a sensible place to start, and the right value is decided with evidence rather than taste: the cross-validation in the next lesson gives you a score for each k on the same rows.

sections.heading: Where it works and where it does not
body: The cost of KNN is that it keeps every training row and, for each prediction, measures the distance to every one of them. On the churn data with 24 training rows that costs nothing. With 500000 customers each single prediction becomes 500000 distance calculations, and the model needs an extra search structure to avoid computing all of them. KNN is easy to fit and expensive to serve.

KNN also fails in two specific ways. It cannot extrapolate: a house of 200 square metres, larger than anything in the training table, gets the price of the largest neighbours and never more, because every prediction is an average of prices that already exist. And it drowns in columns that do not matter: add 50 columns that say nothing about a house and the two useful columns lose their grip on which rows are near which.

One more warning: KNN memorises its training table, so scoring it on rows it has already seen flatters it badly. Always score it on rows it has not seen, and remember that a neighbour model has no weights to explain, which is its real cost when somebody asks why the model predicted that price.

quiz.question: How does a k-nearest neighbours model produce a prediction?
choices: By fitting a straight line through the training rows
By finding the k closest training rows and combining their answers
By averaging every value in the target column of the training data
By multiplying each feature by a weight learned from the target
quiz.explanation: KNN stores the training rows and, for a new row, finds the k nearest ones by distance. A label is taken as the majority among them and a number as their average, which is why the choice of k changes the answer. A straight line is a linear regression, and weights come from fitting, not from looking up neighbours.

quiz_bank.question: What happens to a k-nearest neighbours model when k equals the size of the whole training set?
choices: It becomes a linear regression with one weight per feature
It predicts the most common label of the training data
Every prediction becomes the average of the training targets, so the features stop mattering
It runs faster, because there is no distance left to compute
quiz_bank.explanation: With k equal to the number of training rows, every training row is a neighbour of every new row, so the answer is the average of the training targets whatever the new row contains. On the houses file that average price is 231500 for every house, however large. It is slower, not faster, and it is not a linear model.

lessons.title: Split your data and cross-validate
lessons.goal: Compare models on data they were not trained on, and use cross-validation to make a comparison you can trust.

sections.heading: Why one test set is fragile
body: A single split gives you one number from one arrangement of the rows, and on a small table the arrangement matters as much as the model. Take the churn data with 24 training rows and a model that is allowed to see only tenure_months, the number of months a customer has been with the company. Split the 24 rows into 17 for fitting and 7 for testing, five times with five different random choices of the 7 test rows, and the accuracy comes out 0.43, 0.57, 0.57, 0.71 and 0.43, while the F1 score comes out 0.33, 0.40, 0.40, 0.50 and 0.00.

The model and the data never changed. Only the rows held back changed, and the score moved from 0.00 to 0.50. In the run that scored 0.00 the model caught no churner at all: it flagged 2 of the 5 customers who did not churn and missed both of the 2 who did. In the run that scored 0.50 it caught 1 of the 2 churners and flagged 1 of the 5 who stayed, so it got 5 of 7 rows right. With 7 rows, one row is worth 14 percentage points of accuracy.

The baseline in those same five splits always answered 0 and always scored 0.7143, so in the run where the model managed 0.43 it was worse than doing nothing at all. Two teams can build the same model on the same data and publish different scores, with neither team making a mistake. The fix is not to be careful with one split. It is to let every row take a turn as the test row.

sections.heading: Cross-validation in plain words
body: Cross-validation takes turns. You divide the training rows into k groups, called folds, and then you fit the model k times. In each run one fold is kept back as the evaluation part while the other folds do the fitting, so with 5 folds on 24 rows the held-back group is 5 rows, 5 rows, 5 rows, 5 rows and 4 rows, and every one of the 24 rows is the evaluation row exactly once.

You then score each of the k runs and average the scores. On the churn data the logistic regression that uses both support_tickets and tenure_months scored an F1 of 1.00 on every one of the five folds, so its mean is 1.00 and its spread is 0.00. The model that saw only tenure_months scored 0.00, 0.00, 0.33, 0.33 and 0.00, a mean of 0.13 and a spread of 0.33.

Cross-validation is more work than one split, because you fit the model five times instead of once, and it is the reason your comparison can be trusted. It also gives every training row a job. The model is tested on rows it has not seen, and every row is used for testing once, so no row is wasted and no single row decides the result.

sections.heading: Use it for choices, keep the test set for the verdict
body: Give each job one tool. Cross-validation is for making choices: which features to use, which model family, which threshold. The fixed evaluation set is for the verdict, and you touch it once, after the choices are made. If you look at the evaluation score every time you try a new feature list, the evaluation set stops being a test and becomes part of your training loop.

The churn example shows the payoff. Cross-validation on the 24 training rows chose the model that uses both features, with a mean F1 of 1.00 against 0.13 for the tenure-only model. Scoring that chosen model once on the 12 rows of data/evaluation.csv gave 12 correct out of 12, an accuracy of 1.00 with precision 1.00, recall 1.00 and F1 1.00.

Both numbers are honest because the evaluation rows never entered the fitting or the choosing. If you had tried ten feature lists and kept the one with the best evaluation score, the 1.00 would no longer describe new customers. It would describe the 12 rows you kept looking at, and with 12 rows a single changed prediction moves accuracy by 8.3 percentage points.

sections.heading: Report the variation, not just the mean
body: A mean hides the thing you most need to know. The tenure-only model averaged 0.13 across five folds, but three of those folds were 0.00 and two were 0.33, so on three fifths of the data the model was worth nothing at all. If you report only the average, a reader cannot see that. The spread across folds, 0.33 from the lowest fold to the highest, is the information that says how much the score depends on which rows were held back.

The strong model has a spread of 0.00, which is the opposite warning: every fold gave 1.00, so the score looks completely stable. On 24 rows that is usually a sign that the problem is too easy rather than that the model is excellent, because support_tickets alone already separates the churners from the rest. A perfect score on a small table is a prompt to look for a simpler explanation, not a reason to ship.

So report the mean and the spread, and report how many rows are behind them. A cross-validated F1 of 1.00 with a spread of 0.00 over 5 folds of 24 rows is a very different claim from a mean of 0.13 with a spread of 0.33 over the same 5 folds of the same 24 rows. Both sentences are true, and only one of them lets a reader judge how much to trust the model.

quiz.question: What does cross-validation do that a single split does not?
choices: It uses every training row as the evaluation row once, so the score does not depend on one lucky split
It fits the model on more rows than a single split does
It removes the need for a fixed evaluation set
It guarantees that the model will score well on new data
quiz.explanation: With 5 folds on 24 rows, four folds hold back 5 rows and one holds back 4, and every row is tested once, so the score averages over all the arrangements instead of one. A single split on the same data gave F1 from 0.00 to 0.50 depending only on which rows were held back. Fitting on more rows and guaranteeing future performance are not what folds do.

quiz_bank.question: Which set should you never tune on?
choices: The fixed evaluation set
The training set
The fold that scored highest

quiz_bank.explanation: The evaluation set exists to give one honest number after the choices are made. If you use it to pick features, models or thresholds, it becomes training feedback and its score stops describing rows the model has not seen. The training set and the folds are exactly where tuning belongs, and the scaler is fitted on training rows only.

quiz_bank.question: Why report the spread of the fold scores and not only their average?
choices: Because the spread tells you how much the score depends on which rows were held back
Because the average is always wrong when the folds are small
Because the spread identifies which fold was the hardest

quiz_bank.explanation: The tenure-only model averaged 0.13 over five folds but scored 0.00 on three of them, and only the spread shows that. A high average with a wide spread is a risk that a single number hides. The average is not always wrong, the spread does not name the hardest fold, and publishing rules are not the reason.

lessons.title: Build a baseline before a model
lessons.goal: Compare a candidate model with a simple reference that exposes the value of learning from features.

sections.heading: A baseline makes performance interpretable
body: A baseline is the simplest thing you could do that still produces an answer, and it needs no learning at all. For a label the usual baseline is to predict the most common class every time, which scikit-learn calls a DummyClassifier. The bundled evaluation file holds 12 customers, 8 of whom did not churn and 4 of whom did, so a model that answers 0 for every row gets 8 of 12 right and scores 0.6667.

Now read that number next to a claim of 90 percent accuracy. A model that always says 0 on a table where 8 of 12 rows are 0 already has 66.67 percent accuracy before it has learned anything, so an accuracy figure on its own says nothing about whether the work paid off. This is why the report records the baseline score next to the model score: the gap between them is the part that belongs to your model.

There is a second reason, and it is the more important one. The baseline finds none of the 4 customers who churned, so its recall is 0.00 and a retention team working from it would do nothing at all. A score that hides this is worse than no score, because it looks like evidence. The same idea applies to the regression half of this project: predict the average price of the training houses, 231500, for every house you score.

sections.heading: Compare on the same held-out rows
body: Two numbers can only be compared when they were measured on the same thing. So the baseline and your model must both be scored on the same 12 rows of data/evaluation.csv, and both must be fitted without ever seeing those rows. If you scored the baseline on the 24 training rows and the model on the 12 evaluation rows, the two numbers would describe different data, and the difference would tell you about the rows rather than about the models.

The second rule follows from the first: the evaluation set is also off limits for fitting. A scaler fitted on all 36 rows, or an encoder that has already seen which categories exist, has learned something from the evaluation rows even though your classifier never saw their labels. The fix is in the next lesson, and the reason is that any number derived from the evaluation rows has to stay out of the training process.

Write down what you did so the comparison can be repeated: the rows used for fitting, the rows used for scoring, the rule that split them, the metrics you computed and the definitions of those metrics. In this project the split rule is simple and fixed, the first 24 customers are for fitting and the last 12 are for scoring, and the report records that as data_split = fixed_holdout.

sections.heading: Keep the baseline in the report
body: The report you paste into the submission form holds both numbers: baseline_accuracy 0.6667 and accuracy 1.00, which comes from 12 of 12 correct on the evaluation rows. A reviewer looks at three things. Is the baseline sensible for this data, which here it is, because the majority class really is 8 of the 12. Does the model beat it, which it does. And by how much, in the units of the decision, which is 4 churners caught that the baseline would have missed.

The same shape works for the regression half of the project. The baseline there predicts the average training price, 231500, for every house, and on the four held-back houses that produces an average error of 174500. The fitted linear regression produces an average error of 5351. Reporting both makes the claim checkable, because a reader can see that the model, and not the data, did the work.

A baseline also protects you from a bad surprise. If a carefully built model cannot beat the simplest reference, then something is wrong with the model, the features or the measurement, and the report should say so instead of hiding it behind a respectable-looking score. The baseline is a floor, and knowing your floor tells you how much of your score you actually earned.

quiz.question: Why compare a model against a baseline?
choices: Because a score only means something next to the simplest possible reference
Because the baseline is usually the model you will end up shipping
Because a model that beats a baseline is guaranteed to work on new data
Because accuracy cannot be computed without one
quiz.explanation: On the evaluation file, always answering 0 already scores 0.6667, so a model accuracy of 0.90 says only 0.23 more than doing nothing. The baseline shows what the data gives away for free, and the gap is what your model earned. Beating a baseline is not a guarantee, and accuracy can be computed without one.

The model will also score 0.85 on new data
The baseline was fitted badly and should be improved
The model and the baseline agree on 85 percent of the rows
quiz_bank.explanation: The gap between the two scores, 0.85 minus 0.50, is 0.35, so the model found 35 percentage points more than the simple reference on these rows. It says nothing about new data, and the baseline is not necessarily badly fitted, because its job is to be a sensible floor. Agreement between two models is a different measurement.

lessons.title: Keep preprocessing inside a pipeline
lessons.goal: Fit transformations only on training folds and keep inference behavior reproducible.

sections.heading: Preprocessing learns from data
body: Preprocessing is the work you do to a table before the model sees it, such as filling in missing values, turning words into columns, or putting numbers on a comparable scale. Each of those steps learns numbers from the rows it sees. A scaler learns a mean and a standard deviation, an imputer learns a median, and a one-hot encoder learns which categories exist. That is why they cannot be fitted once on everything and then left alone.

The numbers move very little here, which is exactly what makes the mistake dangerous. On the 24 training rows the mean number of support tickets is 2.125 and the standard deviation is 1.833. A scaler fitted on all 36 rows would use a mean of 2.111 and a standard deviation of 1.838, so the training rows would be transformed with values the 12 evaluation rows helped set. Nothing in the output looks wrong, and the evaluation score is quietly optimistic.

An encoder makes the same point more visibly. One-hot encoding turns a channel such as web, mobile or partner into three columns of ones and zeros, and to do that it has to know the list of channels. If a channel appears only in the evaluation rows, fitting the encoder on everything puts that channel into the vocabulary, and the model has been told something about the evaluation rows before it was scored on them.

sections.heading: Use a pipeline for mixed columns
body: A pipeline is an object that holds the preparation steps and the model together, so that one call fits everything in the right order. A ColumnTransformer is the part of a pipeline that handles mixed columns: you name the columns and give each group its own recipe, and it stacks the results into one table of numbers. In the orders table from the data module, order_total is numeric and channel is text with three values: web on 5 rows, mobile on 4 and partner on 3.

The recipe for order_total is an imputer followed by a scaler, because one total is missing and one is negative. The median of the 11 recorded totals is 29.99, so the missing order gets that value instead of a blank. The recipe for channel is a one-hot encoder, so a mobile order becomes one in the mobile column and zero in the web and partner columns. The classifier comes last, and nothing inside the pipeline is fitted until you call fit.

The order of the steps matters as much as the grouping. The imputer runs before the scaler, because the scaler needs a number in every cell, and the scaler runs before the classifier, because the classifier expects columns on a comparable scale. When the pipeline is fitted on training rows, every step learns its numbers from those rows only, and the same fitted object then scores new rows exactly as it scored the ones it trained on.

sections.heading: Save the whole inference path
body: Save the fitted pipeline, not just the model inside it. The model is a set of weights, and on its own it cannot do anything with a raw row. It needs the mean and the standard deviation that turn a ticket count into a scaled number, the median that fills a missing total, the list of channels that keeps the one-hot columns lined up, and the column order that says which number goes where.

If you keep only the model, one of two things happens. Either the code that loads it rebuilds the transformations by hand, in which case any small difference between that code and the original fit changes the prediction silently, or it cannot rebuild them at all and scoring new rows stops working. Neither failure announces itself, which is why it is worth saving one object that holds the whole path.

Record the other facts beside it: the feature names and their order, the library versions you used, and the metrics you measured, so that a reader can rebuild the same numbers. The report for this project records the feature list, the number of folds and the split rule for exactly this reason, and a saved pipeline plus those notes is enough for somebody else to repeat your work.

quiz.question: Why must a scaler be fitted inside a pipeline rather than before it?
choices: Because the scaler learns a mean and a spread from the rows it sees, and inside the pipeline each training fold learns its own
Because a scaler cannot be used together with a classifier
Because fitting a scaler first always makes the model slower
Because a scaler fitted first will always produce a perfect fit
quiz.explanation: The mean and the standard deviation are numbers learned from data, so fitting the scaler once on all 36 rows lets the 12 evaluation rows influence the training. Inside the pipeline each training fold fits its own scaler, and that fitted scaler is then applied unchanged to the rows being scored. The other three choices describe effects that do not happen.

It does not copy the target, it has nothing to do with the number of folds, and wrapping the model into a pipeline is the Pipeline's job.

quiz_bank.explanation: The scaler, the imputer and the encoder hold numbers the model depends on, such as the mean of 2.125 and the standard deviation of 1.833 for support tickets. Saving only the classifier loses them, so a raw row cannot be prepared in the same way. File size, joblib's abilities and retraining are not the reason.

lessons.title: Measure model quality for the decision
lessons.goal: Select metrics that reflect the costs and consequences of model errors.

sections.heading: Read the confusion matrix
body: A confusion matrix is a 2 by 2 table that counts what a classifier did with four kinds of row. For the churn problem the positive class is the customer who churned within 30 days. On the 12 rows of data/evaluation.csv, the model that uses support_tickets and tenure_months put 8 non-churners in the negative column and 4 churners in the positive column, and made no mistakes at all, so the table holds 8 true negatives, 0 false positives, 0 false negatives and 4 true positives.

The four cells are easier to remember as sentences. A true positive is a customer who really churned and you flagged, which is the cell you want to fill. A false positive is a customer who stayed and you flagged anyway, the wasted call. A false negative is a customer who churned and you did not flag, the missed save. A true negative is a customer who stayed and you left alone.

Read the table as a cost, not as a score. On this data the model produced 4 useful flags and 0 wasted ones, so a retention team would spend 4 calls and catch 4 churners. A model with 4 true positives and 3 false positives would spend 7 calls to catch the same 4, and that difference in work is what your threshold and your metric are really about.

sections.heading: Use metrics with clear meanings
body: Every metric is arithmetic on those four cells. Accuracy is true positives plus true negatives over all rows, which here is (4 + 8) / 12 = 1.00. Precision is true positives over everything you flagged, which is 4 / (4 + 0) = 1.00. Recall is true positives over everything that really churned, which is 4 / (4 + 0) = 1.00. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which is 2 times 1 times 1 divided by 1 plus 1, so 1.00.

The sentence each one means in a report is worth writing down. Accuracy says 12 of the 12 customers were labelled correctly. Precision says of the customers you would call, all 4 really churned. Recall says of the 4 customers who really churned, you found all 4. F1 says one number that balances precision and recall, and it is the one to quote when you cannot say which of the two matters more to the decision.

The same arithmetic on the baseline makes the point. Always predicting 0 gives accuracy (0 + 8) / 12 = 0.6667 and recall 0 / (0 + 4) = 0.00, and precision is not defined because the baseline flags nobody. The orders table from the data module shows the other trap: 4 of its 12 orders were returned, so a model that always says no also scores 0.6667 accuracy while catching nothing at all.

sections.heading: Report the threshold
body: A classifier that outputs a probability does not decide anything by itself. The threshold is the number you compare that probability against, and turning a score into a label is a decision you own, because it encodes what a false positive costs you. On the 24 churn training rows, using out-of-fold predictions so that each row is scored by a model that did not train on it, a threshold of 0.3 gave 8 true positives and 3 false positives, while a threshold of 0.5 gave 8 true positives and 0 false positives.

The model did not change between those two lines, only the threshold, and precision moved from 8 / 11 = 0.73 to 8 / 8 = 1.00 while recall stayed at 1.00. Push the threshold up to 0.8 and the picture changes again: 4 true positives and 4 false negatives, so recall falls to 4 / 8 = 0.50 and F1 falls to 0.67. The same model, the same data, three different reports.

Choose the threshold on validation data and never on the fixed evaluation set, then apply the chosen threshold once to the evaluation rows and report it next to the metrics. A report that gives precision and recall without the threshold is incomplete, because a reader cannot tell whether you were strict or generous without knowing where you drew the line.

quiz.question: In a confusion matrix, what does a false positive mean?
choices: A row that was really negative was labelled positive, a false alarm
A row that was really positive was labelled negative, a missed case
A row that was labelled correctly but with a low probability
A positive row that the model gave a high score to
quiz.explanation: A false positive counts the rows where the truth was negative and your model said positive, so they are wasted calls. A missed case is a false negative. A correct label is a true positive or a true negative, and a high score on a row that was labelled correctly is not an error at all.

Recall
Accuracy

Precision is the one that answers the question about your flagged list.

Because the threshold changes the training data
Because a model cannot produce a probability without one
Because the machine learning library sets the threshold, not you
quiz_bank.explanation: On the churn training rows a threshold of 0.3 gave precision 0.73 and recall 1.00, while 0.8 gave precision 1.00 and recall 0.50, with no change to the model. Where you cut decides how many calls you make and how many churners you catch. The threshold does not change the data, the model produces scores without one, and you choose it.

lessons.title: Validate, compare, and read probabilities carefully
lessons.goal: Estimate variation, make fair model comparisons, and interpret predicted probabilities carefully.

sections.heading: Use cross-validation for model choices
body: When you compare two models, the only thing that should differ is the model. If one model is scored on one split and the other on another, the gap between the scores measures the split as much as it measures the model. Cross-validation removes that problem by giving every candidate the same folds: on the churn data with 24 training rows, 5 folds hold back 5 rows, 5 rows, 5 rows, 5 rows and 4 rows in turn, and every model sees the same five evaluation slices.

The comparison on this data is instructive rather than exciting. A logistic regression on both features and a decision tree of depth 3 both scored an F1 of 1.00 on every fold, so the mean is 1.00 and the spread is 0.00 for each, and the data cannot tell them apart. A logistic regression allowed to see only tenure_months scored 0.00, 0.00, 0.33, 0.33 and 0.00, a mean of 0.13 and a spread of 0.33.

A tie is information too. It tells you that on this data the choice between those two model families does not matter, so you should pick on cost, on speed or on explainability. It also tells you to look again at the data, because support_tickets alone already separates every churner from every stayer, which is a sign that the exercise is easy rather than that your model is brilliant.

sections.heading: Do not tune on the test set
body: Every look at the evaluation set during development is a small leak. Try three feature sets, keep the one with the best evaluation accuracy, and you have used the evaluation rows to make a choice, so the final score no longer describes rows the model has not seen. This is easy to do by accident, because checking the score is the fastest way to know whether a change helped, and the evaluation file is right there.

The numbers make the cost concrete. The evaluation file has 12 rows, so one changed prediction moves accuracy by 8.3 percentage points, and it holds only 4 churners, so one churner is a quarter of everything you could catch. Any model selection done on those rows is working with a very small and very precious number, and repeated selection quietly turns the file into training data.

The same rule protects you from a subtler leak. In this bundled churn table the column cancelled_after_snapshot is 1 for exactly the rows that churn and 0 for exactly the rows that did not, in the training rows and in the evaluation rows alike, so a model that is allowed to use it will look perfect while learning nothing about customers. It is information from after the prediction moment, and the report records it as a leakage feature that must stay out.

sections.heading: A score is not automatically a probability
body: A model that outputs 0.9 is claiming a score, not a 90 percent chance, unless somebody has checked. On the 12 evaluation rows the honest churn model gave an average score of 0.367, while the observed churn rate is 4 / 12 = 0.333, so the model is slightly pessimistic about the average customer. The gap is small here, and it is exactly the kind of gap that grows on real data.

Look closer and the model is doing well. The 8 customers it scored below 0.40 averaged 0.114 and none of them churned, and the 4 it scored between 0.79 and 0.94 averaged 0.872 and all 4 churned. Customer E003 was scored 0.266 and did not churn, and E009 was scored 0.820 and did. Calibration means comparing the average score in each band of scores with the rate you actually observe in that band.

This matters because people act on the number. A retention manager told that an account has a 90 percent chance of leaving will spend real money on a save offer, and if the scores are too high that budget goes to accounts that were never going to leave. If the scores are too low, real churners are ignored. So check the bands, and if the model is badly off, calibrate it on data it was not fitted on before you let anybody act on its numbers.

quiz.question: Why must two models be compared on the same folds?
choices: So that the difference you see comes from the models and not from the rows that were held back
So that both models take the same time to fit
So that the fold scores can be averaged
So that the evaluation set is used more often
quiz.explanation: Cross-validation gives every candidate the same five evaluation slices, so a gap in the scores is a property of the models. With different slices the gap measures the split, which is how a tenure-only model produced F1 scores from 0.00 to 0.50 on the same 24 rows. Averaging is what you do with the scores afterwards, and using the evaluation set more often is the mistake to avoid.
