lessons.title: What a classifier does
lessons.goal: Explain what a classification model produces, how a probability becomes a label, and where classification fits in a product.

sections.heading: A label, not a number
body: A classification model does not output a continuous value like a regression model. Instead it produces one of a fixed set of labels. In the spam problem the labels are spam and not-spam, and the model must pick one of those two for every email. This distinction matters because a user needs to take action based on the label, not admire a decimal number.

sections.heading: Scores become labels at a threshold
body: A classifier first produces a score, a raw number that reflects how strong the evidence is. Choosing a threshold turns that score into a label: above the threshold becomes spam, below becomes not-spam. If the threshold is 0.5 an email with probability 0.6 is flagged as spam, while 0.4 is not. The trainer chooses the threshold based on which error is more costly.

sections.heading: Labels need to be right in the data
body: A model can only learn from the labels you give it. If an email is truly spam but labelled not-spam, the model will learn the wrong rule. Noisy or inconsistent labels mean the model may learn patterns that do not reflect reality, and its predictions will be wrong in ways that are hard to diagnose later.

sections.heading: What good looks like
body: A first spam filter will be wrong often. The goal is not to be right every time but to be wrong in the cheapest direction. If a spam email gets through it may cost the provider in lost trust; if a real email is hidden it costs the user time to retrieve it. A good first model minimises the more expensive error.

quiz.question: What does a classification model output before you choose a threshold?
choices: A continuous regression value
One of a fixed set of labels
A probability between 0 and 1
A confusion matrix
quiz.explanation: A classifier produces a raw score or probability between 0 and 1 before a threshold is applied. That score is then compared to the threshold to decide which label the email receives.

lessons.task: Write down the two labels you would use for the bundled email dataset, state which one your business cares about more, and pick a threshold you would start with and explain why.

A probability between 0 and 1
A confusion matrix
quiz_bank.explanation: A classifier produces a raw score or probability between 0 and 1 before a threshold is applied. That score is then compared to the threshold to decide which label the email receives.

quiz_bank.question: Why does the order of your labels in the data not change the model?
choices: Because the model always predicts the first label
Because swapping label names does not change the model's decisions, only how we read them
Because the data contains only one label per email
Because the model ignores the label column
quiz_bank.explanation: The model learns from the pattern of features, not from which string is called spam. If you swap the label names the model's predictions stay exactly the same; only the human-readable output changes.

quiz_bank.question: Which direction of error costs a mail provider more: a spam email that gets through, or a real email that is hidden?
choices: A spam email that gets through costs more, because the provider loses trust and users see unwanted content
A real email that is hidden costs more, because the user must spend time retrieving it
Both cost exactly the same, so the threshold does not matter
Neither costs anything in a well-trained model
quiz_bank.explanation: A spam email that reaches the inbox erodes user trust and increases abuse reports, which is typically more costly for a provider than a legitimate email being sent to spam, which the user can retrieve in seconds.

lessons.title: Logistic regression: a score that becomes a label
lessons.goal: Train a logistic regression classifier and explain how its weights turn feature values into a probability.

sections.heading: A weighted sum, then a squeeze
body: Logistic regression begins with a weighted sum of the features: each column of the email is multiplied by a learned weight and all those products are added together. The squeeze is the logistic (or sigmoid) function that pushes that sum between 0 and 1, producing a probability. If the weighted sum is large and positive the probability approaches 1 (spam); if it is large and negative the probability approaches 0 (not-spam).

sections.heading: Fitting the weights
body: The weights are chosen so that the model's predicted probabilities match the true labels in the training data. Scikit-learn searches for weights that make wrong predictions expensive, using an optimisation algorithm that adjusts each weight slightly until the loss stops decreasing. The process is automatic once you provide the feature matrix and the label vector.

sections.heading: Reading the coefficient
body: A coefficient tells you how a one-unit change in a feature moves the probability. A positive coefficient pushes the probability toward spam, a negative one toward not-spam. The size of the coefficient depends on the units of the feature: a coefficient of 0.5 on a word-count feature means each additional occurrence of that word increases the spam probability by a measurable amount, but the same coefficient on a feature measured in dollars would have a very different effect.

sections.heading: Where it works well
body: Logistic regression is fast to train, makes few assumptions about the data, and produces a readable set of coefficients. Its main weakness is that it can only draw straight-line boundaries in feature space, so it cannot capture complex interactions unless features are engineered. For many text problems a bag-of-words representation with logistic regression provides a strong first baseline.

quiz.question: What does the logistic regression model do to the weighted sum of features?
choices: It leaves the sum unchanged
It clamps the sum to between -1 and 1
It squeezes the sum between 0 and 1 using the logistic (sigmoid) function
It subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation
quiz.explanation: The logistic (sigmoid) function takes any real-valued number and pushes it into the range (0, 1), producing a probability that can be compared to a threshold to produce a label.

It clamps the sum to between -1 and 1

It subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation
quiz_bank.explanation: The logistic (sigmoid) function takes any real-valued number and pushes it into the range (0, 1), producing a probability that can be compared to a threshold to produce a label.

quiz_bank.question: What does a large positive coefficient for a word tell you?
choices: The word never appears in spam emails
The word pushes the probability toward the spam class
The word must be removed before training
The coefficient must be negative for the model to work
quiz_bank.explanation: A positive coefficient means that as that feature increases, the weighted sum grows, and after the squeeze the probability moves toward 1 (spam). The word is therefore indicative of the spam class.

quiz_bank.question: Why is logistic regression usually a good first classifier?
choices: It is guaranteed to achieve 100 percent accuracy
It is fast to train, makes few assumptions, and produces readable coefficients
It can capture any non-linear boundary without feature engineering
It does not require any labelled data
quiz_bank.explanation: It trains quickly, does not require heavy tuning assumptions, and the learned coefficients tell you which features push the prediction toward each class, which is useful for understanding and debugging.

lessons.title: k-nearest neighbours for labels
lessons.goal: Classify a new example by the labels of its nearest neighbours, and see how the choice of k changes the answer.

sections.heading: The idea in one sentence
body: k-nearest neighbours classifies a new email by looking at the k training emails most similar to it and assigning the most common label among those neighbours. If k=1 the new email takes the label of its single closest neighbour; if k=7 it takes the majority vote of its seven closest neighbours.

sections.heading: Turning text into something you can measure
body: Distance cannot be computed on raw text directly, so each email is turned into a vector of numbers. A simple approach is counting how many times each word appears, which gives a sparse vector that can be compared using Euclidean distance or cosine similarity. Without this step no distance metric can operate on the text.

sections.heading: Choosing k
body: A small k makes the model flexible and likely to overfit, because a single outlier neighbour can change the prediction. A large k makes the model more conservative and likely to underfit, because the majority vote smooths over local patterns. The choice of k trades off bias against variance, and the optimal k is typically found by cross-validation on a held-out set.

sections.heading: Its limits
body: k-nearest neighbours stores every training example, so prediction time grows with the size of the training set. Irrelevant or noisy features can dominate the distance calculation, making all examples appear equally distant. The method also struggles when the feature space has many dimensions relative to the number of training examples.

quiz.question: How does a k-nearest neighbours classifier choose a label?
choices: It computes the weighted average of all training labels
It looks at the k training examples closest to the new example and takes the majority vote of their labels
It uses the label of the single farthest training example
It randomises between all labels present in the training set
quiz.explanation: The k-nearest neighbours rule assigns the new example the most common label among its k closest training neighbours, breaking ties arbitrarily or by distance.

It randomises between all labels present in the training set
quiz_bank.explanation: The k-nearest neighbours rule assigns the new example the most common label among its k closest training neighbours, breaking ties arbitrarily or by distance.

quiz_bank.question: Why do we count words before using distance on text?
choices: So that the text can be stored in a database
So that each email has the same number of characters
So that each email can be represented as a vector of numbers that distance metrics can operate on
So that the model trains faster
quiz_bank.explanation: Distance metrics work on numbers, not on raw strings. Counting words produces a vector where each entry represents how often a word appears, enabling distance computations such as Euclidean or cosine distance.

quiz_bank.question: What happens to a k-nearest neighbours model when the training set grows?
choices: The model becomes faster at prediction time
The model becomes more likely to overfit
The prediction time grows because every training example must be examined
The model automatically reduces the value of k
quiz_bank.explanation: In k-nearest neighbours every training example must be compared to the new example at prediction time, so a larger training set means more distance computations and slower predictions.

lessons.title: Decision trees: rules you can read
lessons.goal: Train a decision tree and read it as a set of if-then rules that a person could follow.

sections.heading: A tree of questions
body: A decision tree is a hierarchical structure of questions about the feature values. Starting at the root the tree asks a question such as 'does the word free appear in the subject?' and follows the 'yes' or 'no' branch depending on the answer. Each internal node is a question and each leaf node carries a label, so traversing the tree from root to leaf produces a sequence of decisions that ends with a predicted class.

sections.heading: How the tree chooses its questions
body: At each node the tree evaluates many possible questions and picks the one that separates the labels most usefully. The measure of usefulness is typically information gain or Gini impurity: the question that reduces impurity the most is chosen. In the spam problem the tree might first ask whether the word 'free' appears, because that split separates most of the spam emails from the normal ones.

sections.heading: Reading a tree without over-trusting it
body: A printed tree can be followed as a set of if-then rules, which is useful for explanation. But a fully grown tree may memorise the training data, including noise and idiosyncrasies that will not appear in new emails. Pruning, limiting depth, or requiring a minimum number of examples per leaf are techniques that prevent the tree from becoming too specific to the training set.

sections.heading: When a tree is a good choice
body: Decision trees handle mixed data types naturally, can work with missing values, and produce rules that are easy for a non-expert to understand. They are a good first choice when interpretability matters. The risk is overfitting: a deep tree can achieve perfect training accuracy while generalising poorly to new emails.

quiz.question: What does each question in a decision tree do?
choices: It selects the next branch to follow, leading to another question or a leaf label
It computes the probability of the spam class
It averages the feature values in the subtree
It decides the learning rate for the subtree
quiz.explanation: Each internal node asks a question about a feature value. The answer directs you to the left or right branch, and you continue until you reach a leaf node that carries the predicted label.

quiz_bank.question: Why can a deep decision tree memorise the training data?

quiz_bank.question: Give one situation where a decision tree is a better fit than logistic regression.
choices: When the relationship between features and the label is perfectly linear

When the number of features exceeds the number of training examples
quiz_bank.explanation: Decision trees handle mixed data types natively, can work with missing values, and produce if-then rules that are easy for a person to read, unlike logistic regression which assumes a linear boundary and requires feature engineering for non-linear patterns.

lessons.title: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix
lessons.goal: Compute the four standard classification metrics from a confusion matrix and choose the one that matches the decision.

sections.heading: The four cells
body: A confusion matrix for the spam problem has four entries. True positives (TP) are spam emails correctly labelled as spam. False positives (FP) are normal emails wrongly labelled as spam. True negatives (TN) are normal emails correctly labelled as not-spam. False negatives (FN) are spam emails wrongly labelled as not-spam. In matrix form the rows are the actual labels and the columns are the predicted labels.

sections.heading: Accuracy: the simple one
body: Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct: (TP + TN) divided by all predictions. It misleads when one class is rare: if 95 out of 100 emails are normal and the model predicts 'not-spam' for every email, accuracy is 95 percent even though the model never detects spam.

sections.heading: Precision and recall: the useful pair
body: Precision is the fraction of predicted spam that are actually spam: TP divided by (TP + FP). Recall is the fraction of actual spam that were caught: TP divided by (TP + FN). The two questions use different denominators, so they can be very different numbers for the same model. In a spam filter precision asks 'of the emails we flagged as spam, how many were really spam?' and recall asks 'of all the spam emails, how many did we catch?'

sections.heading: F1 and the cost of errors
body: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, the harmonic mean being 2 divided by (1 divided by precision plus 1 divided by recall). It gives a single number that balances both concerns. In a spam filter you might deliberately accept more false positives to catch more spam, which raises recall at the expense of precision, and the F1 score reflects that trade-off.

quiz.question: A classifier flags 100 emails and 90 of them really are spam. What is its precision?
choices: 90 percent
10 percent
90 out of the total email count
Cannot be determined from this information alone
quiz.explanation: Precision is TP divided by (TP + FP). Here 90 out of the 100 flagged emails are spam, so precision is 90 percent.

quiz_bank.explanation: Recall is TP divided by (TP + FN). The classifier caught 120 spam, and there are 200 spam in total, so recall is 120 divided by 200, which is 60 percent.

quiz_bank.explanation: If 95 out of 100 emails are normal and the model predicts 'not-spam' for every email, accuracy is 95 percent even though the model never detects spam. Accuracy does not reveal whether the rare class is being modelled correctly.

lessons.title: What unsupervised learning is for
lessons.goal: Explain the difference between a labelled problem and an unlabelled one, and name three situations where you would cluster data.

sections.heading: No labels, just rows
body: A dataset is a table of rows and columns. In a supervised problem, each row already carries a label — such as 'spam' or 'not spam' — so the model learns to predict that label from the other columns. An unsupervised problem has no such label column. The rows are present, and the feature values are present, but nobody has marked which group each row belongs to. A cluster is a group of rows that are similar to one another across their feature columns. The learner discovers the clusters; the meaning of the clusters comes later.

This is the core idea of unsupervised learning: find structure in data that has no pre-assigned answers. The bundled pixels.csv data has 144 rows, each with red, green and blue values plus x and y position. If you ask Python to group the rows without telling it that the image has a blue top, a red middle and a green bottom, the algorithm will find some grouping. The question is whether those groups make sense to a human.

sections.heading: Three real uses
body: Image colour segmentation groups pixels by similar colours, so a 12 by 12 image can be split into a blue band, a red block and a green band. Customer grouping clusters shoppers by purchasing behaviour, so a business can offer different promotions to each segment. Document grouping organizes articles by topic, so a search engine can show related pieces together. All three situations start with a table of rows and no label column, and the clustering step reveals groups that a human must then interpret.

The pixels.csv data is a concrete example: 144 pixels from a synthetic image, with red green blue values and position coordinates. Running k-means on those 144 rows without knowing the true region labels will produce groups that a human can compare to the top-middle-bottom layout. The method works the same way for customer data or text documents, except the features are purchase counts or word frequencies instead of colour values.

sections.heading: The catch: you decide what a group means
body: Without labels, the meaning of a cluster comes from your interpretation, and a cluster is not automatically a useful segment. The algorithm only knows distance; it does not know that one group represents 'customers who buy expensive items' and another represents 'customers who rarely purchase'. That interpretation is up to you, and different people may assign different meanings to the same groups.

A cluster that is mixed — containing pixels from blue, red and green regions all in one group — is less useful than a cluster that contains pixels from only one true region. The algorithm minimizes distance within groups, but it does not maximize separation between groups unless you guide it. Always check what each group contains before you claim it has a meaningful interpretation.

sections.heading: How you will know it worked
body: A cluster is useful when it is stable, separated, and you can say something actionable about it. Stable means that if you ran the algorithm again with a slightly different start, you get similar groups. Separated means that the groups are distinct from one another, not overlapping heavily. Actionable means that you can name the group in a way that helps a decision, such as 'these customers are high-value' or 'these pixels are the blue sky'.

In the pixels case, you would check whether each cluster maps primarily to one of the three true regions: top band, middle red block, or bottom green band. If a cluster contains roughly 48 pixels and they are all similar blue values, that cluster is useful. If a cluster mixes red and green pixels, it does not help anyone make a decision.

quiz.question: What makes a problem unsupervised rather than supervised?
choices: The dataset has no rows, only columns.
The dataset has no label column and no pre-assigned answers.

lessons.title: k-means clustering, step by step
lessons.goal: Run the k-means algorithm by hand on a small example and explain each of its four steps.

sections.heading: Pick k starting points
body: The k-means algorithm begins by placing k initial centres, which are called centroids. The number k is how many groups the algorithm will find, and you must choose it before the run begins. A bad choice of starting points can lead to a poor final arrangement, because the centroids may start in a region where the algorithm converges to a locally optimal solution rather than the best overall one. That is why practitioners often run k-means many times with different starts and keep the best result.

In the pixels data, if we set k = 3, we would place three initial centroids somewhere in the feature space. One common method is to pick k rows at random from the data and use their r g b values as the starting centres. With 144 pixels and k = 3, there are many possible starting configurations, and the choice matters for the final answer.

sections.heading: Assign each point to its nearest centre
body: Once the k centroids are placed, each row in the dataset is assigned to the centroid that is closest in distance. The most common distance measure in k-means is Euclidean distance: the square root of the summed squared differences across all feature columns. For the pixels data, the features are r, g and b, so the distance between one pixel and a centroid is the square root of the squared differences of those three colour values.

If a pixel has r = 30, g = 82, b = 195 and a centroid has r = 28, g = 85, b = 192, the squared differences are (30-28)² = 4, (82-85)² = 9 and (195-192)² = 9, which adds to 22, and the square root of 22 is about 4.7. The pixel is assigned to the centroid with the smallest such distance. This assignment step is repeated for all 144 rows.

sections.heading: Move each centre to the middle of its group
body: After all rows are assigned, each centroid moves to the mean (the average) of the rows that were assigned to it. This is the step that gives k-means its name: the k refers to the number of clusters, and means refers to the arithmetic mean of the assigned points. For the pixels data, if three pixels with r values 30, 31 and 29 are assigned to one centroid, the new r value for that centroid is (30 + 31 + 29) divided by 3, which is 30.

The centroid moves toward the centre of its group, and the groups slowly shift as centroids move. This is why the algorithm is iterative: the new centroid positions change the distances for the next assignment step, which can move more rows, which changes the centroids again.

sections.heading: Repeat until nothing moves
body: The algorithm repeats the assignment and update steps until the centroids stop moving, or until the change is smaller than a very small threshold. When the centroids no longer move, the algorithm has converged. The risk is converging to a poor arrangement, especially if the starting points were not well chosen. Running the algorithm multiple times with different random starts and comparing the results is a common practice.

In the pixels data with k = 3 and three true regions (blue top, red middle, green bottom), the algorithm will typically find centroids that are near the average r g b values of each region. If the blue region has average r about 28, g about 82, b about 193, the centroid for that cluster will have those average values — assuming the algorithm converges to a good arrangement.

quiz.explanation: The four steps are: 1) Pick k starting points (centroids). 2) Assign each point to its nearest centre. 3) Move each centre to the mean of its group. 4) Repeat until the centroids stop moving. This is the standard k-means loop.

lessons.title: Choosing how many groups
lessons.goal: Choose a number of clusters with evidence from the data instead of a guess, and report the trade-off.

sections.heading: More groups always fits better
body: If you increase k, the within-group spread can only decrease or stay the same, because each point has more centres to choose from when finding its nearest centroid. With k = 144 (one cluster per row), the algorithm could assign each row to its own centroid and the within-group spread would be zero. A perfect fit with enough groups means nothing; it is simply overfitting to the quirks of the individual rows rather than finding meaningful structure.

The pixels data has 144 rows. If you run k-means with k = 3, each cluster contains about 48 pixels and the within-group spread is some positive number. If you run with k = 144, every pixel is its own cluster and the spread is zero, but you have not found three colour regions — you have simply labelled each pixel uniquely.

sections.heading: The elbow
body: The elbow method plots the within-group spread (also called inertia or total within-cluster sum of squared distance) against the number of clusters k. As k grows, the spread drops. The elbow is the point where the rate of decrease slows down markedly — the plot bends like an elbow. Choosing k at the elbow gives a good trade-off: adding more groups reduces the spread only a little, so the extra complexity is not justified by the gain.

In the pixels data, running k-means for k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and recording the within-group spread would show a sharp drop from k = 1 to k = 3, because three groups capture the blue top, red middle and green bottom. Going from k = 3 to k = 4 gives a much smaller reduction in spread, so the elbow is often at k = 3 for this dataset.

sections.heading: The silhouette score
body: The silhouette score measures how well separated each point is from its own group compared with the next group. For one point, the silhouette width is (distance to next group minus distance to own group) divided by the larger of those two distances. The width ranges from -1 to 1: a high value means the point is very close to its own group and far from the next group, so the clustering is doing a good job. The average silhouette score across all points summarizes the overall quality for a given k.

For the pixels data with k = 3, the blue pixels would have high silhouette scores because they are far from the red and green groups. Red pixels would also score well, and green pixels would as well. If k were set to 4 or higher, some groups would be very small or mixed, and the average silhouette score would drop, signaling that the extra group is not well supported by the data.

sections.heading: Choose and justify
body: To choose k with the elbow method or silhouette score, record the metric for each k value you test, plot the results, and look for the elbow or the highest average silhouette. Then write down the k you would use and the sentence you would use to defend it. The defence must appeal to the data, not to personal preference. For the pixels data, k = 3 is supported because the within-group spread drops sharply from k = 2 to k = 3 and then slows, and the average silhouette score is highest at k = 3.

Checking stability is also wise: run k-means a few times with different random starts for your chosen k and see whether the groups are similar each time. If the groups change wildly, the chosen k may not be reliable. For the pixels data with k = 3, you would expect the three clusters to map cleanly to the blue top, red middle and green bottom regions across multiple runs; if the cluster labels flip-flop between runs, the grouping is not stable and you should reconsider your k.

choices: Because each centroid can move to a more precise location with more groups.

Because the algorithm runs faster with larger k.

quiz.explanation: With more clusters, every row has more centroids to compare its distance to, so the nearest centroid is always at least as close as it was with fewer centroids. This means the within-group distance for each row can only decrease or stay the same, and the total spread drops.

lessons.title: Look at and read your clusters
lessons.goal: Visualise a clustering result and describe it without overclaiming what the algorithm found.

sections.heading: Draw the clusters
body: Visualising clusters helps you see what the algorithm found. A simple scatter plot can show each row as a point, coloured by its cluster label. For the pixels data, the three features r, g and b are colour values, and the x and y coordinates give the pixel position. A plot of x versus y coloured by cluster label will show the three true regions as horizontal bands: blue at the top, red in the middle, green at the bottom. If the algorithm found different groups, the plot would show those groups in the same coordinate system.

To make the plot readable, use clear colours, a legend that shows which label corresponds to which colour, and enough white space that the points do not run together. Avoid plotting all 144 points in a way that makes the image unreadable; a 12 by 12 grid with colour-coded cells is one effective approach.

sections.heading: Describe each group
body: After plotting, describe each group in words. Give the average r, g and b values for the group, and name how many pixels it contains. For example, a group might have average r = 28, g = 82, b = 193 and contain 48 pixels — that colour profile matches the blue band at the top of the image. Another group might have average r = 201, g = 45, b = 42 and contain 48 pixels — that matches the red middle block. Always ground your description in concrete numbers from the data.

Describing groups with average colour values is especially intuitive for the pixels data, because the three regions have very different colour profiles. The blue band has relatively low red values and relatively high green and blue values. The red middle has high red values and low green and blue values. The green bottom has moderate red values, high green values and moderate blue values.

sections.heading: The label problem
body: Cluster numbers are arbitrary: if you ran k-means twice with different random starts, the cluster labelled 0 in the first run might be labelled 1 or 2 in the second run. The algorithm does not guarantee that cluster 0 means the same thing across runs. This is why you should name groups by their characteristics — such as 'the blue group' or 'the red group' — rather than by their assigned number.

If you say 'cluster 0 is blue', a reader might think that cluster 0 is always blue, but another run could label the blue group as cluster 1. Naming groups by what they contain — 'the group with average r = 28, g = 82, b = 193' — survives a rerun of the algorithm.

sections.heading: What you may claim
body: You may claim that the data has structure that this method found, but you may not claim that you discovered the absolute truth about the data. The algorithm found groups that are useful for the purpose at hand, and a different method or a different k might find different groups. State what the data shows, not what the algorithm proved.

An honest summary for the pixels data would be: 'k-means with k = 3 found three groups of 48 pixels each. The groups have distinct average colours, matching the blue top, red middle and green bottom of the original image.' You can say the method found structure, but you cannot say that the groups are the only possible ones or that no other method could find others.

One run may place a blue-centroid at label 0, another at label 1. The numbers are not intrinsic to the data; the group characteristics are what matter.

lessons.title: Fewer columns with PCA
lessons.goal: Reduce many features to a few combined features with PCA, and judge how much information was kept.

sections.heading: Why squeeze the columns
body: Having many features slows down computation and makes plots harder to draw. If you have 50 features, plotting all pairs is impossible. Reducing the number of features speeds up the code, makes visualisations possible, and can remove noisy columns that do not carry signal. In practice, you often reduce a dataset to two or three principal components so you can draw a 2D or 3D plot.

The pixels data has three feature columns: r, g and b. That is already a small number, but even here PCA can show how two components capture the variation across the 144 pixels. With more features — such as texture measurements or colour histograms — PCA becomes increasingly useful.

sections.heading: The idea of a principal component
body: PCA finds the directions in which the data varies the most. The first principal component is the single direction in feature space along which the data varies the most. The second principal component is the direction orthogonal (perpendicular) to the first that captures the most remaining variation, and so on. Each principal component is a weighted combination of the original feature columns. For the pixels data, the first principal component might be a combination such as 0.5 times r plus 0.5 times g plus 0.3 times b, and the second would be orthogonal to it.

The weights are called loadings, and they tell you how much each original feature contributes to the new component. A large positive loading means the feature contributes in the same direction, a large negative loading means it contributes in the opposite direction, and a loading near zero means the feature hardly contributes at all.

sections.heading: How much did you keep
body: The explained variance ratio tells you how much of the original data's variation is captured by each principal component. If the first principal component has an explained variance ratio of 0.7, it means 70 percent of the total variation in the data is captured by that one component. The second component's ratio adds to the first, so if it is 0.2, the first two components together capture 90 percent of the variation. You choose the number of components that keeps most of the variation while reducing the column count to a manageable level.

For the pixels data, the three colour columns r, g and b are highly correlated because each pixel has one colour from a limited set. PCA on those three columns might show that the first component captures about 60 percent of the variance and the second captures about 30 percent, so two components keep about 90 percent of the information. That means you can work with two columns instead of three with little loss.

sections.heading: When not to use it
body: PCA assumes that the relationship between features is linear, so it will not capture curved or nonlinear structure in the data. If the clusters in your data follow a circular pattern, PCA's linear combinations may spread them out rather than pulling them together. PCA also requires that features be on comparable scales; if one feature is measured in thousands of dollars and another in cents, the feature with the larger numerical range will dominate the principal components unless the features are scaled first — typically by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.

The new columns from PCA cannot be read directly as 'red value' or 'green value'. They are abstract combinations, and the loadings that produce them depend on the dataset you applied PCA to. If you apply PCA to one dataset and then try to use the same components on new data, you must apply the same scaling and the same weighting, or the numbers will not mean the same thing.

lessons.title: From one neuron to a network
lessons.goal: Explain what a single artificial neuron computes and how stacking neurons into layers builds a model.

sections.heading: One neuron, one number
body: An artificial neuron is the simplest building block of a deep learning model. It takes several numbers, multiplies each by a stored weight, adds them all together, and then adds a single number called a bias. The bias shifts the result up or down without changing any of the weights. This computation is exactly a weighted sum plus an offset, the same kind of arithmetic you use when you compute a total bill from item prices and quantities.

During training, the learning process is the only thing that changes the weights and biases. All weights and biases start as random numbers, typically drawn from a small range so they are not huge. No human writes the feature-to-output rule by hand; the training loop nudges each weight a little bit at a time until the model produces the right answers often enough. The neuron's raw output before any activation function is this weighted sum plus bias.

sections.heading: Layers pass numbers to layers
body: A layer is a group of neurons that work in parallel. Each neuron in the layer takes the same input numbers, produces its own output number, and the layer passes all those output numbers upward to the next layer. The width of a layer — how many neurons it contains — is a design choice you make. More neurons let the model represent more complex patterns, but each one adds weights that must be trained.

If a layer has N neurons, its output is a row of N numbers, one per neuron. The next layer takes that row as its input and applies its own set of weights and biases. Stacking layers this way builds a network, and the depth — how many layers you have — is another design choice. Each additional layer increases the functions the model can compute, but also increases the number of weights that the training loop must find.

sections.heading: Where the numbers come from
body: All the weights and biases start as random numbers, typically drawn from a small range so they are not huge. During training, the learning process is the only thing that changes these numbers. No human writes the feature-to-output rule by hand; the training loop nudges each weight a little bit at a time until the model produces the right answers often enough.

The training loop computes gradients and updates each weight a tiny amount at a time. The bias terms are updated the same way, shifting the neuron's output left or right. Because the weights start random, different initialisations can lead to different final models, which is why practitioners often run training several times with different random seeds.

sections.heading: Why bother with layers
body: A single-layer neuron computes a weighted sum, which draws one straight-line (hyperplane) boundary in the space of its inputs. That can only separate two classes when they are linearly mixable. Stacking layers lets the model draw curved boundaries, even circles or spirals, at the cost of more weights to get right.

The trade-off is that a deeper network can represent far richer functions than a single neuron alone. A two-layer network with ReLU activation can approximate any continuous function given enough neurons, which is why deep learning models almost always have at least one hidden layer. The cost is that more weights must be trained, and the model becomes harder to interpret.

quiz_bank.explanation: Training adjusts every weight and bias value, moving each one a small amount at a time so the model's output better matches the correct labels. The architecture, such as the number of layers, stays fixed during training.

quiz_bank.question: What can a stack of layers compute that a single linear neuron cannot?
choices: Only faster computation, not richer patterns
Curved decision boundaries, not just straight ones
Only one extra class of output
No difference at any depth
quiz_bank.explanation: A single neuron draws one straight-line boundary (hyperplane). Adding layers with activation functions between them lets the model draw curved boundaries, such as circles or spirals, which a single linear model cannot produce.

lessons.title: Activation functions
lessons.goal: Explain what an activation function does and choose between sigmoid, tanh and ReLU for a hidden layer.

sections.heading: Why a layer needs an activation
body: Without an activation function, every layer of a neural network computes only a weighted sum, and stacking several linear layers together still gives just one linear result. The composition of linear functions is always linear, so the whole network would collapse to one neuron no matter how many layers you add. An activation function squashes each neuron's output into a new range, and that nonlinearity is what lets the model compute and draw curved boundaries.

Without nonlinearity, a deep network has no more representational power than a single neuron. This is why every hidden layer in a practical deep learning model uses an activation function. The choice of activation changes how gradients flow during training and what kinds of patterns the model can learn.

sections.heading: Sigmoid and tanh
body: The sigmoid function squashes any input number into a range between 0 and 1, which is useful when the output must be read as a probability. The tanh function does the same squashing but its range is between -1 and 1, zero-centred, which makes learning easier for the layers below. Both functions saturate when their input is very far from zero: the gradient becomes almost zero, so learning slows to a crawl.

A beginner's mistake is to use sigmoid for hidden layers where tanh often works better because of its zero-centred range. When inputs to sigmoid or tanh are large in magnitude, the output saturates at 0 or 1 respectively, and the gradient near zero means the weights receive almost no update. This is why ReLU became the default choice for many hidden layers.

sections.heading: ReLU
body: ReLU, which stands for rectified linear unit, keeps the input unchanged if it is positive and outputs zero otherwise. Its computation is simply max(0, x), which makes it very fast to calculate. Because ReLU does not saturate when the input is positive, learning flows through it more easily than through sigmoid or tanh.

The main risk with ReLU is the 'dead ReLU' problem: if a neuron receives only negative inputs during training, its gradient becomes zero forever and the neuron stops learning entirely. This means the model permanently loses that weight. Variants such as leaky ReLU or parametric ReLU were introduced to keep a tiny gradient even when the input is negative, so the neuron can recover.

sections.heading: Choosing the output activation
body: The output activation depends on the task type. A binary classification problem — deciding between two classes — typically uses a single output with sigmoid, which produces a number between 0 and 1 that can be interpreted as the probability of the positive class.

A multi-class classification problem with ten or more classes, such as classifying handwritten digits, uses one output unit per class with softmax, which spreads the outputs so they sum to 1 across all classes. A regression problem, where the target is a continuous number, typically uses no activation at the output layer at all, so the model can produce any real-valued prediction.

quiz.question: What happens if you stack layers without any activation function?

The network's output is always zero, regardless of input

The weights automatically become binary values
quiz.explanation: Without activation functions, every layer computes only a weighted sum, and the composition of any number of linear transformations is itself linear. The network would be equivalent to a single neuron no matter how many layers it contains, which is why activation functions are essential for deep learning.

quiz_bank.question: Why does a ten class problem need ten output units instead of one?
choices: Because one output unit cannot store the number 10
Because the ten outputs are multiplied together to produce the final score

One output unit cannot represent ten distinct classes simultaneously.

lessons.title: How a network learns: backpropagation in plain words
lessons.goal: Describe backpropagation as a two-step loop of measuring each weight's contribution to the error and adjusting it, without needing the calculus behind it.

sections.heading: The loss measures how wrong you are
body: A loss function is a number that measures how poorly the model's predictions match the true labels. For a regression task, mean squared error is common: it squares the difference between the predicted and actual value, so larger errors loom even larger. For a classification task, cross-entropy loss measures the surprise of the predicted probability given the true class. In both cases, the training loop's job is to make this number smaller and smaller.

The loss number answers one question: 'how wrong are we right now?' A smaller loss means the model's outputs are closer to the correct answers. The loss function provides the target that the training loop will try to minimize, and it is the single number that drives every update to the model's weights.

sections.heading: Step one: blame the weights
body: The backward pass works backwards from the error: it asks, 'If I nudge this weight a tiny amount, how much does the loss change?' The gradient tells the model how much each weight contributed to the current error. This is not a human judgment; it is a precise arithmetic calculation using the chain rule, and it assigns a blame score to every weight in the network.

The gradient is a vector of partial derivatives, one per weight. Each entry says how much the loss would change if that weight were increased slightly, holding everything else steady. The backward pass computes these derivatives efficiently, propagating the error signal from the output layer back through every hidden layer.

sections.heading: Step two: nudge the weights
body: Gradient descent takes the blame scores (the gradient) and subtracts a small fraction of each one from the current weight. The learning rate controls how large that fraction is: a larger learning rate moves the weights farther each step, a smaller one moves them less. After the nudge, the forward pass recomputes the output and the loss, and the loop starts over.

The update rule for one weight is: weight_new = weight_old - learning_rate × gradient. If the gradient is positive, the weight decreases; if the gradient is negative, the weight increases. The learning rate is the knob you turn to control step size, and choosing it well is one of the most important practical decisions in training.

sections.heading: Repeat many times, on small batches
body: Training loops over many iterations, and in each iteration the model sees a small batch of examples rather than the whole dataset at once. Mini-batch training makes learning faster and more stable than using the entire dataset in one go, and it also introduces a little noise that can help the model escape shallow local minima.

The loss usually falls in a bumpy way, not straight down, because each batch gives a slightly different gradient direction. An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset, and typical training runs for many epochs. The model's loss on the training set may keep falling while the validation loss tells you whether you have trained too long.

quiz.question: What are the four steps of every training loop?

quiz.explanation: Every training loop runs through four stages: the forward pass computes the model's output, the loss measures how wrong it is, the backward pass computes gradients, and the update step nudges the weights. These four repeat until training stops.

quiz_bank.explanation: When the learning rate is too large, the weight updates overshoot the low-loss region and land somewhere worse, so the loss goes up instead of down. The steps become too big and the training diverges or bounces around without ever settling.

lessons.title: Training, validating and spotting overfitting
lessons.goal: Train a network while watching the training and validation curves, and recognise overfitting when you see it.

sections.heading: Three sets of data, three jobs
body: Every neural network training uses three separate sets of data: training, validation, and test. The training set is used in every training iteration, the model's weights are updated after each batch, and this is the only set that drives the learning process. The validation set is not used for weight updates; instead, after each epoch the model's performance on the validation set is checked to decide when to stop training or which model checkpoint to keep.

The test set is held out until the very end, and its result is reported once as the final evaluation — it must never influence training decisions, or the reported accuracy will be artificially inflated. Using the test set during training would give an optimistically biased result that does not generalise to completely new data. The three sets together form the complete data pipeline.

sections.heading: Reading a learning curve
body: A learning curve plots the model's loss (or accuracy) versus the training epoch. A healthy curve shows both training loss and validation loss falling together over the early epochs. A broken curve shows training loss continuing to fall while validation loss starts to rise: the model is learning patterns that are specific to the training examples rather than general patterns, which is the sign of overfitting.

The epoch number is on the x-axis and the loss value is on the y-axis. When you see the two curves (training and validation) diverge, with training going down and validation going up, you are looking at classic overfitting. The vertical distance between the curves measures how much the model has over specialised to the training data.

sections.heading: What is overfitting
body: Overfitting happens when the model memorises the training examples instead of learning the general patterns. In a digit classification task, the model might learn that a particular pixel arrangement always goes with a specific digit in the training set, but that memorisation does not transfer to new digits. On the training set the model gets very high accuracy, but on completely new digits its accuracy drops.

The gap between training performance and validation (or test) performance is the diagnostic marker. A model that has overfitted will show training accuracy near 100 percent but validation accuracy much lower. The model has not learned to recognise digits in general; it has learned to recognise the specific digits that happened to be in the training set.

sections.heading: The four usual cures
body: The first remedy is to get more training data, because a model with too few examples can memorise them all. Data augmentation is another technique: for digit classification, small random rotations, shifts, or contrasts of the existing digits create synthetic new training examples without collecting new data.

Dropout randomly turns off a fraction of neurons during each training step, which prevents the model from relying on any single path and makes it learn more robust features. Early stopping monitors the validation loss and stops training the moment it starts rising, so the model does not keep refining memorisation patterns after the general pattern has already been learned. Of these, getting more data or using augmentation is usually the first thing to try, because it addresses the root cause rather than the symptom.

quiz.question: Which set of data is used to decide when to stop training?
choices: The training set, because it has the most examples
The validation set, because its loss is monitored across epochs
The test set, because it represents the real-world data distribution
All three sets are used equally for stopping decisions
quiz.explanation: The validation set is explicitly held aside from weight updates; its loss is computed after each epoch and used as the signal for early stopping or model checkpointing. The test set must remain untouched until the final evaluation.

quiz_bank.explanation: Dropout randomly drops neurons during training, forcing the model to learn robust features, and early stopping halts training before the model starts memorising training-specific patterns. Both are standard techniques for reducing overfitting.

lessons.title: Your first network in Keras
lessons.goal: Build, compile, train and evaluate a classifier for handwritten digits with a few lines of Keras.

sections.heading: The shape of the code
body: A Keras digit classifier follows four steps. First, build the model by stacking layers: an input layer that accepts 64 pixels (8 times 8 greyscale values), one hidden layer with 32 ReLU units, and an output layer of 10 units (one per digit class) with softmax activation. Second, compile the model by choosing the loss function (sparse categorical crossentropy for integer labels), the optimizer (Adam is a good default), and the metric to track (accuracy).

Third, train the model on the training data, specifying the number of epochs and a validation split so you can watch the learning curves. Fourth, evaluate the model on the held-out test set, which reports the test loss and test accuracy. The data shape at each step is: input of 64 pixels per example, hidden layer produces 32 numbers, output produces 10 probabilities that sum to 1.

sections.heading: The compile step is where you choose the loss
body: Compiling a Keras model is where you specify the three core ingredients: the loss, the optimizer, and the metrics. The loss is the function the model minimises during training; for integer labels across ten classes, sparse categorical crossentropy is the standard choice. The optimizer, such as Adam, determines how the weights are updated each step based on the gradients.

The metric, usually accuracy, is the proportion of predictions that match the true label and is reported at the end of every epoch and at evaluation time. These three choices — loss, optimizer, metrics — define how the model learns and what is reported, and they are set once before training begins.

sections.heading: Pixels are numbers between 0 and 1
body: The digits dataset stores each image as 8 by 8 greyscale pixels, and each pixel value is an integer from 0 to 255, where 0 is white and 255 is black. Before feeding these values into a neural network, it is standard practice to scale them to the range 0 to 1 by dividing by 255. This scaling keeps the weighted sums in a reasonable range and makes the optimization landscape easier for the training algorithm.

The input layer then receives a flat vector of 64 numbers, each between 0 and 1, one per pixel. Without scaling, the pixel values would dominate the weighted sums because 255 is much larger than the random starting weights, and the model would learn more slowly or poorly.

sections.heading: Read the evaluation output
body: After model.evaluate() runs on the test set, the output includes the test loss and the test accuracy. On a ten class digit problem, a test accuracy of 98 percent means the model correctly classified 98 out of every 100 digits it has never seen before. The test loss tells you the average loss per example on that held-out set.

Comparing the training loss to the test loss tells you whether the model generalises well or shows signs of overfitting. If training loss is much lower than test loss, the model has memorised the training examples rather than learning patterns that transfer to new data. A close gap between training and test loss indicates good generalisation.

lessons.title: How a computer sees an image
lessons.goal: Explain how an image becomes a grid of numbers and what information is lost when you flatten it.

sections.heading: Pixels are numbers
body: Each image in the bundled data is 8 pixels by 8 pixels, giving 64 pixel values per image. The image I001 has p0=15 as its top-left pixel, p1=20 as the next pixel to the right, and so on across each row. A pixel value represents brightness, with larger numbers meaning brighter pixels. In this synthetic dataset the smallest value is 12 and the largest is 214, so the images use the full available range. When you look at the grid, you can see patterns — a row of high numbers might look like a bright stripe, and a row of low numbers like a dark stripe. The computer stores these numbers but discards the visual shape unless you keep the 8-by-8 layout in mind.

A brightness value of 12 is very dark, near black, while 214 is very light, near white. The 64 values for I001 average about 118, which is close to mid‑grey. If you see a pixel with value 200 you know it is brighter than average, and a pixel with value 30 is noticeably darker. These numbers let you compare brightness across images, but only if you remember which position each number came from. Without the position information you cannot tell whether a bright pixel is in the top-left corner or the bottom-right, and that position matters for recognising shapes.

sections.heading: Greyscale has one channel
body: Most colour images have three channels — red, green and blue — so every pixel needs three numbers, one for each colour. The bundled images are greyscale, which means each pixel is stored as a single brightness value. That single number is the perceived lightness, and it combines the three colour channels into one shade of grey. A pixel with value 150 in a greyscale image might correspond to red 150, green 150, blue 150 in a colour image, producing a neutral middle‑grey. Having just one number per pixel makes the data smaller and easier to work with, especially when you have many images to process.

A greyscale image discards colour information, so you cannot tell a red shirt from a blue shirt — both become just a brightness number. That loss matters if colour is the feature you need, but for many tasks such as detecting whether a digit is written clearly or judging the lightness of a surface, colour is irrelevant and the single channel is sufficient. The trade-off is that you give up the ability to distinguish objects that differ only in colour, but you gain speed and simplicity in every step that follows.

sections.heading: Flattening loses the picture
body: Flattening an image means putting the 64 pixel values into one long list of 64 numbers, going from a two‑dimensional grid to a one‑dimensional line. The image I001 has its top‑left pixel first, then the next pixel to the right, and so on until the 64th pixel at the bottom‑right. When you flatten you keep the numbers but you lose the knowledge that position seven is next to position eight and far from position fifty-seven. A flat list tells you how bright each spot is, but not where that spot lives in the picture.

Because human vision relies on neighbouring pixels to recognise edges and shapes, a model that receives a flat list must re‑learn the spatial structure from scratch. Keeping the 8-by-8 layout lets the model use neighbouring pixels the way our visual system does: a bright pixel next to a dark pixel signals an edge, and a small cluster of bright pixels suggests a feature. When the grid shape is preserved, a convolution or simple rule can detect patterns such as a bright corner or a dark line without extra processing.

sections.heading: Brightness values across the dataset
body: Across the 30 images in the dataset the individual pixel values range from 12 to 214, a span of 202 units. Image I001 has its 64 pixels clustered between 15 and 20, giving a uniformly dark appearance, while image I011 has pixels spread from 180 to 214, producing a very bright image. Some images, such as I005, have a mix of very dark pixels (around 15) and very bright pixels (around 200), creating high contrast. Knowing the overall range helps you normalise the data later, but each image has its own brightness character that a single number cannot capture.

If you compute the mean pixel value for each image you get a single number summarising its overall brightness: I001 averages about 118, I011 averages about 197, and I005 averages about 108. These means tell you which images are generally brighter or darker, but two images can have the same mean and look very different — one might have a bright spot on a dark background, the other a medium‑grey scene. The mean is a useful summary, yet it hides the detail that a histogram of pixel values would reveal.

lessons.title: Preparing image data
lessons.goal: Resize, scale and organise image data so that every training image looks the same to the model.

sections.heading: Every image the same size
body: Neural networks require every input image to have the same width and height, because the layers expect a fixed number of pixels. The bundled images are already 8-by-8, but real photographs come in many sizes — a portrait might be 1200-by-1600 and a snapshot might be 800-by-600. Resizing every image to 8-by-8 before training is not optional; it is the first step that makes every image compatible with the model's fixed‑size input layer. Without resizing the model would crash or produce unpredictable results when shown images of different dimensions.

When you resize an image you change its pixel count but keep the meaning of each position — the top‑left corner stays the top‑left corner after resizing. A common beginner mistake is to stretch the image non‑uniformly, making objects look wider than they are tall. Always resize both dimensions by the same scaling factor, or use a library function that maintains the aspect ratio and then crops the excess. This ensures that a square object in the original photo remains approximately square in the resized version.

sections.heading: Scaling the numbers
body: Pixel values in the bundled data run from 12 to 214, but most machine learning models work best when input numbers are centred around zero and lie in a narrow range such as 0 to 1. Dividing every pixel value by 255 — the maximum possible value in an 8‑bit greyscale image — scales the bundled data so that the smallest becomes about 0.05 and the largest becomes about 0.84. This process, called normalisation, makes the initial training steps more stable because the model does not start with one feature that is orders of magnitude larger than the others.

After normalisation a pixel that was 12 becomes 0.047 and a pixel that was 214 becomes 0.839. The difference between neighbouring pixels is now much smaller in absolute terms, which helps the gradient descent steps stay modest at the start of training. If you skip this scaling and feed raw values into the model the first updates can be huge because a single large pixel value dominates the weighted sum. That is why normalisation is standard practice before the first training epoch.

sections.heading: Labels and folders
body: Each image in the dataset carries a label — a single number that tells the model what that image depicts. In the bundled data the label is 0 or 1, where 0 means one kind of pattern and 1 means another. Most tools expect a folder-per-class layout: all images with label 0 go in one folder, all images with label 1 go in another. When the folder name itself carries the class name the model can read the label directly from the file path, which is convenient for the training loop. If you put all images in one folder and write a separate CSV file with image IDs and labels you must ensure the CSV is error‑free, because the model will not guess the label from the filename.

If you store all images in one folder and keep a separate CSV file that maps each image ID to its class, the model must read that CSV instead of inferring the label from the directory. A common mistake is to mismatch the image ID in the CSV with the actual filename, causing the model to learn the wrong class for each image. Always verify that the number of rows in the CSV equals the number of image files, and that every label is either 0 or 1, with no missing or extra entries.

sections.heading: Augmentation: making new images on purpose
body: Data augmentation creates additional training examples by applying small changes to each image, such as flipping it left‑right, rotating it by a few degrees, or cropping a random section. These techniques teach the model to ignore minor variations so it still recognises the same pattern when the image is slightly turned or mirrored. In this synthetic dataset the pixels are fixed, so augmentation would be applied in software before the model sees the image, not by changing the CSV file itself.

A warning specific to this domain: a flipped digit is not always valid, because the written form of a digit matters — a reversed 6 looks like a 9, and a reversed 3 can be confusing. Unlike natural images where left‑right symmetry is common, structured patterns such as digits or letters have a canonical orientation. If you augment by rotating, be sure the rotation angle stays within a range that does not destroy the recognisable shape. Always check a few augmented examples visually before starting training, to be sure the changes are helpful rather than noise.

quiz.explanation: Neural network layers are built with a fixed number of input units, so every image must have the same width and height. If images vary in size the model cannot process them in a single batch without resizing first.

lessons.title: Convolutional neural networks
lessons.goal: Describe what a convolution does to an image and why it lets a model find a feature anywhere in the picture.

sections.heading: A small filter slides across the image
body: A convolution filter is a small grid of numbers, also called a kernel, that slides across the image one pixel at a time. The filter at position one multiplies each of its numbers by the pixel values underneath, adds the products together, and produces a single new number. As the filter moves to the next location it produces another number, and so on until every position in the image has been covered. For an 8-by-8 image with a 3-by-3 filter the output is a 6-by-6 grid of numbers, because the filter fits six positions horizontally and six vertically.

Each number in the output grid is called a feature map value, and it tells you how strong that pattern was at that location. If the filter is looking for a vertical edge and the image has a vertical line at that spot the product will be large and the feature map value will be high. If there is no edge the value will be low. The filter learns what to look for during training, starting with random numbers and gradually changing so that the feature map values highlight the patterns that matter for the task.

sections.heading: Early filters find edges
body: In a convolutional network the first few layers have filters that respond to very simple patterns such as a dark pixel next to a bright pixel, which is an edge, or a slight change in colour texture. These early filters are useful because almost every image feature — corners, lines, curves — is built from edges at some scale. As you go deeper into the network the filters respond to more complex patterns such as curves, then shapes like eyes or wheels, because each layer combines the responses from the layer below.

Imagine a filter that detects a horizontal line and another that detects a vertical line; when both are active in the same region the next layer can combine them to recognise a corner. With each successive layer the model builds up from parts to wholes: edges → parts of objects → whole objects. This hierarchy is why convolutional networks are so much better at image tasks than a fully connected network, which would have to learn edge detection from scratch for every new image and would not scale to the richness of natural pictures that humans recognise instantly.

sections.heading: Pooling and shrinking
body: Pooling is a operation that reduces the size of a feature map by keeping only the strongest number in each small region. For example, a 2-by-2 max-pooling takes four numbers and outputs the single largest of those four, so the feature map shrinks by half in width and height. This operation makes the model invariant to small translations: if a pattern shifts by one or two pixels the pooled result can stay the same, which helps the model recognise the same feature even when its exact position varies.

After pooling the feature map is smaller, which means fewer numbers for the next layer to process. This reduces computation and helps prevent overfitting, because the model relies on whether a feature is present rather than exactly where it sits. A common beginner mistake is to use pooling too early, before the first few convolutional layers have had a chance to learn meaningful patterns, which can cause the model to lose useful detail before it is even recognised.

sections.heading: From feature maps to a label
body: After several convolutional layers and pooling steps the feature maps have been reduced to a compact set of numbers that describe the most important patterns found in the image. These numbers are then flattened into a one‑dimensional list and fed into one or more dense layers, where each neuron connects to every number from the previous layer. The dense layers compute weighted sums and apply a non‑linear activation, finally producing a small vector of scores — one score per class.

The last step is usually a softmax function that turns those raw scores into probabilities that add up to one. A score of 3.2 might become a probability of 0.78, a score of 1.1 becomes 0.15, and a score of -0.5 becomes 0.07, leaving the remaining probability for other classes. The class with the highest probability is the model's prediction, and during training the model adjusts its filters and dense‑layer weights so that the correct class receives the highest probability for each image.

It resizes the image to a smaller grid
It converts the image from colour to greyscale
quiz.explanation: The filter slides across the image position by position, multiplying each filter value by the pixel value underneath and adding the products. This produces one new number per position, forming a feature map that highlights where the pattern exists.

lessons.title: Transfer learning: start from what is already known
lessons.goal: Reuse a pre-trained model as a feature extractor or as the starting point for your own training.

sections.heading: Why training from scratch is expensive
body: Training a convolutional neural network from scratch means randomly initializing all weights and then adjusting them using your own dataset. This process can require millions of labelled images and many hours of computing time, because the model must discover edge detectors, color patterns and object parts entirely on its own. Models that have already been trained on large datasets such as ImageNet have learned these basic patterns already, so starting from those learned weights saves vast amounts of data and compute time. In practice, fine‑tuning a pre‑trained model on a new task can take minutes or hours instead of days or weeks.

Because the early layers of a pre‑trained model already detect edges and textures, only the later layers need to change when you fine‑tune on your own data. This means your own labelled dataset can be small — often just a few hundred images — and still produce a working model. If you tried to learn everything from scratch you would need thousands of examples for each class just to discover the same edge detectors that the pre‑trained model already knows.

sections.heading: Feature extraction
body: Feature extraction means keeping all the layers of a pre‑trained model fixed (frozen) and training only a new, small classifier on top of them. The pre‑trained layers have already learned to produce useful feature representations from the raw pixel values — they map each image patch to a vector of numbers that capture edges, shapes and textures. You add one or more dense layers on top, with the number of output units equal to the number of classes you want to distinguish, and train those new layers using your own data. The heavy lifting of pattern detection is already done; you only teach the model how to map those patterns to your specific labels.

Think of it like reusing a trained chef's prep work: the chef has already chopped onions, measured spices and heated pans so that the final dish comes together quickly. You do not need to teach the chef from scratch; you just add your own seasoning and cooking steps to finish the recipe. In the same way, the pre‑trained model provides ready‑made pattern detectors, and you add a new classifier that learns which patterns matter for your own classes.

sections.heading: Fine-tuning
body: Fine‑tuning means unfreezing some of the pre‑trained layers so that their weights can change during training on your own data. The early layers, which detect generic edges and textures, often stay frozen because those features are useful across many tasks. The later layers, which are closer to the final classification decision, are unfrozen so they can adapt to your specific classes. A small learning rate is used because the pre‑trained weights are already in a good region; large steps would move them too far and hurt performance rather than help.

A common practice is to freeze the first two of five convolutional layers and unfreeze the last two, then train for a few epochs with a learning rate around 0.001. You monitor the validation loss and if it stops improving you reduce the learning rate further or freeze the layers again. This careful adjustment lets the model specialize without losing the general knowledge it already carries.

sections.heading: Checking the result
body: After fine‑tuning you evaluate the model on the held‑out evaluation set and compute a confusion matrix that counts true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives for each class. Comparing the accuracy and precision of your fine‑tuned model against a simple baseline — such as a model that always predicts the most common class — tells you whether the pre‑trained weights actually helped. If the confusion matrix shows many false positives you may need to adjust the decision threshold or collect more labelled examples.

A useful visual aid is to misclassify some images and look at what the model was actually responding to — sometimes a model predicts 'class 1' because it detected a bright patch that happens to correlate with that class in the training data but is not the true feature. The lesson here is that transfer learning speeds up development but you still need to check the results honestly, because a model can be confident and wrong if the data does not fully support the task.

quiz.explanation: Transfer learning starts from weights that have already learned to detect edges and textures from a large dataset, so your new task needs far fewer labelled examples and much less compute time to reach good performance.

lessons.title: Detection and segmentation: what comes after labels
lessons.goal: Tell classification, object detection and image segmentation apart, and say what each is used for.

sections.heading: One label for the whole image
body: Image classification gives the model one label for the entire image, such as 'this picture shows a cat'. The model looks at all the pixels and outputs a single class name, which is useful when you only need to know whether the desired object is present. But classification cannot answer where the cat is located inside the image, nor can it tell if there are multiple cats or other objects sharing the frame. For tasks that require spatial information the single-label approach is too coarse.

Suppose you have a dataset of 1,000 photos of rooms and you want to know whether each room has a window. A classification model can give you 1,000 yes/no answers, but it won't tell you which of the 1,000 rooms have windows and which do not, because the 'window' or 'no window' decision is the only output the model produces. To find the location you need a different kind of model that produces spatial output such as boxes or a pixel‑wise mask.

sections.heading: Boxes around objects
body: Object detection produces a set of boxes around the objects it finds in the image, together with a label for each box and a confidence score that says how sure the model is about that prediction. For example, a detector might output 'cat at position (120, 45) with size 80-by-60 and confidence 0.92'. The confidence score is the model's estimated probability that the box actually contains the stated object. Well‑known families of detectors such as YOLO (You Only Look Once) and Faster R‑CNN scan the image once or multiple times and output all detected objects in a single pass.

A confidence score above a chosen threshold — commonly 0.5 or 0.7 — is taken as a detection; scores below the threshold are discarded. If the same object is detected with two overlapping boxes the model usually keeps the one with the higher score and discards the other, a procedure called non-maximum suppression. YOLO's architecture makes it particularly fast, which is why it is used in real‑time applications such as counting cars in traffic video feeds.

sections.heading: A label for every pixel
body: Semantic segmentation gives every pixel in the image a label, so the output is a full‑resolution mask that shows which pixels belong to which class. All pixels that are part of the same class receive the same label — for instance, every pixel that is sky gets label 'sky' and every pixel that is grass gets label 'grass'. This lets you measure exactly how much of the image is covered by each class, which is useful for tasks such as medical image analysis or mapping land cover.

Instance segmentation goes a step further by giving each separate object its own mask, even when all objects belong to the same class. If there are three cars in the image, instance segmentation produces three distinct masks — car‑1, car‑2, car‑3 — so you can count the cars and tell them apart. This is essential for applications that need to track individual objects over time, such as counting floating particles in a fluid or tracking pedestrians in a crowd.

sections.heading: Choosing the right task
body: The choice of task depends on what question you want to answer. If you need a yes/no answer — does this image contain a cat? — use classification. If you need to know where objects are and how many there are, use object detection, which gives you boxes and labels with confidence scores. If you need to measure how much of the image is occupied by a certain class, use semantic segmentation to get a pixel‑wise mask. The decision summary is: classification for yes/no, detection for boxes and counts, segmentation for per‑pixel area measures.

Counting the cars in a photo needs detection, measuring how much of the photo is road needs segmentation, and a yes or no answer about whether the photo contains a cat needs classification. Each task produces a different kind of output and requires different evaluation metrics, so choosing the right one before you start training saves time and leads to more meaningful results.
