quiz.explanation: Object detection returns a set of bounding boxes, each with a class label and a confidence score, while a classifier only returns one label for the entire image, with no spatial information.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning, storytelling and peer review
lessons.goal: Plan a computer vision project, present it clearly, and use a peer review to find the gaps before an employer does.

sections.heading: Scope the project in one sentence
body: A good project sentence follows a simple four‑part structure: data, task, model, and the decision it supports. You state which data you are using, what prediction or classification task the model will perform, which type of model you have chosen, and what decision the result will inform. For example: 'Using the 30 bundled 8‑by‑8 greyscale images, I will train a convolutional network to classify each image as class 0 or class 1, so that a new image can be quickly categorised without human inspection.' This one sentence tells anyone reading exactly what you built and why it matters.

Writing the sentence first forces you to think about what data you have, what you want to predict, and what you will do with the answer before you start spending hours on training. If you cannot write a clear four‑part sentence, it is a sign that the project scope is not well defined and you should clarify your data, your goal, or your model choice before you begin.

sections.heading: Plan before you train
body: Before you start training write down the data split you will use, the evaluation metric you will track, and a simple baseline model you can beat. For example: 'I will use 20 images for training and 10 for evaluation, I will report accuracy, and a baseline that always predicts the majority class achieves 50% accuracy.' Having these numbers recorded before you train prevents you from accidentally overfitting to the evaluation set and gives you a clear rubric to judge whether your model is actually improving.

The split should be stratified so that both the training and evaluation sets have roughly the same proportion of each class, and the metric should be chosen before you look at the results. A common beginner mistake is to pick the metric after seeing that the model does well, which inflates the apparent performance. Write down your plan, then train, then evaluate exactly against that plan.

sections.heading: Tell the story with evidence
body: A good project presentation follows a clear shape that reviewers can follow quickly. Start with the problem the project addresses, then describe the data you used, then the method (model type and key steps), then the numbers (accuracy, confusion matrix, anything else), then the limits of what the model can do, and finally the next step you would take. This six‑part structure ensures that no important aspect is omitted and that the reviewer can judge the work on its own terms.

In the bundled computer vision project the problem is to classify new 8‑by‑8 greyscale images, the data are the 30 images with their labels, the method is a convolutional network with transfer learning, the numbers include the accuracy and confusion matrix on the 10 evaluation images, the limits are that the model cannot localisation objects, and the next step is to collect more varied images and try object detection. Writing these six sentences in your README lets a reviewer quickly check that you have addressed every component.

sections.heading: Peer review that helps
body: When you review a classmate's project, give specific feedback that mentions what they did well and exactly what could be improved, such as 'your project sentence clearly states the data and task, but the confusion matrix section is missing so I cannot tell if the model performed well.' Receiving feedback is easier when you remember that the reviewer is trying to help you make your project stronger, not criticise you personally. Always ask for at least two pieces of feedback so you see the same issue mentioned by more than one person, which signals that the improvement is real.

Give the story and the six‑part presentation to your classmate and ask for two pieces of feedback: one about the clarity of the project description and one about whether the numbers reported match what the confusion matrix shows. When you receive feedback, read it once without defending your work, then go back and address the points that were mentioned by both you and your reviewer. This loop of draft‑feedback‑revise is what makes peer review valuable practice for employer evaluations later.

lessons.title: Make a training run repeatable
lessons.goal: Identify the inputs and controls needed to reproduce a model training run.

sections.heading: A model file is not a training record
body: A model file such as a .pkl or .h5 contains the learned weights of a classifier, the numbers the model learned from data. It does not contain the code that produced those weights, the data that was shown during training, or the random seed that started the run. Two people can have identical model files and get different answers when they apply them, because the model file says what the model knows but not how it was taught.

The training record is what ties everything together: the exact Python script, the CSV file with its row count and column names, the configuration file with learning rate and regularization strength, and the random seed that makes the run deterministic. Without that record, a model file is just a set of numbers with no context. The record answers the question: 'Exactly what data and settings produced these weights?'

sections.heading: Separate configuration from code
body: Putting parameters such as the learning rate, regularization strength, or number of epochs inside a config file means you can change them without editing a single line of Python code. The training script reads the config at startup, so the same script can produce many different runs just by switching the config. This matters because editing code to change a number introduces the risk of accidentally saving a changed script that you did not intend.

A beginner might keep everything inside the script and later forget which value belonged to which experiment. With a config file, the entire run is described in one place: the code version, the data fingerprint, and every parameter that changed the result. When you later want to repeat the run, you read the config, set the seed, load the same data, and you know the output will match.

sections.heading: Repeat before you trust
body: The cheapest possible check for reproducibility is to run the exact same command twice and compare the resulting numbers. If the model weights, the evaluation metric, and the predictions all match, you have strong evidence that the run is deterministic. If they differ, you know immediately that something in the code, data, or environment changed between runs, which points you toward the record you need to fix it.

In practice this means running your training script, saving the output metrics to a file, then running it again from a clean state. A clean state means the same code, the same data file, and the same config file, started from the same directory. If the two runs produce different results, you have not yet separated configuration from code, or you have not fixed the randomness that makes one run differ from the next.

quiz.question: Why is a saved model file not enough to reproduce a training run?
choices: A model file only contains the learned weights and says nothing about the code, data, or random seed that produced them
A model file is always smaller than the training script that created it
A model file cannot be loaded by Python without a separate configuration file
A model file overwrites the original data used during training
quiz.explanation: A model file stores only the learned weights, not the code that produced them, the dataset they were trained on, or the random seed that started the run. Without those other pieces, the file has no context for reproduction.

lessons.title: Version datasets and model artifacts
lessons.goal: Track which data and model files a run used without placing sensitive raw data in experiment logs.

sections.heading: Fingerprint the data you used
body: A checksum is a short string of letters and numbers that acts as a fingerprint of a file's contents. If even a single character changes in the file, the checksum changes completely. This is better than relying on a filename, because a filename does not guarantee the file's contents have not been altered, and two files with the same name can carry different data.

In practice you compute the SHA256 hash of your training CSV and your evaluation CSV and record those strings in your run manifest. The train.csv file has fingerprint 45e50618d7167f6f14ef9e6797116f3a6f5767671c943739251d6b0e706bd254 and the evaluation.csv file has fingerprint 54fe0bab10f9dbe75c6c348bf5fa0ff2f8f87fc75bc03113e5b9a0c3fc36f2da. If either file changes, the fingerprints will not match, and you know you are not working with the same data.

sections.heading: Version the complete inference artifact
body: When you save only a model's weights, you capture the numbers the model learned, but you lose the preprocessing steps that turned raw rows into those weights. Scaling, encoding categorical features, and imputing missing values are part of how the model was built, and without them you cannot apply the model to new data with confidence. The inference artifact must include the complete pipeline, not just the final weights, so that anyone can use the model tomorrow as reliably as today.

A beginner might save clf.pkl and assume it contains everything needed for prediction, but the preprocessing object, the column order, and the imputation constants are separate files that must travel together. If you load the model without the scaler that was fitted on the training data, the feature scales will be wrong and the predictions will be garbage. Version the scaler, the encoder, and the model together as one artifact, and record the version string so you can prove which preprocessing went with which model.

sections.heading: Keep an experiment index
body: An experiment index is a simple table, often a CSV or a markdown file, that lists every run you have completed with columns for the run name, the date, the data version, the parameters, and the metric that mattered. You read the index before you start a new experiment so you can see what has already been tried and avoid repeating the same configuration. A minimal index might have one row per run and five columns: name, date, data fingerprint, key parameters, and validation score.

Suppose you ran two experiments: one with learning rate 0.1 and data fingerprint 45e50618d7167f6f14ef9e6797116f3a6f5767671c943739251d6b0e706bd254 and another with learning rate 0.01 and the same data fingerprint. The first achieved a validation F1 of 0.72 and the second achieved 0.76. By reading the index you can decide which configuration to promote, and you can later reproduce the winning run because all the inputs are recorded. Without the index you must rely on memory, which is the beginner mistake that leads to wasted compute and irreproducible results.

lessons.title: Search parameters without overfitting validation
lessons.goal: Tune models on training data while preserving a final evaluation set for one honest comparison.

sections.heading: Search inside training folds
body: A parameter search must be validated inside the training data using a pipeline so that each fold refits the scaler on its training portion only. When the scaler is fit on the entire dataset before the search begins, information from the validation portion leaks into the training process, and the resulting parameter choices are overly optimistic. Cross-validation splits the training data into folds, trains on each fold while refitting the scaler, and evaluates on the held-out fold, giving an unbiased estimate for every candidate parameter value.

For example, with 5-fold cross-validation on the 24-row training set, each fold uses 20 rows for training and 4 rows for validation, and the scaler is refitted on those 20 rows before the model is trained and evaluated. The mean validation score across the 5 folds is the number you compare across different parameter values, and the parameter with the highest mean score is the candidate you promote.

sections.heading: Keep the final test set out of the search
body: A test set used for choosing parameters stops being a test set, and the score you record from that point on is no longer an honest estimate of performance on unseen data. If you look at the final evaluation set while tuning hyperparameters, you risk overfitting to that set without realizing it, because the parameter choices have already been shaped by the information you gained from it. The final evaluation set must be held out until the parameter search is complete, then consulted once to report the final result.

In practice this means you search over parameter values using cross-validation on the training data, select the best candidate, and only then evaluate that single candidate on the test set. The test set remains untouched throughout the search, and its score is the one number you report to stakeholders or record in the run manifest.

sections.heading: Promote artifacts deliberately
body: When a candidate parameter value wins the cross-validation search, you record which value won, save its artifact, and note the metric that justified the promotion. The run manifest captures the winner's parameter value, the cross-validation mean score, the data fingerprint, and the final evaluation metric earned on the held-out test set. This record lets anyone look at the promotion decision and understand why one set of parameters was chosen over all others.

A beginner might save the model file without recording which parameter value it used, or might promote the candidate that performed best on the test set without showing the cross-validation results. Both practices make it impossible to reproduce the reasoning behind the chosen model, which defeats the purpose of a reproducible training workflow.

lessons.title: Tensors, autograd and where the code runs
lessons.goal: Understand tensor operations, automatic differentiation, and the PyTorch workflow.

sections.heading: Tensors are numbers with a shape
body: A tensor is a grid of numbers that has a shape describing how many dimensions it has and how many values are in each dimension. A plain Python list can hold numbers but does not track its shape, so you cannot easily tell whether [1, 2, 3, 4] is a row of four or a column of four. A tensor with shape 4 tells you there are four values in a single dimension, and a shape of 2 by 2 tells you there are two rows of two values each. The bundled churn data has 24 rows, and each row is a tensor of shape 2, with one value for support_tickets and one for tenure_months.

Reshaping a tensor does not change the values, only the way they are grouped; for example, a tensor of shape 12 can be viewed as two rows of six or three rows of four, and the underlying data stays the same. This is why it is important to know the expected shape before you pass a tensor into a layer, because the same values laid out differently will produce different results.

sections.heading: Autograd records the path
body: PyTorch autograd records every operation applied to a tensor that requires gradients. When you ask for a gradient, PyTorch replays those operations backwards to compute how much each parameter changed the output. For example, if you square a number and then add 5, the gradient of the result with respect to the original number is twice that number. The recording stops the moment you detach the tensor, so only the recorded path contributes to the gradient.

A common beginner mistake is to forget that autograd only tracks operations on tensors requires_grad=True; if you create a new tensor inside the forward path without requiring gradients, the backward pass will produce a zero gradient for that part, which can be confusing when the loss does not change.

sections.heading: Device placement
body: A device is the hardware where a tensor lives, typically a CPU or a GPU. Moving a tensor to a GPU with .to('cuda') makes operations run faster, but if you try to add a CPU tensor to a GPU tensor PyTorch raises a RuntimeError because the two tensors are on different devices. Always check that the model and the input data are on the same device before you run a forward pass, and use .device to inspect where a tensor currently lives.

A common beginner mistake is to forget to move the model to the same device as the data; if the model is on GPU and the batch is on CPU, the forward pass will silently produce incorrect results or raise an error, so always .to(device) both the model and every input tensor before training.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a tensor and a plain Python list for this work?
choices: A tensor has a shape that tracks its dimensions, while a plain list does not.
A tensor can hold only numbers, while a list can hold any Python object.
A tensor is always on a GPU, while a list is always on the CPU.
A tensor requires a gradient, while a list does not.
quiz.explanation: A tensor stores its shape as part of its data, so you can reshape, transpose or query dimensions. A plain list has no shape attribute and cannot be reshaped directly. The other choices misrepresent what tensors can do.

lessons.title: Build a neural network in PyTorch
lessons.goal: Define a neural network module and forward pass for tabular data.

sections.heading: A module holds the layers
body: nn.Module is a container for layers that also knows its own parameters. When you define a class that inherits from nn.Module, you add layers in the __init__ method and the framework collects all learnable weights for you. The forward method describes how data flows through those layers, one after another, and the output is the model's prediction. In the churn use case, the model takes support_tickets and tenure_months as input and produces a score that indicates how likely a customer is to cancel.

Every nn.Module also has a named parameter dictionary named parameters() that lets you inspect or modify each learnable weight, and you can zero them all at once with named_parameters() if you need to debug. This is how optimizers like SGD or Adam find the parameters to update; they ask the module for its parameters rather than looking them up by name yourself.

sections.heading: Choosing the shape of the network
body: The input size comes from the number of features in your table. The churn data has two features, support_tickets and tenure_months, so the input layer must have two units. A hidden layer of 16 ReLU units gives the model enough capacity to learn nonlinear patterns without becoming too large. The output layer has one unit that produces a raw score; a later step will turn that score into a probability with a sigmoid function. The total number of learnable parameters is (2 times 16) plus 16 bias terms for the hidden layer, plus (16 times 1) plus 1 bias term for the output layer, which is 49 parameters.

Using ReLU activation means that negative values become exactly zero, which keeps the model sparse and speeds up training compared to sigmoid, which squashes values between 0 and 1 and can cause vanishing gradients. A beginner mistake is to apply ReLU before the linear transformation, but the standard order is linear first, then activation.

sections.heading: The forward pass
body: The forward pass runs the input tensor through each layer in order. With an input of shape 2, the hidden layer transforms it to shape 16 applying the ReLU activation (which replaces negative values with zero). The output layer then transforms shape 16 to shape 1, producing a single score per row. For a batch of four rows the input tensor has shape 4 by 2, the hidden layer produces shape 4 by 16, and the output produces shape 4 by 1. Each step is a matrix multiplication followed by adding the bias term.

The ReLU activation function outputs the input unchanged if it is positive and zero otherwise, so it does not change the magnitude of positive values and completely removes negative values. A common beginner mistake is to apply dropout before the ReLU, but the standard practice is to apply dropout after the activation, zeroing out entire feature maps to prevent co-adaptation.

quiz.question: What does an nn.Module keep besides the layers?
choices: The module also keeps track of all learnable parameters, including weights and bias terms.
The module stores the training history and the loss value after each epoch.
The module remembers the exact order in which the training data was presented.
The module keeps a copy of the input data for the forward pass.
quiz.explanation: nn.Module registers every nn.Parameter (weight or bias) so that autograd can find and update them. It does not store training history, data order, or the input data itself.

lessons.title: Choose a prediction serving pattern
lessons.goal: Choose batch or online inference based on the decision's latency, volume, and reliability needs.

sections.heading: Batch and online inference solve different timing needs
body: Batch inference scores a group of records all at once, typically once a day or once an hour. The churn model can score all 24 training rows in a single batch job that runs overnight. This is efficient when the people who need the scores do not need them instantly.

Online inference scores one record at a time, while a person or another system waits. An customer service representative opening a support ticket might want the churn risk score before the conversation continues. Online inference adds latency, typically one to five seconds, but returns a result immediately. Batch inference has zero wait time for the person who triggers it, but the scores are stale by the time they are used. Choosing between them means trading off the acceptable wait time against how recently the data must be.

sections.heading: Define a stable prediction contract
body: A prediction contract is a documented promise that says what input fields the service expects and what it returns. The churn model's contract requires two fields: support_tickets, which must be a whole number between zero and one thousand, and tenure_months, which must be a whole number between zero and twelve hundred. Each field has a type, a valid range, and a clear error message if the caller provides something else.

Changing the contract later breaks every caller who wrote code against the old shape, which is why the contract must be stable before the service goes live. The contract also says what comes back: the predicted churn risk as a number, the model version as a string, and the probability as a decimal between zero and one.

sections.heading: Protect the application boundary
body: Validation belongs at the edge of the service, where the application meets the outside world. If a caller sends a negative support_tickets value the service should reject the request with a 422 response that says support_tickets must be zero or greater. If a caller sends a string where a number belongs the service should reject the request and explain which field was wrong and what type was expected.

Extra fields that the contract does not list must also be rejected, because they may indicate a caller who is trying to probe the service boundaries. Good error messages name the field, state the requirement, and give an example of a valid value, so the caller can fix the request without guesswork.

quiz.question: When is batch inference the better choice over online inference?
choices: When the people who need the scores can wait until the next batch run
When the model is too large to run on a server
When the input data has more than five features
When the model must predict probabilities above 0.9
quiz.explanation: Batch inference scores a group of records once a day or hour, which is efficient when the consumers do not need immediate results. Online inference scores one record at a time with seconds of latency, which is needed when a person waits for the answer.

lessons.title: Monitor data and model behavior
lessons.goal: Detect service failures, input shifts, and changes in model quality with appropriate signals.

sections.heading: Monitor the service and the model separately
body: A healthy service can serve bad predictions, so uptime and latency are not enough. The churn model might have 99.9 percent availability and still return a churn risk that is far from reality. Service signals such as error_rate and latency tell you whether the HTTP server is responding, but they say nothing about whether the prediction is correct.

Model signals such as error_rate on holdout data and latency per prediction tell you whether the model's quality has changed. Input drift measures how the incoming feature values differ from the values the model saw during training. Prediction drift measures whether the distribution of predicted risks has shifted. Monitoring both service and model signals gives you the full picture: the system is up, and the model is still accurate.

sections.heading: Drift is a signal to investigate
body: Input drift occurs when the statistical distribution of support_tickets or tenure_months changes relative to the training data. In the 24-row training set the mean support_tickets is 1.4 and the mean tenure_months is 18. If the recent mean support_tickets rises to 3.5 that is a noticeable shift, but it does not by itself prove the model is worse.

The model may still make accurate predictions on the new input shapes. Input drift alone is not a reason to retrain or to sound an automatic alarm. What it does signal is that the world has changed and the team should investigate whether the model's assumptions still hold. The team should check if the churn quality metrics have also changed before taking action.

sections.heading: Set actions before alerts fire
body: Every monitoring alert should have a written action plan that says who does what when a signal moves. For example if input drift is detected the action might be: the data engineer checks the source system for a schema change, the model owner runs a quality check on a held-out batch, and the engineering lead decides whether to pause new deployments.

If the error_rate on holdout data exceeds ten percent the action might be: rollback to the last known-good model version and page the on-call engineer. If latency exceeds two seconds the action might be: investigate the inference endpoint metrics and scale the service horizontally. Writing these plans in advance means that when an alert fires the team is not guessing what to do, and the response is faster and more consistent.

quiz.question: Why can a service be up and still serve bad predictions?
choices: Because the HTTP server may return 200 even when the model returns a wrong answer
Because the model runs on a different machine than the service
Because the service does not check the model's predictions before responding
Because uptime measures network health, not model accuracy
quiz.explanation: The service can report success while the model inside returns incorrect predictions. Uptime does not guarantee correctness.

Because the service does not check the model's predictions before responding
Because uptime measures network health, not model accuracy
quiz_bank.explanation: The service can report success while the model inside returns incorrect predictions. Uptime does not guarantee correctness.

quiz_bank.question: What does input drift tell you and what does it not tell you?
choices: Input drift tells you the model is worse and must be retrained immediately, and it not tell you the direction of the change
Input drift tells you the incoming data has a different distribution from the training data, and it does not tell you whether the model quality has changed
Input drift tells you the model coefficients are wrong, and it does not tell you the feature names
Input drift tells you the service is overloaded, and it does not tell you the latency
quiz_bank.explanation: Input drift measures whether the feature distribution has shifted from training. It does not by itself prove the model is worse, because the model may still be accurate on the new data.

quiz_bank.question: What must accompany every monitoring alert?
choices: A written action plan that says who does what when the signal moves
A direct phone call to the model trainer
A decision to retrain the model within twenty-four hours
A confirmation from the service owner that the server is healthy
quiz_bank.explanation: Every alert needs a written action plan so the team knows who does what when the signal moves, which makes the response faster and more consistent.

lessons.title: Release with a canary and rollback
lessons.goal: Limit the impact of a model update and restore a known-good version safely.

sections.heading: Treat model promotion as a release
body: A new model version is a production change with the same care as a code change. The churn model moving from version 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 affects every prediction the service serves, so the team should treat it like a code deployment with testing, documentation, and a rollback plan.

The canary release pattern sends a small share of traffic to the new version while the majority continues on the current version. If the new version's error_rate exceeds the guardrail the canary is stopped and traffic is shifted back. If the new version meets the guardrail it can be promoted to serve all traffic. This pattern limits the number of users affected by a bad release and gives the team a rehearsed way to restore the prior version.

sections.heading: Use stop and rollback conditions
body: A canary deployment has stop conditions that automatically halt the release when a signal crosses a threshold. The churn model's canary has an error_rate_limit of ten percent: if the candidate version 1.1.0 observes an error rate above ten percent on the canary traffic the release is stopped and the active version remains 1.0.0.

The rollback steps are rehearsed ahead of time: shift traffic from the candidate version back to the current version, verify that the health endpoint returns status 200, and confirm that the prediction contract still validates inputs correctly. These steps are practiced in a staging environment before any production canary is attempted, so the team knows exactly what to do when the guardrail fires.

sections.heading: Retraining is a governed decision
body: Data drift alone is not a significant reason to retrain a model. The churn model may experience input drift as the business collects new customer segments, but if the model's quality metrics on held-out data have not degraded the team should not retrain.

Retraining costs engineering time, compute, and review, and it introduces a new model that must be validated from scratch. The team should retrain only when the model's quality has demonstrably fallen, such as the holdout error_rate rising above the guardrail, and when the team has new labeled data that represents the current population. Every retraining decision should be documented with the trigger metric, the new data used, and the validation results on a held-out test set.

quiz.question: What is a canary release and why is it called that?
choices: A canary release sends a small share of traffic to the new version and gets its name from the canary bird that was historically used to detect toxic gas in mines
A canary release runs the new version on a separate canopy of servers, and the name refers to the cloud architecture
A canary release is a type of unit test, and the name refers to the canary testing framework
A canary release deletes the old version first, and the name refers to the canary in the deployment pipeline
quiz.explanation: The term comes from the practice of using canary birds in mines; if the bird showed signs of distress the miners knew toxic gas was present. Similarly a canary release tests the new version on a small traffic share before fully deploying it.

Rehearse these rollback steps in the staging environment before the first production canary. choices: The exact stop condition and guardrail threshold, such as an error_rate limit

quiz_bank.explanation: The stop condition and its threshold, such as an error_rate limit of ten percent, must be documented so the automatic check knows when to halt the release.

quiz_bank.question: Why is data drift on its own not a reason to retrain?
choices: Because drift always improves model quality
Because the model may still make accurate predictions on the new data distribution, and retraining costs engineering time and compute without guaranteed benefit
Because drift can only be detected on the training data, not on new data
Because the model cannot be retrained once it is in production
quiz_bank.explanation: Data drift means the input distribution has changed, but the model may still be accurate. Retraining costs time and compute and the new model must be validated from scratch, so the team should retrain only when quality has demonstrably fallen.

lessons.title: Orchestrate the full ML pipeline
lessons.goal: Combine data preparation, model training, and evaluation into a single orchestrated pipeline that runs with one command.

sections.heading: Pipeline frameworks
body: Most machine learning work lives in separate scripts: one for loading data, another for training, a third for evaluation. A pipeline runner combines them so every stage runs in the correct order without manual coordination. The runner reads a configuration that lists each stage and passes the output of one stage as the input to the next. This means a single command such as `make train evaluate` can replace three separate invocations, and the order is guaranteed by the configuration rather than by remembering which script to run first.

The beginner mistake here is to run scripts in the wrong order and wonder why the model trains on incomplete data. Another common error is to hard-code file paths between scripts, which breaks when the data location changes. A pipeline runner avoids both problems by declaring dependencies explicitly and by passing artifacts from one stage to the next through a shared location.

sections.heading: Artifact management
body: An artifact is any output produced by one pipeline stage that another stage later requires. Examples are the cleaned dataset, the trained model weights, the evaluation report, and the confusion matrix. The pipeline runner stores each artifact in a versioned location, typically a timestamped folder or a content-addressable store, so that stage N+1 can always find the exact output of stage N even if earlier runs used different parameters. When the runner starts a new execution, it can skip stages whose artifacts are already up to date, saving time on long-running training.

A frequent beginner error is to re-read the raw data in every stage instead of passing the intermediate artifact forward, which makes the pipeline slow and fragile. Another mistake is to forget to version the model weights, so a later stage might accidentally use a weights file from an experiment run three weeks earlier. Explicit artifact management solves both by recording what was produced and when.

sections.heading: End-to-end test
body: An end-to-end test runs the pipeline from the very first step—raw data loading—to the very last step, such as generating a model performance report. The test verifies that every stage succeeds and that the final report contains the expected numbers, such as the baseline accuracy and the count of evaluation rows. If any stage fails or produces unexpected output, the test fails immediately, catching problems such as a broken import statement or a mismatch in column names before the report is published.

A typical beginner mistake is to test only the training step in isolation and assume the other steps work because they ran successfully last week. Data files change, library versions update, and a script that worked on a laptop may fail in continuous integration. The end-to-end test catches these regressions by confirming that the full chain, from raw data to report, produces consistent results every time it runs.

quiz.question: What does a pipeline runner give you that separate scripts do not?
choices: A single command that runs every stage in order, with dependencies declared between stages.
Faster training because the runner parallelizes every stage.
Automatic selection of the best model among all runs.
A graphical interface for monitoring loss during training.
quiz.explanation: A pipeline runner declares which stage depends on which output, so a single command runs them in the correct order. Separate scripts require you to remember and run each one manually, and they often fail when a later script expects data that an earlier script omitted.

lessons.task: Write a single shell command that runs data preparation, training, and evaluation in order and prints the final report line. Then add one test that runs the entire chain from raw data to report and fails if any step produces unexpected output.

quiz_bank.question: How do stages pass work to each other in a pipeline?
choices: Each stage writes its output to a shared location that the next stage reads from, and the pipeline runner tracks the artifact between stages.
Stages pass variables directly through function calls in the same Python process.
Stages exchange work by overwriting a single global file after each run.
Stages do not pass work to each other; they all read the original raw data independently.
quiz_bank.explanation: The pipeline runner stores the output of each stage such as the cleaned dataset or trained model as an artifact, and the next stage reads that artifact from the shared location. This decouples the stages and makes the pipeline resilient to individual changes.

quiz_bank.question: Why does the pipeline need an end-to-end test?
choices: Because running each stage separately is too slow for regular execution.
Because it runs the whole chain from raw data to report and catches problems such as broken imports or column mismatches before the report is published.
Because the end-to-end test trains the model faster than any other test.
Because it automatically fixes any mismatch in column names between stages.
quiz_bank.explanation: An end-to-end test confirms that every stage runs successfully from start to finish, so a failure points to a real problem such as a missing import or a changed data format, rather than a fluke in one isolated step.

lessons.title: Design monitoring and canary deployment
lessons.goal: Design monitoring signals and a canary deployment strategy for model updates, with explicit thresholds and rollback steps.

sections.heading: Monitoring signals
body: A monitoring signal is a number computed from recent production data that reveals a change in model behaviour. The four families are error rate, latency, input drift, and prediction drift. Error rate tracks how often the service returns an incorrect response, latency measures how long a request takes, input drift compares the distribution of recent feature values to the distribution seen during training, and prediction drift compares the distribution of recent model scores to the scores from training. Each signal answers a different question: error rate catches misclassifications, latency catches performance degradation, input drift detects when the world has changed around the model, and prediction drift detects when the model's own outputs have shifted.

A beginner often ignores prediction drift because error rate looks healthy, but a model can produce correct labels on stale data, so the score distribution changes without any immediate error. That is why all four signal families are needed: each one reveals a different failure mode, and a monitoring dashboard should display all four simultaneously rather than relying on a single number.

sections.heading: Canary deployment strategy
body: A canary deployment releases a new model version to a small fraction of traffic, typically 5 percent, while the majority continues on the current version. The canary runs alongside the production version, and its predictions are collected but not used to serve customers. After a watch window—such as 30 minutes or 100 requests—the team compares the canary's error rate, latency, and drift signals against predefined stop conditions. If any signal exceeds its threshold, the canary is considered unsuccessful and traffic remains on the old version.

The stop conditions must be written before the deployment: for example, error rate must not increase by more than 2 percentage points, latency must not grow by more than 200 milliseconds, and prediction drift must stay below a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.2. If all conditions stay within bounds for the entire watch window, the team gradually increases the canary's traffic share until it serves 100 percent of requests.

sections.heading: Rollback conditions
body: Rollback is the process of returning traffic to the previous model version when the canary deployment shows signs of failure. The rollback plan should state exactly when to trigger the rollback, such as when the error rate rises by more than 3 percentage points within a 10-minute window or when prediction drift exceeds 0.25 for two consecutive watch windows. The plan should also describe how to shift traffic back, such as by updating a load balancer rule or by rolling the container image to the previous version.

Before a release, the team should rehearses the rollback steps in a staging environment and confirm that the previous version serves traffic correctly within a minute. This rehearsal proves that the rollback works and that the team is familiar with the commands, so a real rollback is faster and less error-prone. The rollback condition and the rehearsal together ensure that a failed deployment can be reversed before it damages many users.

quiz.question: Which monitoring signal would catch a service that is down?
choices: Error rate, because a down service returns a high rate of errors or timeouts.
Latency, because a down service always has infinite latency.
Input drift, because a down service changes the feature distribution.
Prediction drift, because a down service changes the model score distribution.
quiz.explanation: Error rate tracks how often the service returns an incorrect response or times out; when the service is completely down the error rate spikes, making it the signal that reveals a service outage.

quiz_bank.explanation: A canary plan must declare the traffic share how many requests go to the new model the watch window how long to observe and stop conditions thresholds for each signal. Without these the team cannot decide whether the canary succeeded or failed.

Never; rollback is a manual process that should not be practiced.
quiz_bank.explanation: Rehearsing the rollback before release proves the steps work and makes the team familiar with the commands so a real rollback is faster and less likely to cause a second outage.
